shard.title: East, Southern and Nile Africa
shard.author: regional historian: East, Southern and Nile Africa
shard.note: Covers southern Africa (the Cape to the Rhodesias), the Nile (Egypt and the Sudans), East Africa and the Horn, plus the British wartime administrations in the Horn and Libya and the Indian Ocean occupations of Madagascar and Bourbon. Territories carry their own accurate region value, so several differ from this shard's single region field. GEO GAPS - places this dataset needed and the 302-unit vocabulary cannot draw, recorded here rather than invented: Zululand as distinct from Natal (annexed 1887, merged 1897); Griqualand West and the Transkeian territories inside the Cape; British Bechuanaland south of the Molopo, now inside South Africa; Barotseland inside Northern Rhodesia; Buganda and Bunyoro inside Uganda; the ten-mile Kenyan coastal strip leased from Zanzibar until 1963 and the Northern Frontier District; the Zanzibar sultanate's mainland dominions before 1886; the Ogaden, the Haud and the Reserved Area inside Ethiopia; the three southern provinces of Sudan are drawn by the south-sudan unit but the Abyei, Nuba and Blue Nile disputed areas are not; Cyrenaica, Tripolitania and the French-run Fezzan inside Libya; Walvis Bay inside Namibia; the Caprivi Strip; and Diego Suarez inside Madagascar. Where a territory covered only part of a drawn unit the coverage period marks it partial.

territories.name: Cape Colony
territories.formalName: Colony of the Cape of Good Hope
territories.subregion: The Cape and the eastern frontier

namesOverTime.name: Kaap de Goede Hoop
namesOverTime.note: A refreshment station of the Dutch East India Company (VOC), not a plantation colony: ships to Asia needed vegetables and water.

namesOverTime.name: Cape Province
namesOverTime.note: Split in 1994 into the Western, Northern and Eastern Cape.

namesOverTime.name: Western Cape, Northern Cape and Eastern Cape
namesOverTime.note: The Cape Province was divided into three provinces of South Africa on 27 April 1994. There has been no 'Cape Colony' on this ground since 1910 and no 'Cape' province since 1994.

modernSuccessors.name: South Africa
modernSuccessors.note: The old Cape Colony is now the Western, Northern and Eastern Cape provinces, plus the part of the Northern Cape that was British Bechuanaland.

geoCoverage.label: The south-western Cape only
geoCoverage.change: British authority in 1795 reached only a few days ride from Cape Town; the drawn shape is the colony's later maximum.

geoCoverage.label: Growing east and north
geoCoverage.change: Britain came back in 1806 and then pushed the border east across the Fish and Kei rivers in nine frontier wars, and north to the diamond fields in 1871.

geoCoverage.label: The Cape at its full extent
geoCoverage.change: The annexation of British Bechuanaland on 16 November 1895 gave the Cape the shape it carried into the Union.

acquisitions.how: A British fleet under Admiral Keith Elphinstone and General James Craig beat the Dutch East India Company's burgher militia at Muizenberg in August 1795 and took the garrison's surrender on 16 September.

counterparties.name: Dutch East India Company and its burgher settlers
counterparties.lost: The VOC lost its Asian supply station and, within four years, went bankrupt and was wound up.

counterparties.name: Khoikhoi and San peoples
counterparties.lost: They had already lost most of their land and cattle to the VOC over 140 years; British rule confirmed the loss and added pass laws in 1809.
counterparties.note: Smallpox in 1713 and 1755 had destroyed the western Khoikhoi as independent societies before any Briton arrived.

counterparties.name: Xhosa chiefdoms of the Zuurveld
counterparties.lost: Nothing yet in 1795 - but the new rulers inherited a frontier war and would fight seven more against them.

people.name: James Henry Craig
people.role: commanded the landing force and became the first British governor

people.name: Abraham Josias Sluysken
people.role: Dutch commissioner-general who surrendered the Cape

acquisitions.resistance: The burgher militia fought at Muizenberg and Wynberg and then gave up; the frontier republics of Graaff-Reinet and Swellendam refused British authority until troops arrived in 1799.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: A History of South Africa
evidence.supports: The two British occupations and their strategic motive.

acquisitions.how: Britain handed the Cape back to the Dutch in 1803, then took it again three years later: General David Baird beat the Batavian garrison at Blaauwberg on 8 January 1806 and Governor Janssens capitulated at Papendorp on the 10th.

counterparties.name: Batavian Republic
counterparties.lost: The Netherlands lost the Cape permanently, and with it any Dutch route to the East.

counterparties.name: Khoikhoi soldiers of the Batavian garrison
counterparties.lost: Khoikhoi troops fought on the Dutch side at Blaauwberg and were absorbed into a British-officered Cape Regiment.

people.name: David Baird
people.role: commanded the British invasion force

people.name: Jan Willem Janssens
people.role: Batavian governor who surrendered the colony

acquisitions.resistance: The Batavian force of about 2,000, including Khoikhoi troops and French sailors, held for one morning against roughly 5,000 British troops before withdrawing.

acquisitions.how: At the peace settlement the Netherlands signed the Cape away for good, and Britain paid six million pounds covering the Cape and the Guiana colonies together.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of the Netherlands
counterparties.lost: Sovereignty over the Cape, sold rather than fought for, in exchange for money and a strengthened Dutch state in Europe.

instrument.name: Anglo-Dutch Treaty (Convention of London), 1814
instrument.note: Historians differ on how much of the six million pounds was for the Cape as against Demerara, Essequibo and Berbice; the treaty does not itemise it.

contested.note: The six million pounds is often quoted as the price of the Cape alone. The treaty covers the Cape and the Guiana colonies together and does not break the sum down.

acquisitions.how: Four years after the first diamonds were found on the Vaal, Britain accepted a cession from the Griqua captain Nicolaas Waterboer and proclaimed the diamond fields British, beating the Orange Free State to them.

counterparties.name: Orange Free State
counterparties.lost: The richest diamond deposits on earth, for which Britain later paid it 90,000 pounds in compensation.

counterparties.name: Griqua people under Nicolaas Waterboer
counterparties.lost: Within a decade the Griqua had lost their land to speculators and their captaincy to a magistrate; Waterboer was tried for his part in the 1878 Griqua rising.

counterparties.name: Tlhaping and Kora communities of the Vaal
counterparties.lost: Their land was overrun by 20,000 diggers within two years and their claims were never heard.

instrument.name: Governor Barkly's proclamation annexing Griqualand West
instrument.note: Rested on the Keate Award of 17 October 1871, an arbitration by the Lieutenant-Governor of Natal that the Orange Free State always said was rigged.

evidence.author: Robert V. Turrell
evidence.work: Capital and Labour on the Kimberley Diamond Fields, 1871-1890
evidence.supports: The annexation of the diamond fields and the labour system built on them.

date.note: Annexed piece by piece: Fingoland and Idutywa in 1879, Thembuland and Bomvanaland in 1885, Pondoland in 1894.

acquisitions.how: After the ninth and last frontier war of 1877-78 the Cape swallowed the independent Xhosa-speaking country between the Kei River and Natal, chiefdom by chiefdom, over fifteen years.

counterparties.name: Gcaleka, Thembu, Mpondo and Mfengu chiefdoms
counterparties.lost: Their independence, their courts and their control of land; chiefs became salaried headmen under Cape magistrates.

counterparties.name: Sarhili, paramount chief of the Gcaleka Xhosa
counterparties.lost: His country in 1878 and his throne; he died in exile in Bomvanaland in 1892.

acquisitions.resistance: Sarhili fought the war of 1877-78 and was driven across the Mbashe; the Mpondo submitted in 1894 only after Cape artillery gave a demonstration shoot in front of their assembled regiments.

acquisitions.how: British Bechuanaland, a crown colony since 1885, was folded into the Cape without asking the Tswana people who lived in it.

counterparties.name: Tlhaping and Rolong communities south of the Molopo
counterparties.lost: Their land was opened to Cape settlers, and Britain reneged on land guarantees given in 1885.

statusPeriods.label: First British military occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British general governed by proclamation, kept VOC law and the VOC's officials, and reported to the War Office in London.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Burghers petitioned; the enslaved and the Khoikhoi could not even do that.

statusPeriods.label: Second British occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Military government again, but this time permanent: the governor issued the Hottentot Proclamation of 1809, which tied Khoikhoi workers to farms by pass.
statusPeriods.gapReason: Britain returned the Cape to the Batavian Republic under the Treaty of Amiens on 1 January 1803. For three years it was Dutch again, under Governor Janssens.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony under a governor
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The governor made law by ordinance with a nominated council; London could veto anything, and did, most famously by emancipating enslaved people in 1834 over settler objections.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cape Town, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: No elections at all until 1854.
statusPeriods.note: Ordinance 50 of 1828 removed the pass laws from Khoikhoi and free people of colour and made them equal before the law - a real change, and one that Boer trekkers cited in 1836 as a reason to leave.

statusPeriods.label: Elected parliament, appointed government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Cape men elected a parliament, but the governor chose the ministers, so the voters could refuse taxes and little else.
statusPeriods.franchise: The 1853 constitution set a low, deliberately colour-blind qualification: 25 pounds of property or 50 pounds a year in wages. Black and Coloured men who met it could and did vote.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government at the Cape
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: From 1872 a Cape prime minister answerable to the Cape parliament ran everything except foreign policy and defence; Cecil Rhodes held the office from 1890 to 1896.
statusPeriods.franchise: Still colour-blind in law, and steadily narrowed in practice: the Parliamentary Voters Registration Act of 1887 struck off communal landholders, the 1892 Act raised the bar to 75 pounds and added a literacy test, and the Glen Grey Act of 1894 excluded most Transkeian land from qualifying.
statusPeriods.note: By 1909 African and Coloured voters were about 15 per cent of the Cape roll. It was the only non-racial franchise anywhere in southern Africa, and it died with the colony.

departures.how: The Cape stopped being a colony and became a province of the new Union of South Africa, taking its parliament building and its prime minister but not its franchise into the new state.

led.name: John X. Merriman
led.role: last prime minister of the Cape; argued at the National Convention that the Cape franchise should be extended to the whole Union, and lost

led.name: William Philip Schreiner
led.role: led a delegation to London in 1909 to ask Parliament to strike the colour bar out of the South Africa Bill

led.name: Abdullah Abdurahman
led.role: president of the African Political Organisation; went with the 1909 delegation to defend Coloured voting rights

led.name: John Tengo Jabavu
led.role: editor of Imvo Zabantsundu and the leading African voice in Cape politics

departures.movement: South African Native Convention and the 1909 delegation to London

cost.note: Nobody was killed in the merger. The cost was the Cape franchise: the House of Commons was warned in 1909 that entrenching a colour bar would be regretted, and passed the bill anyway. African voters were struck off the common roll in 1936, Coloured voters in 1956.

departures.borders: The Cape's boundaries simply became provincial boundaries and did not move a metre; what moved was the constitutional floor under a quarter of a million non-white British subjects.

instrument.name: South Africa Act 1909
instrument.note: Section 35 entrenched the Cape franchise behind a two-thirds joint sitting - a lock the National Party picked in the 1950s by packing the Senate.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: The Unification of South Africa, 1902-1910
evidence.supports: The National Convention, the franchise argument and the 1909 London delegation.

slavery.note: The Cape was a slave society for 180 years before Britain arrived: the VOC imported people from Madagascar, Mozambique, India and Indonesia, and by 1795 there were more enslaved people than free burghers.

abolitionDate.note: The Slave Trade Act stopped fresh imports to the Cape; it freed nobody already there.

emancipationDate.note: Emancipation took effect on 1 December 1834 and was followed by four years of unpaid apprenticeship.

toll.money: Cape slave-owners were awarded roughly 1.2 million pounds, payable only in London, so most sold their claims to agents at a discount. The freed received nothing. The award is entered in the Legacies of British Slavery database at UCL, which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers.
toll.note: Roughly 36,000 people were freed at the Cape in 1834; the exact registry total is usually given as 35,745, and different counts include or exclude Cape apprentices.
toll.source: The Legacies of British Slavery database (UCL), which transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission's registers of 1835-36 award by award.

warrant.author: Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery, University College London
warrant.work: Legacies of British Slavery database
warrant.supports: Cape slave-owners were awarded roughly 1.2 million pounds, payable only in London, so most sold their claims to agents at a discount.
warrant.check: ucl.ac.uk/lbs — browse by colony. Every award transcribes the Slave Compensation Commission’s registers, T 71, The National Archives, Kew.

violence.note: Nine frontier wars between 1779 and 1879 pushed the Xhosa off the land between the Fish and the Kei; Britain fought six of them.

toll.note: No reliable count exists for Xhosa dead across a century of frontier war. The best-documented catastrophe is the cattle-killing of 1856-57, when tens of thousands starved after a prophecy that killing the herds would drive the British into the sea.

populationTransfer.note: About 4,000 British settlers were landed at Algoa Bay in 1820 and placed on the Xhosa frontier on hundred-acre plots, as a human buffer paid for by Parliament.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Kei River line and the old Transkeian annexations became the borders of the Transkei and Ciskei bantustans in the 1970s, and are visible in South Africa's Eastern Cape today.
consequences.economicLegacy: Diamonds at Kimberley in 1867 turned a farming colony into an industrial one and created De Beers, the compound labour system and the migrant contract that later staffed the gold mines.
consequences.languageAndLaw: South African law is still Roman-Dutch at its base with English procedure on top, because Britain kept the VOC's civil law in 1806 and never replaced it.

peak.populationNote: 1904 census of the Cape Colony. About 580,000 were counted as white.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Cape Colony’s largest recorded population: 2,409,804 people, counted in 1904.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: A History of South Africa
evidence.supports: The overall narrative from the VOC to Union.

evidence.author: Noel Mostert
evidence.work: Frontiers: The Epic of South Africa's Creation and the Tragedy of the Xhosa People
evidence.supports: The frontier wars and the destruction of Xhosa independence.

evidence.author: Nigel Worden
evidence.work: The Making of Modern South Africa: Conquest, Apartheid, Democracy
evidence.supports: Slavery at the Cape, emancipation and the shape of the colonial economy.

pedagogy.hook: Britain conquered the Cape twice, handed it back in between, and only kept it the second time because of a sea route to India that nobody uses now.

misconception.belief: Britain took the Cape in order to settle white farmers in Africa.
misconception.correction: Britain took it as a naval station: whoever held Table Bay controlled the sailing route to India, and in 1795 France was the danger. The 1820 settlers - about 4,000 people - were sent 25 years later, and were placed on the Xhosa frontier as a buffer, not on the good land near Cape Town.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Cape is where two British decisions collided: the empire abolished slavery here in 1834 and gave black men the vote in 1853, then traded that franchise away in 1910 to buy a union with the Boer republics it had just defeated. The road to apartheid runs through a British Act of Parliament.

keyDates.what: British troops take the Cape from the Dutch East India Company
Britain takes it back for good after Blaauwberg
About 36,000 enslaved people at the Cape are emancipated
A colour-blind property franchise is written into the Cape constitution
Diamonds found near the Vaal; Britain annexes the field in 1871
The Cape becomes a province of the Union of South Africa

territories.name: Natal
territories.subregion: The south-east coast and Zululand

namesOverTime.name: KwaZulu

from.note: A rough marker for the consolidation of the Zulu kingdom under Shaka; there is no founding date.

namesOverTime.note: The kingdom north of the Thukela; the coast south of it was contested ground.

namesOverTime.name: Natalia
namesOverTime.note: The Voortrekker republic founded after the defeat of the Zulu at Blood River.

namesOverTime.name: Natal
namesOverTime.note: From Terra Natalis, the name Vasco da Gama's fleet gave the coast at Christmas 1497.

modernSuccessors.name: South Africa
modernSuccessors.note: Natal and Zululand together are now the province of KwaZulu-Natal.

geoCoverage.label: Natal without Zululand
geoCoverage.change: Britain annexed the Voortrekker republic of Natalia; the Zulu kingdom north of the Thukela stayed independent for another 36 years.

geoCoverage.label: Natal with Zululand
geoCoverage.change: Zululand, conquered in 1879 and annexed as a separate British territory in 1887, was handed to the Natal settlers on 30 December 1897.

acquisitions.how: Britain annexed the Boer republic of Natalia four years after the trekkers founded it, partly to stop an independent Boer port at Durban and partly because thousands of African refugees were being pushed off their land by it.

counterparties.name: Republic of Natalia
counterparties.lost: Its independence. Most of its Voortrekkers loaded their wagons and left for the highveld rather than live under British rule.

counterparties.name: Zulu kingdom under Mpande
counterparties.lost: A British colony on its southern border, and the ability to control who settled the Thukela lowlands.

instrument.name: Letters patent annexing Natal
instrument.note: Natal was ruled as a district of the Cape Colony from 1844 and became a separate colony on 15 July 1856.

people.name: Andries Pretorius
people.role: Voortrekker commandant-general of Natalia; left for the Transvaal after the annexation

people.name: Theophilus Shepstone
people.role: Diplomatic Agent then Secretary for Native Affairs from 1845; designed the reserve-and-chief system that became the model for indirect rule

acquisitions.resistance: The Boers besieged the British camp at Congella in May 1842 until Dick King rode 960 kilometres to Grahamstown in ten days to fetch relief; after the annexation most trekked out rather than submit.

acquisitions.how: Britain invaded the Zulu kingdom in January 1879 on an ultimatum written to be refused, lost 1,300 men at Isandlwana on 22 January, and burned the royal homestead at Ulundi six months later.

counterparties.name: Zulu kingdom under Cetshwayo kaMpande
counterparties.lost: Its army, its king and its unity: Sir Garnet Wolseley cut the kingdom into thirteen chiefdoms designed to fight each other, and they did, for eight years.

people.name: Cetshwayo kaMpande
people.role: king of the Zulu; defeated at Ulundi, captured on 28 August 1879, exiled, taken to London in 1882, partly restored in 1883 and dead in 1884

people.name: Ntshingwayo kaMahole
people.role: commanded the Zulu army that destroyed the British centre column at Isandlwana

people.name: Henry Bartle Frere
people.role: High Commissioner who issued the ultimatum without London's approval, to force a confederation of South Africa

people.name: Frederic Thesiger, 2nd Baron Chelmsford
people.role: commanded the invasion; split his force before Isandlwana

acquisitions.resistance: The Zulu army destroyed a British column of about 1,800 men at Isandlwana, the worst defeat regular British troops ever suffered at the hands of an African army, and fought on for six months against Martini-Henry rifles and Gatling guns.

cost.note: British and colonial dead are recorded as about 1,750, of whom roughly 1,300 fell at Isandlwana. Zulu dead are estimated between 8,000 and 12,000 and were never counted; roughly 1,000 to 3,000 died at Isandlwana alone and about 1,500 at Ulundi.

evidence.author: John Laband
evidence.work: Rope of Sand: The Rise and Fall of the Zulu Kingdom in the Nineteenth Century
evidence.supports: The 1879 war, the partition of Zululand and the civil wars that followed.

acquisitions.how: Zululand had been annexed as a separate British territory in 1887; ten years later London handed it to Natal's settler government, which opened two and a half million acres of it to white farmers in 1904.

counterparties.name: Zulu people of Zululand
counterparties.lost: Direct imperial administration, which had at least protected the land, and then about 40 per cent of the land itself to the 1902-04 delimitation commission.

statusPeriods.label: A district of the Cape, then a colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A lieutenant-governor under Cape Town ran Natal, while Theophilus Shepstone gathered Africans into locations under government-appointed chiefs applying customary law.
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1856.

statusPeriods.label: Settler legislature, imperial governor
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An elected Legislative Council spoke for about 15,000 white colonists; the governor kept the executive and the imperial garrison.
statusPeriods.franchise: In law non-racial; in practice the Native Franchise Act of 1865 made an African voter prove twelve years of exemption from customary law and get the governor's signature. By 1905 there were fewer than ten African voters in a colony of about a million Africans.

statusPeriods.label: Responsible government under the settlers
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: From 1893 a settler ministry governed the colony, and used its power at once: a poll tax in 1905, martial law in 1906, and the flogging and shooting of tax resisters.
statusPeriods.franchise: White adult men, plus a handful of exempted Africans. Indians were struck off the roll in 1896 unless already registered.
statusPeriods.note: Winston Churchill, then a junior minister, called Natal in 1906 'the hooligan of the British Empire' over its handling of the Bambatha rising.

departures.how: Natal, the most reluctant of the four colonies, voted by referendum in June 1909 to join the Union rather than face the Transvaal alone, and became a province on 31 May 1910.

led.name: Frederick Moor
led.role: last prime minister of Natal; took the colony into the Union

led.name: John Langalibalele Dube
led.role: Zulu educator and editor of Ilanga lase Natal; first president of the South African Native National Congress in 1912

led.name: Mohandas Gandhi
led.role: lawyer in Durban from 1893; organised Natal's Indians against the 1896 disenfranchisement and invented satyagraha here in 1906

cost.note: The merger itself was bloodless and decided by a whites-only referendum: 11,121 votes for union, 3,701 against.

departures.borders: Natal carried Zululand into the Union as a single province, so the border drawn by the 1879 conquest disappeared into a provincial boundary and the Zulu kingdom vanished from the map for eighty-four years.

populationTransfer.note: Between 1860 and 1911 about 152,000 indentured labourers were shipped from India to cut Natal's sugar cane on five-year contracts; their descendants are the largest population of Indian origin in Africa.

toll.note: Indentured arrivals are counted from the Protector of Indian Immigrants' registers, which are good; mortality on the estates is not well recorded.

violence.note: The Bambatha rebellion of 1906 against a one-pound poll tax ended with about 3,000 to 4,000 Zulu dead against roughly 30 on the government side, and about 7,000 arrests.

toll.note: Colonial returns give around 3,000 to 4,000 African dead in 1906, including 500 or more killed at the Mome Gorge on 10 June; the figure comes from the side doing the killing.

warrant.author: The Natal colonial government, in its own returns
warrant.work: Natal colonial returns of the Bambatha rebellion
warrant.supports: Colonial returns give around 3,000 to 4,000 African dead in 1906, including 500 or more killed at the Mome Gorge on 10 June; the figure comes from the side doing the killing.
warrant.check: Colonial administration returns are printed in the territory’s annual Blue Book and administration report; the British copies are in the CO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The side doing the killing counted its own dead precisely and the other side’s by estimate. That asymmetry is in the figure, not just in the footnote.

consequences.borderLegacy: The reserves Shepstone marked out in the 1840s were still the map of KwaZulu in the 1980s: the bantustan boundary followed lines drawn by one British official a century and a half earlier.
consequences.economicLegacy: Sugar built Natal, and it was cut by indentured Indian labour because Zulu households with land of their own refused to work for the wages offered.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Shepstone's system of ruling Africans through appointed chiefs and codified customary law was exported to Nigeria, Tanganyika and beyond as indirect rule.

peak.populationNote: 1904 census, including Zululand: about 97,000 whites, 100,000 Indians and roughly a million Africans.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Natal’s largest recorded population: 1,194,043 people, counted in 1904.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: John Laband
evidence.work: Rope of Sand: The Rise and Fall of the Zulu Kingdom in the Nineteenth Century
evidence.supports: The Zulu kingdom, the 1879 war and the annexation of Zululand.

evidence.author: Jeff Guy
evidence.work: The Destruction of the Zulu Kingdom: The Civil War in Zululand, 1879-1884
evidence.supports: The deliberate partition of Zululand after 1879 and its consequences.

evidence.author: Shula Marks
evidence.work: Reluctant Rebellion: The 1906-8 Disturbances in Natal
evidence.supports: The poll tax, the Bambatha rising and its suppression.

pedagogy.hook: In January 1879 a Zulu army armed mainly with spears destroyed a British column at Isandlwana; the news reached London before the war had been approved there.

misconception.belief: African kingdoms could not seriously fight European armies, so colonisation was quick and one-sided.
misconception.correction: The Zulu kingdom beat a modern British force in a stand-up battle at Isandlwana on 22 January 1879, killing about 1,300 men. Britain won in the end by sending far more troops than it had planned and by breaking the kingdom into thirteen pieces afterwards - which tells you what it thought of Zulu military power.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Natal is where indirect rule was invented. Theophilus Shepstone's system of ruling Africans through appointed chiefs and codified custom, on reserved land, was copied across British Africa and became the administrative skeleton of apartheid.

keyDates.what: Britain annexes the Boer republic of Natalia
The first indentured labourers arrive from India on the SS Truro
Isandlwana: a British column is destroyed by the Zulu army
Zululand handed to Natal's settler government
The Bambatha rebellion against the poll tax is crushed
Natal becomes a province of the Union

territories.name: Transvaal (first annexation)
territories.subregion: The highveld north of the Vaal

namesOverTime.name: Zuid-Afrikaansche Republiek
namesOverTime.note: Britain recognised the republic's independence at the Sand River Convention in 1852.

namesOverTime.name: Gauteng, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North West
namesOverTime.language: English, Afrikaans, Sesotho sa Leboa and others
namesOverTime.note: The Transvaal was divided into four provinces of South Africa on 27 April 1994.

modernSuccessors.name: South Africa
modernSuccessors.note: The old Transvaal is now Gauteng, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North West province.

geoCoverage.label: The bankrupt Boer republic
geoCoverage.change: Britain annexed a republic that could not pay its officials and could not beat the Pedi kingdom on its eastern border.

acquisitions.how: Theophilus Shepstone rode into Pretoria with 25 mounted policemen and a clerk, read a proclamation, and annexed a sovereign republic that had twelve shillings and sixpence in its treasury and was losing a war to Sekhukhune's Pedi.

counterparties.name: Zuid-Afrikaansche Republiek
counterparties.lost: Independence Britain itself had recognised in writing in 1852 - which is why the Boers thought the annexation not just hostile but dishonest.

counterparties.name: Pedi kingdom under Sekhukhune
counterparties.lost: Everything. Britain took over the Boers' war, invaded with 2,000 British troops and 8,000 Swazi allies in November 1879, and destroyed the Pedi capital; Sekhukhune was jailed in Pretoria.

instrument.name: Shepstone's proclamation annexing the Transvaal
instrument.note: Shepstone claimed a majority of burghers wanted annexation. Two petitions with about 6,500 signatures against it, gathered by Paul Kruger, say otherwise.

people.name: Theophilus Shepstone
people.role: special commissioner who annexed the republic on his own reading of his instructions

people.name: Paul Kruger
people.role: vice-president of the republic; travelled to London twice to ask for the annexation to be reversed and was refused both times

people.name: Sekhukhune
people.role: Pedi king who had beaten the Boers and was then destroyed by the British army in 1879

acquisitions.resistance: The republic protested rather than fought in 1877, because the annexation followed a war it was losing. Armed resistance came three and a half years later, once the British had beaten the Pedi and the Zulu for them.

evidence.author: Peter Warwick
evidence.work: The South African War: The Anglo-Boer War 1899-1902
evidence.supports: The confederation policy behind the 1877 annexation and its collapse.

statusPeriods.label: Annexed, then lost
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An administrator governed by proclamation with a nominated executive council; the promised elected assembly was never called, which is the grievance that started the war.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Pretoria, under the High Commissioner at Cape Town
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Boer burghers had voted for their own president before 1877 and did not vote again until 1881.

departures.how: The Transvaal Boers declared their republic restored in December 1880, wiped out a British column at Bronkhorstspruit, killed a general and 92 men on Majuba Hill on 27 February 1881, and Gladstone chose to negotiate rather than reconquer.

led.name: Paul Kruger
led.role: member of the triumvirate that declared the republic restored; president of the ZAR from 1883 to 1900

led.name: Piet Joubert
led.role: commandant-general; commanded the Boer force at Majuba

led.name: George Pomeroy Colley
led.role: British commander and Natal governor; killed leading the attack on Majuba

led.name: William Ewart Gladstone
led.role: prime minister who decided that reconquering the Transvaal was not worth the cost

departures.movement: The Transvaal burgher commandos

cost.note: British dead across the ten-week war are usually given as about 400, including 92 at Majuba. Boer losses were far lower - roughly 40 killed - because they fought from cover with accurate rifles against troops in the open.

departures.borders: The borders went back exactly where they had been in 1877, but the London Convention of 1884 quietly fixed the western boundary in Britain's favour, keeping the road north to Bechuanaland out of Boer hands.

instrument.name: Pretoria Convention, 1881
instrument.note: Gave the Transvaal self-government under British suzerainty; the London Convention of 27 February 1884 dropped the word suzerainty from the preamble, and Britain and Kruger argued about whether it still applied right up to 1899.

contested.note: Whether Britain retained suzerainty over the Transvaal after 1884 was the legal core of the quarrel that led to the 1899 war. Britain said the 1881 preamble survived; Kruger said the 1884 convention replaced it. No court ever ruled.

violence.note: The main killing of the annexation years was not of Boers but of the Pedi: a British-led force of about 10,000, most of them Swazi, stormed Sekhukhune's stronghold in November 1879.

toll.note: No count of Pedi dead was made. British and Swazi losses at the storming of Tsate are recorded; African losses on the winning and losing sides were not.

consequences.borderLegacy: Majuba fixed the western border question: Britain kept the missionaries' road to the north, which is why Bechuanaland and Rhodesia exist and why the Transvaal never reached the sea.
consequences.economicLegacy: Britain gave the republic back nine years before it discovered it was sitting on the largest goldfield in the world - and spent the next two decades trying to get it back.

peak.populationNote: Roughly 40,000 Boer burghers and perhaps 800,000 Africans, on estimates only; the republic never held a census.

evidence.author: Thomas Pakenham
evidence.work: The Boer War
evidence.supports: Majuba, the conventions of 1881 and 1884, and the road to 1899.

evidence.author: Peter Delius
evidence.work: The Land Belongs to Us: The Pedi Polity, the Boers and the British in the Nineteenth-Century Transvaal
evidence.supports: The destruction of the Pedi kingdom under British annexation.

pedagogy.hook: In 1877 one British official annexed an entire republic with 25 policemen; four years later the Boers took it back and Britain let them.

misconception.belief: Britain always won its colonial wars, and only left when it chose to.
misconception.correction: The First Anglo-Boer War of 1880-81 was a straight British defeat. After Majuba, Gladstone's cabinet calculated the cost of reconquest and handed the republic back. Britain retreated because fighting was not worth it - and remembered the humiliation so well that 'Remember Majuba' was a British slogan in 1899.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the empire's limits before the gold rush changed the arithmetic. Britain would not spend blood on a poor republic in 1881; after 1886 it spent 22,000 lives and 200 million pounds on a rich one.

keyDates.what: Sand River Convention: Britain recognises Transvaal independence
Shepstone annexes the Transvaal with 25 policemen
Majuba Hill: the Boers defeat and kill General Colley
Pretoria Convention hands the republic back

territories.name: Transvaal Colony
territories.subregion: The Witwatersrand and the highveld

namesOverTime.name: Gauteng, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North West
namesOverTime.language: English, Afrikaans, Sesotho sa Leboa and others
namesOverTime.note: The Transvaal Province was divided into four provinces of South Africa on 27 April 1994.

modernSuccessors.name: South Africa
modernSuccessors.note: Now Gauteng, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and most of North West province.

geoCoverage.label: Conquered by proclamation, held by war
geoCoverage.change: Britain proclaimed the annexation of the republic in September 1900; Boer commandos then fought on across the same ground for twenty more months, so the map and the control did not match until May 1902.

acquisitions.how: Britain invaded the South African Republic in October 1899 over the voting rights of foreign miners and the ownership of the world's largest goldfield, took Pretoria in June 1900 and proclaimed the republic annexed on 1 September.

counterparties.name: Zuid-Afrikaansche Republiek
counterparties.lost: Its independence, its gold revenue and, in the camps, a tenth of its Boer population.

counterparties.name: African communities of the Transvaal
counterparties.lost: They were promised the vote by British propaganda and denied it at Vereeniging; over 100,000 worked for the British army and 14,000 or more died in the black concentration camps.
counterparties.note: Kruger's republic had barred Africans from the franchise; the British peace terms of 1902 postponed the question until after self-government, which meant never.

instrument.name: Proclamation annexing the South African Republic
instrument.note: The Treaty of Vereeniging, signed 31 May 1902, is what actually ended the war and Boer sovereignty.

people.name: Alfred Milner
people.role: High Commissioner who forced the crisis and then ran the conquered colonies

people.name: Paul Kruger
people.role: president of the republic; left for Europe in September 1900 to seek help that never came, and died in Switzerland

people.name: Sol Plaatje
people.role: court interpreter and diarist of the siege of Mafeking; later first secretary-general of the South African Native National Congress

acquisitions.resistance: After the capitals fell, about 20,000 Boers fought a guerrilla war for twenty months under Christiaan de Wet, Koos de la Rey and Jan Smuts; Britain answered with blockhouses, farm burning and camps.

cost.note: Across both republics: about 22,000 British and imperial dead, roughly 6,000 Boer fighters, 27,927 Boer civilians in the camps, and at least 14,154 recorded African deaths in separate camps, with historians estimating up to 20,000. Ranges differ because African camp deaths were poorly recorded and were left out of official totals for eighty years.

warrant.author: The British camp superintendents’ own registers, and the historians who reworked them
warrant.work: Death registers of the South African War concentration camps
warrant.supports: Across both republics: about 22,000 British and imperial dead, roughly 6,000 Boer fighters, 27,927 Boer civilians in the camps, and at least 14,154 recorded African deaths in separate camps, with historians estimating up to 20,000. Ranges differ because African camp deaths were poorly recorded an…
warrant.check: Colonial administration returns are printed in the territory’s annual Blue Book and administration report; the British copies are in the CO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The 27,927 Boer deaths were registered; the 14,154 African deaths were registered separately and less completely, which is why the historians’ figure runs to 20,000.

evidence.author: Thomas Pakenham
evidence.work: The Boer War
evidence.supports: The course of the war, the guerrilla phase and the peace of Vereeniging.

statusPeriods.label: Under martial law while the war went on
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Lord Kitchener governed by martial law: 8,000 blockhouses, farms burned, and the civilian population of the veld moved into camps.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Milner's reconstruction
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Milner and his young Oxford recruits, the Kindergarten, rebuilt the mines, imported 63,000 Chinese indentured miners, and tried and failed to anglicise the schools.
statusPeriods.franchise: None; a nominated legislative council from 1903.
statusPeriods.note: The Chinese labour scheme of 1904-07 became a British election issue - 'Chinese slavery' - and helped bring down the Conservatives in 1906.

statusPeriods.label: Self-government under Botha and Smuts
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Four years after losing the war the Boers won the election: Louis Botha, a Boer general, became prime minister of the colony Britain had conquered.
statusPeriods.franchise: White men only. The 1906 letters patent settled the point the peace treaty had dodged: no African or Indian in the Transvaal would vote.

departures.how: The conquered republic became the richest province of a self-governing dominion run by the men who had commanded its commandos eight years earlier.

led.name: Louis Botha
led.role: Boer general, then Transvaal premier, then first prime minister of the Union

led.name: Jan Smuts
led.role: guerrilla commander, then Transvaal colonial secretary, then the Union's dominant politician for forty years

led.name: Mohandas Gandhi
led.role: led Transvaal Indians in mass resistance to the 1907 registration law and was jailed three times

cost.note: Nobody died in the merger. The bill had been paid in 1899-1902 and was still being paid by the 63,000 Chinese labourers repatriated between 1907 and 1910.

departures.borders: The republic's borders became the Transvaal province's borders unchanged, so a war fought to erase a country left its outline on the map for another eighty-four years.

violence.note: In the concentration camps of 1900-1902 about 27,927 Boer civilians died, roughly 22,000 of them children under sixteen, and at least 14,154 Africans died in separate camps.

toll.note: Boer camp deaths of 27,927 come from the camp registers and are firm. African camp deaths were recorded separately and carelessly; the official 14,154 is a floor and historians such as Peter Warwick and Stowell Kessler put the real figure nearer 20,000.

warrant.author: Peter Warwick
warrant.work: Black People and the South African War 1899-1902
warrant.supports: Boer camp deaths of 27,927 come from the camp registers and are firm.
warrant.check: Cambridge University Press, 1983. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

populationTransfer.note: Britain moved roughly 115,000 Boer and 115,000 African civilians off the land into camps, and shipped in 63,000 indentured Chinese miners between 1904 and 1907 to restart the gold mines.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Witwatersrand gold mines were rebuilt on a system Milner protected: African migrant workers on short contracts in closed compounds, paid a fraction of white wages. That system outlived the empire by eighty years.
consequences.borderLegacy: The peace of Vereeniging promised that the African franchise question would be settled only after self-government. Self-government came to white men in 1906, and the question was never reopened.

peak.populationNote: 1904 census of the Transvaal Colony: about 300,000 whites and 970,000 Africans.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Transvaal Colony’s largest recorded population: 1,268,716 people, counted in 1904.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Thomas Pakenham
evidence.work: The Boer War
evidence.supports: The war, the camps and the peace.

evidence.author: Peter Warwick
evidence.work: Black People and the South African War 1899-1902
evidence.supports: African participation in the war and the African concentration camps.

evidence.author: Shula Marks and Stanley Trapido
evidence.work: The Politics of Race, Class and Nationalism in Twentieth-Century South Africa
evidence.supports: Reconstruction, the mining economy and the making of the Union.

pedagogy.hook: Britain invented the concentration camp system here, and about 22,000 of the roughly 28,000 Boers who died in the camps were children.

misconception.belief: The South African War was a white man's war between Britons and Boers.
misconception.correction: At least 100,000 black Africans worked for the British army as scouts, drivers and labourers, and some were armed. About 115,000 Africans were interned in camps of their own, where at least 14,154 died - a figure left out of the official death toll until the 1980s. The British and Boer negotiators then agreed at Vereeniging that Africans would not get the vote.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The war cost Britain 22,000 lives and about 200 million pounds to win a goldfield, and Britain then handed the government of it to the losers within eight years - on terms that excluded everyone else. That bargain, white reconciliation paid for with black rights, is the foundation of modern South Africa.

keyDates.what: Gold found on the Witwatersrand
The South African War begins
Britain proclaims the republic annexed
Treaty of Vereeniging ends the war
Self-government returned to the Transvaal, for white men only
The Transvaal becomes a province of the Union

territories.name: Orange River Sovereignty
territories.subregion: The highveld between the Orange and the Vaal

namesOverTime.name: Oranje-Vrystaat
namesOverTime.note: The Orange Free State, an independent Boer republic for 46 years.

namesOverTime.name: Free State
namesOverTime.note: The province created in 1994 as the Orange Free State dropped 'Orange' in 1995; the 1996 constitution names it Free State.

modernSuccessors.name: South Africa
modernSuccessors.note: Now the Free State province.

geoCoverage.label: Six years of British sovereignty
geoCoverage.change: Harry Smith proclaimed British sovereignty over the country between the Orange and the Vaal, over the objections of both the trekker farmers and the Sotho kingdom whose land it partly was.

acquisitions.how: Governor Harry Smith proclaimed everything between the Orange and the Vaal British, to bring the Voortrekkers who had left the Cape back under British law, and beat the trekker commandos at Boomplaats in August when they refused.

counterparties.name: Voortrekker communities north of the Orange
counterparties.lost: The independence they had trekked 1,000 kilometres to obtain; Andries Pretorius was declared an outlaw with 2,000 pounds on his head.

counterparties.name: Basotho kingdom under Moshoeshoe I
counterparties.lost: Their claim to the fertile Caledon valley: Britain drew the Warden Line in 1849 across land the Basotho farmed, then fought Moshoeshoe at Berea in 1852 and lost.

counterparties.name: Griqua of Philippolis under Adam Kok III
counterparties.lost: Their treaty status and eventually their land; the Griqua trekked over the Drakensberg to Kokstad in 1861-63.

instrument.name: Proclamation of the Orange River Sovereignty

people.name: Harry Smith
people.role: Cape governor who annexed the country and then could not afford to hold it

people.name: Moshoeshoe I
people.role: founder and king of the Basotho; fought the British to a draw at Berea in December 1852 and then wrote a letter letting them claim victory

people.name: Andries Pretorius
people.role: Voortrekker commandant defeated at Boomplaats in 1848

acquisitions.resistance: Pretorius's commandos fought Smith at Boomplaats on 29 August 1848 and lost; Moshoeshoe's Basotho beat a British force under Sir George Cathcart at Berea on 20 December 1852, which is the defeat that persuaded London to withdraw.

statusPeriods.label: Six expensive years
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Resident at Bloemfontein governed with a small garrison, an empty treasury and no way to enforce the boundary he had drawn between Boer farmers and the Basotho.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

departures.how: Britain decided the territory cost more than it was worth, sent a commissioner to hand sovereignty to the Boer inhabitants, and had to persuade a reluctant meeting of them to accept it.

led.name: George Russell Clerk
led.role: special commissioner sent from London to give the territory away

led.name: Josias Hoffman
led.role: first president of the Orange Free State, and a friend of Moshoeshoe

led.name: Moshoeshoe I
led.role: king of the Basotho, who was not consulted about the withdrawal and lost his best land to the new republic in 1866-69

cost.note: Nobody died in the withdrawal itself. The cost fell on the Basotho: without a British buffer they fought the Free State three times and lost the Caledon valley, the country's best arable land, at the Convention of Aliwal North in 1869.

departures.borders: Britain's withdrawal left the Warden Line in place as a republican border, so a boundary drawn by a British major in 1849 became the frontier that stripped Lesotho of its wheat fields.

instrument.name: Bloemfontein Convention, 1854
instrument.note: Britain also promised in it to make no treaties with African polities north of the Orange - abandoning its own allies.

contested.note: Historians disagree whether the 1854 withdrawal was a considered policy of limiting expense - the Colonial Office's own line - or a panic after the defeat at Berea in 1852. Both readings use the same despatches.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Warden Line of 1849 and the Aliwal North convention of 1869 together give Lesotho its border: a mountain state that lost its farmland to a republic Britain had created and then abandoned.
consequences.economicLegacy: Britain walked away from the Orange in 1854 and annexed the diamond fields on its western edge seventeen years later, which tells you what changed its mind about the interior.

peak.populationNote: Perhaps 15,000 white inhabitants and a much larger African population that was never counted.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: Survival in Two Worlds: Moshoeshoe of Lesotho, 1786-1870
evidence.supports: Moshoeshoe, the Warden Line, Berea and the British withdrawal.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: A History of South Africa
evidence.supports: The Orange River Sovereignty and the conventions of 1852 and 1854.

pedagogy.hook: In 1854 Britain gave a territory away because it was too expensive, and had to talk the inhabitants into taking it.

misconception.belief: The British Empire only ever expanded until decolonisation began in the twentieth century.
misconception.correction: Britain abandoned the Orange River Sovereignty in 1854 and recognised the Transvaal's independence in 1852, because the Treasury would not pay for the highveld. The empire contracted whenever a place cost more than it earned - and expanded again when diamonds were found on the same ground in 1867.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest case of the empire retreating for money. It also shows who pays for a British withdrawal: the Basotho, who lost their allies in 1854 and their farmland by 1869.

keyDates.what: Harry Smith proclaims the Orange River Sovereignty
Boer commandos beaten at Boomplaats
Moshoeshoe's Basotho fight the British to a standstill at Berea
Bloemfontein Convention: Britain hands the territory to the Boers

territories.name: Orange River Colony
territories.subregion: The highveld between the Orange and the Vaal

namesOverTime.name: Orange Free State province
namesOverTime.note: Renamed simply Free State in 1995.

modernSuccessors.name: South Africa
modernSuccessors.note: Now the Free State province.

geoCoverage.label: Annexed in 1900, subdued in 1902
geoCoverage.change: Lord Roberts proclaimed the Orange Free State annexed in May 1900, but Christiaan de Wet's commandos rode over the same country for two more years.

acquisitions.how: The Orange Free State had no gold and no quarrel with Britain, but it had a treaty with the Transvaal, honoured it in October 1899, and was annexed by proclamation seven months later.

counterparties.name: Orange Free State
counterparties.lost: Its independence and its farms: British columns burned about 30,000 farmhouses across the two republics and interned the families.

counterparties.name: Basotho and Barolong communities of the colony
counterparties.lost: They were interned in separate camps, used as army labour and scouts, and then written out of the peace.

instrument.name: Proclamation annexing the Orange Free State
instrument.note: Confirmed by the Treaty of Vereeniging on 31 May 1902.

people.name: Christiaan de Wet
people.role: the Free State's guerrilla commander, never caught in two years of pursuit

people.name: Marthinus Steyn
people.role: president of the Orange Free State; refused to surrender and was too ill to sign at Vereeniging

people.name: Emily Hobhouse
people.role: English campaigner whose 1901 report on the camps forced the government to appoint the Fawcett Commission

acquisitions.resistance: De Wet's commandos fought on for two years after the capital fell, which is why Kitchener built 8,000 blockhouses and moved the civilian population into camps.

evidence.author: Thomas Pakenham
evidence.work: The Boer War
evidence.supports: The invasion of the Free State and the guerrilla war.

statusPeriods.label: Martial law and the camps
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Military government under Kitchener: farms burned, livestock destroyed, and roughly 45,000 Free State civilians moved into camps where the death rate for children reached appalling levels in late 1901.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony under Milner
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A lieutenant-governor under Milner's High Commission repatriated the camp survivors, paid out three million pounds of reconstruction money and tried to teach the schools in English.
statusPeriods.franchise: None; a nominated council from 1903.

statusPeriods.label: Orangia Unie takes power
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Five years after the surrender, Abraham Fischer's Orangia Unie won the first election and governed the colony; Britain had conquered the republic and then handed it back to its own people, minus the crown.
statusPeriods.franchise: White men only, exactly as under the republic.

departures.how: The colony joined the Union as the Orange Free State province and got the judicial capital, Bloemfontein, as its consolation prize in the deal between the four colonies.

led.name: Abraham Fischer
led.role: last prime minister of the Orange River Colony

led.name: James Barry Munnik Hertzog
led.role: Free State general and minister; founded the National Party in 1914 and became prime minister in 1924

led.name: Marthinus Steyn
led.role: former president; at the National Convention he insisted on equality for the Dutch language, and won it

cost.note: No deaths at the merger. The colony entered the Union having lost roughly one in ten of its Boer population, mostly children, in the camps eight years before.

departures.borders: The republic's boundaries became provincial boundaries unchanged, including the Caledon line that had taken the Basotho wheat fields in 1869 - so Lesotho's loss was locked into South Africa's internal map.

violence.note: About 45,000 Free State civilians were interned; camp registers for the two republics together record 27,927 Boer deaths, mostly children, and at least 14,154 African deaths.

toll.note: Figures are for both republics together, since the camps were administered as one system. Boer deaths come from camp registers; African camp deaths were recorded separately and are generally treated as an undercount.

consequences.economicLegacy: Britain paid three million pounds in reconstruction grants at Vereeniging and rebuilt the farms of the people it had just defeated - a deliberate purchase of Boer goodwill that helped produce a united white South Africa in 1910.
consequences.borderLegacy: The Free State's frontier with Basutoland, drawn by British officials in 1849 and 1869, is now the international border of Lesotho.

peak.populationNote: 1904 census of the Orange River Colony: about 143,000 whites and 244,000 Africans.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1904 census of Orange River Colony
populationWarrant.supports: Orange River Colony’s largest recorded population: 387,315 people, counted in 1904.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Thomas Pakenham
evidence.work: The Boer War
evidence.supports: The invasion, the guerrilla war and the camps.

evidence.author: Elizabeth van Heyningen
evidence.work: The Concentration Camps of the Anglo-Boer War: A Social History
evidence.supports: Camp administration, mortality and the arguments about the figures.

pedagogy.hook: The Orange Free State had no gold and no argument with Britain; it was invaded because it kept a promise to its neighbour.

misconception.belief: Britain fought the Boer War to free black South Africans from Boer oppression.
misconception.correction: British propaganda used the treatment of Africans in the republics as an argument, and Africans were told the war would bring them rights. At Vereeniging in 1902 Britain agreed that the African franchise would not be settled until after the conquered colonies had self-government - which meant white voters would decide it. They decided no.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Free State shows how quickly Britain moved from conquest to conciliation of white settlers: annexed in 1900, defeated in 1902, self-governing in 1907, and running a dominion in 1910.

territories.name: Union of South Africa
territories.subregion: The four South African colonies joined

modernSuccessors.name: South Africa
modernSuccessors.note: The same state, continuously, since 1910; a republic since 1961 and a democracy since 1994.

to.note: South Africa has no single independence date. 1910: a self-governing dominion. 11 December 1931: the Statute of Westminster ends Westminster's power to legislate for it. 1934: the Union's own Status Act says so in South African law. 31 May 1961: the Union becomes a republic and leaves the Commonwealth, ending the last formal tie — the shared Crown. This atlas keeps South Africa on the map to 1961, the same way it keeps Canada to 1982 and Australia to 1986, so that the four dominions are treated alike.

geoCoverage.label: The four colonies as one dominion
geoCoverage.change: The Cape, Natal, the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony merged into a single self-governing dominion under the South Africa Act 1909.

acquisitions.how: Britain joined four of its own colonies into one dominion by Act of Parliament, on a constitution written by white South Africans at a convention where no black or Indian South African had a seat.

counterparties.name: The four South African colonies
counterparties.lost: Their separate legislatures and, in the Cape's case, a franchise open to men of any colour that could not be extended beyond the province and was destroyed in 1936.

counterparties.name: The African, Coloured and Indian majority of South Africa
counterparties.lost: Any prospect of the vote for two generations. The South African Native Convention of 1909 and the London delegation of the same year asked Parliament to strike out the colour bar; Parliament declined.

instrument.name: South Africa Act 1909
instrument.note: Passed at Westminster. It is the only constitution in the Commonwealth that a British Parliament wrote knowing it entrenched a racial bar, and was told so at the time.

people.name: Louis Botha
people.role: first prime minister of the Union; a Boer general nine years earlier

people.name: Jan Smuts
people.role: architect of the union constitution and of the Native Affairs machinery under it

people.name: Walter Rubusana
people.role: the only African ever elected to the Cape Provincial Council, in 1910, under the Cape franchise

people.name: Pixley ka Isaka Seme
people.role: lawyer who called the 1912 meeting that founded the South African Native National Congress, the future ANC

acquisitions.resistance: Black and Coloured South Africans organised against the constitution before it passed - the South African Native Convention met in Bloemfontein in March 1909, and Schreiner's delegation lobbied Westminster - and founded the South African Native National Congress on 8 January 1912 in response to losing.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: The Unification of South Africa, 1902-1910
evidence.supports: The National Convention and the making of the 1909 Act.

statusPeriods.label: Dominion under the Crown
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: South Africa ran its own affairs through its own parliament under a governor-general; Britain kept foreign policy in theory, and the Union went to war in 1914 as part of the empire and conquered German South West Africa for it.
statusPeriods.franchise: White men everywhere; in the Cape alone, African and Coloured men who met the property test, about 15 per cent of that province's roll. White women got the vote in 1930, and no African woman ever voted in the Union.
statusPeriods.note: The Natives Land Act of 19 June 1913 reserved about 7 per cent of the country for African occupation and made sharecropping illegal outside it. Sol Plaatje's Native Life in South Africa (1916) opens with the sentence that South Africa's black population awoke to find itself a pariah in the land of its birth.

This atlas keeps South Africa on the map to 1961, the same way it keeps Canada to 1982 and Australia to 1986, so that the four dominions are treated alike.

statusPeriods.label: Equal in status after the Balfour formula
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The 1926 Imperial Conference declared the dominions equal in status to Britain and in no way subordinate; South Africa's own Nationality Act of 1927 and its own flag followed within a year.
statusPeriods.franchise: Unchanged, and about to narrow: Hertzog's bills to strip the Cape's African voters from the common roll were introduced in 1926 and finally passed in 1936.

date.note: South Africa has no single independence date. 1910: a self-governing dominion. 11 December 1931: the Statute of Westminster ends Westminster's power to legislate for it. 1934: the Union's own Status Act says so in South African law. 31 May 1961: the Union becomes a republic and leaves the Commonwealth, ending the last formal tie — the shared Crown. This atlas keeps South Africa on the map to 1961, the same way it keeps Canada to 1982 and Australia to 1986, so that the four dominions are treated alike.

departures.how: The Statute of Westminster made South Africa legally sovereign: Westminster gave up the power to legislate for it, and its own Status of the Union Act of 1934 spelled the point out.

led.name: J.B.M. Hertzog
led.role: prime minister who pressed hardest at the 1926 and 1930 imperial conferences for a written statement of dominion sovereignty

led.name: Jan Smuts
led.role: opposition leader who had helped design the dominion idea and thought the statute unnecessary

led.name: Josiah Tshangana Gumede
led.role: ANC president 1927-30, who went to Brussels and Moscow arguing that this independence was for whites only

departures.movement: Afrikaner nationalism, through Hertzog's National Party

cost.note: No one died. This independence transferred power from London to a white electorate of about a million and a half people, in a country of eight million.

departures.borders: No border moved. The change was who could no longer be overruled: after 1931 Britain could not disallow a South African law, which is why the Cape franchise could be destroyed in 1936 with nobody to appeal to.

instrument.name: Statute of Westminster 1931
instrument.note: South Africa's Status of the Union Act 1934 declared the Union a sovereign independent state.

contested.note: When did South Africa stop being British? 1910 (self-governing dominion), 1931 (Westminster gives up legislative power), 1934 (the Union's own Status Act), or 1961 (republic and exit from the Commonwealth)? This atlas uses 1931, because that is when Britain lost the legal power to overrule a South African law. Many textbooks say 1961, which is the date South Africa left the Commonwealth, not the date it became sovereign.

positions.claim: Sovereignty came in 1931, when Westminster surrendered the power to legislate for the dominions.
Sovereignty came in 1961, when South Africa became a republic and left the Commonwealth after a whites-only referendum.

violence.note: The state built in 1910 shot 69 people at Sharpeville on 21 March 1960, most of them in the back, and banned the ANC and PAC nine days later.

toll.note: The official inquiry counted 69 dead and 180 wounded at Sharpeville; the number is not seriously disputed, though the number of shots fired and the order to fire are.

warrant.note: The number of dead is not seriously disputed. The number of shots fired and the order to fire are, and the inquiry is where that argument lives.

populationTransfer.note: The Natives Land Act 1913 and the Native Trust and Land Act 1936 confined African land ownership to 13 per cent of the country, and forced removals moved about 3.5 million people between 1960 and 1983.

toll.note: The Surplus People Project's 1983 survey counted about 3.5 million people removed under apartheid between 1960 and 1983; the figure is an estimate built from local case studies.

warrant.author: The Surplus People Project
warrant.work: Forced Removals in South Africa: the Surplus People Project reports

warrant.check: Surplus People Project, Cape Town, 1983, five volumes; held at the University of Cape Town libraries.
warrant.note: Built up from local case studies rather than counted centrally, because the state that did the removing did not publish a total.

commonwealth.note: After a whites-only referendum on 5 October 1960 carried the republic by 52.29 per cent, other Commonwealth members made clear South Africa's apartheid policy would be attacked at the 1961 conference, and Verwoerd withdrew the application to remain. South Africa rejoined on 1 June 1994.

consequences.borderLegacy: Britain kept Bechuanaland, Basutoland and Swaziland out of the Union in 1910 pending a transfer that was never made, so three independent states sit inside or against South Africa's borders today.
consequences.economicLegacy: Gold and diamonds paid for the Union, and the migrant labour system that mined them - compounds, pass laws, single-year contracts - was already in place before apartheid gave it a name.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The Westminster parliamentary form, an entrenched racial franchise and Roman-Dutch law came together in 1910 and held until 1994.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: A History of South Africa
evidence.supports: Union, segregation, the road to apartheid and 1961.

evidence.author: Sol Plaatje
evidence.work: Native Life in South Africa
evidence.supports: The effect of the 1913 Natives Land Act, reported by an eyewitness who travelled the country recording it.

evidence.author: Saul Dubow
evidence.work: Apartheid, 1948-1994
evidence.supports: How the Union's segregationist framework became apartheid, and the 1961 republic.

contested.note: Historians divide over how far apartheid after 1948 was a continuation of the segregation built into the 1910 settlement and how far it was a new departure. Dubow and Marks stress continuity from the Union's founding; others stress the National Party's radicalisation after 1948.

pedagogy.hook: The British Parliament wrote South Africa's first constitution in 1909, was warned in the debate that it entrenched a colour bar, and passed it anyway.

misconception.belief: South Africa left the British Empire in 1961, and apartheid was invented in 1948 by Afrikaners with nothing to do with Britain.
misconception.correction: South Africa became legally sovereign in 1931, not 1961; 1961 is when it left the Commonwealth. And the machinery apartheid used was already built: the 1913 Land Act reserving 7 per cent of the country, the pass system, mine compounds and the exclusion of black voters were all in place under British-era governments, several of them designed by British officials.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: South Africa is where the empire's habit of buying white settler loyalty with other people's rights produced its most durable result. It is also the clearest test of what a dominion was: independent enough by 1936 to destroy a franchise Britain had created, with Britain unable to stop it.

territories.name: South West Africa
territories.formalName: Mandated Territory of South West Africa
territories.subregion: The Atlantic desert coast and the Namib interior

namesOverTime.name: Namibia
namesOverTime.note: The name the United Nations adopted in 1968 at the request of the Namibian liberation movements.

modernSuccessors.name: Namibia
modernSuccessors.note: Independent after a 23-year war and a UN-run transition; Walvis Bay, a British enclave since 1878, was handed over by South Africa in 1994.

to.note: South West Africa was a League mandate held, in the words of the mandate itself, by the King 'for and on behalf of' South Africa. It therefore left the British Empire exactly when South Africa did, and the answer to that is contested: 1931 in law, 1961 when the Union became a republic. South African rule itself lasted until Namibian independence on 21 March 1990.

geoCoverage.label: Conquered for Britain, run by South Africa
geoCoverage.change: South African troops took the German colony's surrender at Khorab on 9 July 1915; the League handed the mandate to the British Crown in 1920, to be exercised by the Union government.

acquisitions.how: At Britain's request the Union of South Africa invaded German South West Africa in 1915, put down an Afrikaner rebellion against doing so, and took the German surrender at Khorab in July.

counterparties.name: German Empire
counterparties.lost: Its oldest settler colony, and with it the harbours from which German cruisers might have worked the Cape route.

counterparties.name: Herero, Nama, Damara and Ovambo peoples
counterparties.lost: One occupier for another. Germany had killed perhaps 65,000 Herero and 10,000 Nama in 1904-08; South African rule kept the German settlers, their farms and the pass laws, and added its own.

people.name: Louis Botha
people.role: prime minister of the Union; personally commanded the invasion

people.name: Mandume ya Ndemufayo
people.role: king of the Oukwanyama, who resisted the new rulers and was killed by South African forces in February 1917

people.name: Theodor Seitz
people.role: the last German governor, who surrendered at Khorab

acquisitions.resistance: About 12,000 Afrikaners rebelled in 1914 rather than fight for Britain and were defeated; in the north the Kwanyama king Mandume fought until 1917.

cost.note: The 1915 campaign itself was short and comparatively cheap in lives - a few hundred dead in the South African and German forces together. The killing had been done a decade earlier by Germany, in a campaign the German parliament itself debated and that historians now generally call a genocide.

acquisitions.how: The League of Nations conferred a Class C mandate over the territory on His Britannic Majesty, to be exercised on his behalf by the government of the Union of South Africa - so a British mandate was administered by a dominion as if it were a province.

counterparties.name: German Empire
counterparties.lost: Formal title, stripped by the Treaty of Versailles along with all its colonies.

counterparties.name: The peoples of South West Africa
counterparties.lost: The self-determination the mandate system claimed to hold in trust for them; a Class C mandate could be governed as an integral portion of the mandatory's own territory, and was.

instrument.name: League of Nations mandate for German South-West Africa
instrument.note: The wording naming His Britannic Majesty as mandatory is what later let the International Court of Justice treat the mandate as a real trust that South Africa could not simply annex.

people.name: Jan Smuts
people.role: co-author of the mandate system at Versailles, and the man who wanted South West Africa annexed outright

acquisitions.resistance: The Bondelswarts Nama rose in 1922 against a dog tax and grazing restrictions and were bombed from the air by the South African Air Force; about 100 people were killed, and the League's Permanent Mandates Commission criticised the Union for it.

evidence.author: Marion Wallace
evidence.work: A History of Namibia: From the Beginning to 1990
evidence.supports: The 1915 conquest, the mandate and South African rule.

statusPeriods.label: South African military occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A South African military administration governed under martial law, kept the German settlers on their farms and repatriated most German officials.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.governedFrom: Windhoek, under the Union government in Pretoria

statusPeriods.note: About 1,100 German settler families kept their farms, and South Africa settled a further 1,500 Afrikaner families on land taken from Herero and Nama survivors.

It therefore left the British Empire exactly when South Africa did, and the answer to that is contested: 1931 in law, 1961 when the Union became a republic. departures.how: When the Statute of Westminster made South Africa sovereign, the mandate held in the King's name passed in practice to Pretoria alone, and Britain never exercised it again.

becomes.name: South West Africa under South African administration

led.name: J.B.M. Hertzog
led.role: South African prime minister who pressed for dominion sovereignty and treated South West Africa as a fifth province in all but name

led.name: Sam Nujoma
led.role: founding president of SWAPO in 1960 and of independent Namibia in 1990

led.name: Herman Toivo ya Toivo
led.role: SWAPO founder; told a Pretoria court in 1968 that South Africa was a foreign country to him, and served sixteen years on Robben Island

cost.note: Nothing was paid in 1931. The bill came later: the war for Namibian independence from 1966 to 1989 killed something in the order of 20,000 to 25,000 people, on estimates that no one has been able to verify.

departures.borders: The German colonial boundaries survived intact, including the Caprivi Strip that Germany had obtained in 1890 to reach the Zambezi, and Walvis Bay, a British enclave since 1878, which South Africa kept until 1994.

contested.note: There is no clean date for the end of the British connection. Candidates are 1920, when the Union began administering the mandate; 1931 or 1934, when South Africa became sovereign and the King acted on Union advice alone; and 1990, when the territory finally became independent. The mandate instrument names the British Crown throughout, which is why the International Court of Justice could still rule on it in 1966 and 1971. This atlas records 1931 and flags the uncertainty.

violence.note: South Africa refused UN supervision, was ruled illegal in the territory by the International Court of Justice in 1971, and fought SWAPO there and in southern Angola until 1989.

toll.note: Casualty totals for the Namibian war of independence are contested and were counted by the South African Defence Force, an interested party. No agreed figure exists.

consequences.borderLegacy: Namibia's shape is German: the Caprivi Strip, drawn in 1890 to give Germany the Zambezi, still gives Namibia a 450-kilometre panhandle to the Zimbabwean border.
consequences.economicLegacy: Diamonds from the Sperrgebiet and later uranium from Rossing were mined under South African law by companies registered elsewhere; independent Namibia inherited one of the world's most unequal economies.

contested.note: Whether South West Africa should be counted as British at all is disputed. pedagogy.hook: The mandate over South West Africa was granted to the British King, and no British official ever governed the place - a dominion did it for him.

misconception.belief: Mandates were a temporary international trust that prepared colonies for independence.
misconception.correction: Class C mandates like South West Africa could be governed as an integral part of the mandatory's own territory, and were. South Africa treated it as a fifth province, refused to convert it to a UN trusteeship in 1946, and gave it up only in 1990 after a 23-year war and a World Court ruling that its presence was illegal.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows sub-imperialism: an empire lending its name while a settler dominion did the ruling. It also shows the mandate system's real teeth were slow but not nothing - the words in the 1920 instrument gave the World Court its jurisdiction fifty years later.
