territories.name: Bechuanaland
territories.subregion: The Kalahari and the eastern Tswana states

namesOverTime.name: Botswana
namesOverTime.note: The country of the Batswana; the colonial name was an English rendering of the same word.

modernSuccessors.name: Botswana
modernSuccessors.note: A continuous multiparty democracy since independence, and by the 1990s one of the fastest-growing economies in the world.

geoCoverage.label: The protectorate north of the Molopo
geoCoverage.change: Britain declared a protectorate over Tswana country to block a German-Boer link across the continent and to keep the road north open.

acquisitions.how: After the Warren Expedition marched 4,000 men north without a shot, Britain declared a protectorate over Tswana country - not to develop it, but to stop the Transvaal and the new German colony on the Atlantic joining hands across the road to the north.

counterparties.name: Ngwato, Kwena, Ngwaketse, Tawana and Kgatla states
counterparties.lost: External sovereignty, and the right to make their own treaties. Their chiefs had asked for British protection against Boer land raids, and got a protectorate that later tried to hand them to a mining company.
counterparties.note: Khama III of the Ngwato had petitioned for protection since 1876; this is a case where African rulers actively sought a British umbrella, and then had to fight to keep it from turning into something worse.

counterparties.name: Zuid-Afrikaansche Republiek
counterparties.lost: Its westward expansion and the freebooter republics of Stellaland and Goshen its citizens had set up on Tlhaping land.

instrument.name: Proclamation of the Bechuanaland Protectorate
instrument.note: Territory south of the Molopo became the separate Crown Colony of British Bechuanaland in September 1885, and was annexed to the Cape Colony in 1895. That land is now South Africa's North West and Northern Cape.

people.name: Khama III
people.role: kgosi of the Ngwato; asked for protection, then went to London in 1895 to stop the protectorate being handed to Cecil Rhodes

people.name: Charles Warren
people.role: commanded the expedition that established the protectorate without fighting

acquisitions.resistance: There was no war of conquest here. The fight was diplomatic: in 1895 three kgosi crossed the sea to argue their own case in Britain, and won.

evidence.author: Neil Parsons
evidence.work: King Khama, Emperor Joe and the Great White Queen: Victorian Britain through African Eyes
evidence.supports: The 1895 mission of Khama III, Bathoen I and Sebele I to Britain.

statusPeriods.label: A road, not a colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain spent as little as possible: a resident commissioner, a handful of officials, and chiefs left to govern their own people under their own law as long as the road north stayed open.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Tswana political life ran through the kgotla, the public assembly at which any adult man could speak.

statusPeriods.label: Saved from the company, run from abroad
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After the chiefs' London mission the protectorate stayed under the Crown, administered from Mafeking - a town inside South Africa, 24 kilometres outside the territory it governed, for the next seventy years.
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1961; an African Advisory Council of chiefs met from 1920 and a Legislative Council with elected members only from 1961.
statusPeriods.note: Britain expected to hand Bechuanaland, Basutoland and Swaziland to South Africa under section 151 of the South Africa Act 1909. It never did: African opposition and then apartheid made the transfer politically impossible.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government from Gaborone
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Lower than the protectorate default of 3: from the March 1965 general election an elected prime minister ran internal affairs, with Britain retaining only defence, external affairs and the civil service.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Seretse Khama's Botswana Democratic Party won 28 of 31 seats in the first universal-suffrage election and formed a government in a brand-new capital built from nothing at Gaborone.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage from 1965.

departures.how: Britain left a country it had barely governed: independence came by agreement, without a shot, on the anniversary of the day the protectorate's southern half had been annexed to the Cape 71 years earlier.

led.name: Seretse Khama
led.role: heir to the Ngwato chieftaincy, exiled by Britain from 1950 to 1956 for marrying an Englishwoman, then first president of Botswana

led.name: Ruth Williams Khama
led.role: his wife, whose marriage to him in 1948 triggered the British ban

led.name: Quett Ketumile Masire
led.role: co-founder of the Botswana Democratic Party and Khama's successor as president

led.name: Motsamai Mpho
led.role: founder of the Bechuanaland People's Party, the more radical nationalist movement

departures.movement: Botswana Democratic Party

cost.note: Nobody died. Botswana at independence had about 12 kilometres of tarred road, a handful of secondary school graduates and almost no state revenue; Britain paid most of its budget until 1972.

departures.borders: Britain handed over the straight desert lines drawn between 1885 and 1899, including the Caprivi Strip border with Namibia and a four-country meeting point on the Zambezi that lawyers still argue about.

evidence.author: Thomas Tlou and Alec Campbell
evidence.work: History of Botswana
evidence.supports: The protectorate, the transfer question and independence.

commonwealth.note: A republic from the day of independence, with an elected president rather than a governor-general.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 1885 line along the Molopo left the Tlhaping and Rolong of British Bechuanaland inside South Africa, so one Tswana people has been split by an international border for 130 years.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Roman-Dutch common law inherited through the Cape, English as the official language, Setswana as the national one, and the kgotla assembly still functioning in law.

acquisitions.resistance: The Basotho had already beaten the British at Berea in 1852 and fought the Free State to exhaustion three times; what they could not survive was the burning of the harvest year after year.

statusPeriods.franchise: None; the pitso, a national assembly, continued to meet.

statusPeriods.label: Annexed to the Cape - and the Cape loses control
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Cape Colony took Basutoland over, taxed it, and then in 1880 tried to disarm the Basotho under its Peace Preservation Act. The Basotho refused, fought the Gun War, and the Cape could not beat them.
statusPeriods.franchise: Basotho paid Cape taxes and did not vote in Cape elections, because the territory returned no members.
statusPeriods.note: The Gun War of 1880-81 cost the Cape about three million pounds and it lost: the settlement of 1881 let the Basotho keep licensed guns. It is one of the very few colonial disarmament campaigns that simply failed.

statusPeriods.label: Back under the Crown, ruled through chiefs
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain took the territory back from the Cape and ruled it lightly: a Resident Commissioner, a tiny budget, and the paramount chief and his sub-chiefs administering their own law.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Maseru, under the High Commissioner for South Africa
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1960; a Basutoland Council of chiefs and nominees met from 1910, and the first elections were held in 1960.
statusPeriods.note: Basutoland was one of the three High Commission Territories that Britain expected, under the South Africa Act 1909, to hand over to South Africa. Basotho opposition and then apartheid killed the idea.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Lower than the protectorate default of 3: after the April 1965 election a Basotho prime minister ran internal affairs while Britain kept defence and external relations for eighteen months.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Leabua Jonathan's Basotho National Party won the 1965 election by four seats, and formed the government that took the country to independence.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage from 1960.

departures.how: Basutoland became the Kingdom of Lesotho by agreement, with Moshoeshoe II as constitutional monarch and no violence at the handover - and with its economy already wholly dependent on wages earned in South African mines.

led.name: Leabua Jonathan
led.role: leader of the Basotho National Party and first prime minister; annulled the 1970 election when he lost it

led.name: Ntsu Mokhehle
led.role: leader of the Basutoland Congress Party, the main nationalist movement, which won the popular vote in 1970 and was denied power

led.name: Moshoeshoe II
led.role: paramount chief who became king at independence

departures.movement: Basutoland Congress Party and Basotho National Party

cost.note: No one was killed at independence. The violence came in January 1970, when Jonathan lost the first post-independence election, declared a state of emergency and had opponents killed; hundreds died over the following years.

departures.borders: Britain handed over the border it had accepted in 1869: Lesotho keeps the mountains and South Africa keeps the wheat fields of the Caledon valley, which is why a country with excellent rain imports most of its food.

commonwealth.note: A kingdom in its own right: the head of state is the King of Lesotho, not the British monarch.

consequences.economicLegacy: By the 1970s roughly 40 per cent of Lesotho's adult men were working in South African mines at any one time, and their wages were a larger part of national income than everything produced inside the country.
consequences.borderLegacy: The Conquered Territory lost in 1869 is now South Africa's eastern Free State, and Lesotho has never recognised the loss as just; its border claim is a live political issue.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Sesotho and English are both official; Roman-Dutch law arrived through the Cape and still governs, alongside chiefs' courts applying Sesotho customary law.

peak.populationNote: 1966 census, taken in the year of independence; a further 100,000 or so Basotho were working in South Africa at the time.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Basutoland’s largest recorded population: 969,634 people, counted in 1966.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: Survival in Two Worlds: Moshoeshoe of Lesotho, 1786-1870
evidence.supports: Moshoeshoe, the wars with the Orange Free State and the 1868 protectorate.

evidence.author: Elizabeth A. Eldredge
evidence.work: A South African Kingdom: The Pursuit of Security in Nineteenth-Century Lesotho
evidence.supports: The kingdom's economy, land loss and the Gun War.

pedagogy.hook: Lesotho exists because a king asked to be colonised: Moshoeshoe chose the British blanket over destruction by the Orange Free State, and the country he saved is still there.

misconception.belief: Colonisation always happened against the will of local rulers.
misconception.correction: Moshoeshoe I asked Britain for protection in the 1860s because the alternative was annihilation by Boer commandos burning his crops. He got protection and lost his best farmland anyway, in the Convention of Aliwal North in 1869. Choosing the least bad option is still not the same as consent - but it is not the same as conquest either.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Lesotho is the sharpest example of a colonial border with a permanent economic consequence: Britain confirmed the loss of the Caledon wheatlands in 1869, and a mountain kingdom with good rainfall has depended on South African wages ever since.

keyDates.what: The Basotho fight a British force to a standstill at Berea
Britain declares a protectorate at Moshoeshoe's request
The Convention of Aliwal North hands the Caledon valley to the Orange Free State
The Gun War: the Basotho defeat Cape attempts to disarm them
Britain takes the territory back from the Cape
Lesotho becomes independent

territories.name: Swaziland
territories.subregion: The Lubombo escarpment and the middleveld

from.note: A rough marker for the kingdom under Mswati II, whose name it carries; there is no founding date.

namesOverTime.name: Eswatini
namesOverTime.note: King Mswati III restored the siSwati name on the fiftieth anniversary of independence.

modernSuccessors.name: Eswatini
modernSuccessors.note: Africa's last absolute monarchy: King Sobhuza II repealed the independence constitution in 1973 and political parties are still banned.

geoCoverage.label: The kingdom under British protection
geoCoverage.change: Britain took over the administration after defeating the Transvaal, which had run Swaziland since 1894 with British consent.

acquisitions.how: Britain had twice guaranteed Swazi independence in writing, then let the Transvaal administer the kingdom from 1894; after winning the South African War it simply took over the administration itself by Order in Council.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of Swaziland under the queen regent Labotsibeni
counterparties.lost: Independence twice promised by treaty, and then two thirds of the land: the partition proclamation of 1907 allotted about a third of the country to the Swazi and the rest to white concessionaires and the Crown.

counterparties.name: Zuid-Afrikaansche Republiek
counterparties.lost: The protectorate it had held since 1894, and its only realistic route to the sea.

instrument.name: Swaziland Order in Council, 1903
instrument.note: Placed the territory under the Governor of the Transvaal; a further Order in Council in December 1906 transferred it to the High Commissioner for South Africa.

people.name: Labotsibeni Mdluli
people.role: queen regent from 1899 to 1921; raised money from Swazi across the region to buy back land Britain had given away

people.name: Sobhuza II
people.role: king from 1899 to 1982; took the land question to the Privy Council in 1926 and lost, then spent fifty years buying land back

acquisitions.resistance: The Swazi fought this in courtrooms, not in the field: Sobhuza II's case against the 1907 land partition went to the Privy Council in London in 1926, which ruled that a protecting power could do as it liked with land in a protectorate.

evidence.author: Philip Bonner
evidence.work: Kings, Commoners and Concessionaires: The Evolution and Dissolution of the Nineteenth-Century Swazi State
evidence.supports: The concession scramble, the Transvaal administration and the British takeover.

statusPeriods.label: Administered from Pretoria
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British special commissioner governed under the Governor of the Transvaal, sorting through hundreds of overlapping land, mineral and even sanitation concessions that Swazi kings had signed in the 1880s.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Mbabane, under the Governor of the Transvaal
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: High Commission Territory, two thirds of it alienated
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Resident Commissioner under the High Commissioner ran the territory, and the 1907 partition proclamation left the Swazi with about a third of their own country, much of it already occupied by white ranchers.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Mbabane, under the High Commissioner for South Africa
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The Swazi National Council under the king and the queen mother spoke for Swazi opinion; European settlers had an advisory council of their own.
statusPeriods.note: Like Bechuanaland and Basutoland, Swaziland was earmarked in 1909 for eventual transfer to South Africa. It was never transferred; apartheid ended the argument.

statusPeriods.label: Constitution, elections, and a king who won them
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Lower than the protectorate default of 3: from 1963 there was a legislature and from 1967 internal self-government, with Britain keeping external affairs and defence.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain wrote a constitution to produce a modern party system; Sobhuza II's Imbokodvo National Movement won every seat in 1964 and again in 1967, and he then dismantled the system that had elected him.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage from 1964, on a roll with separate European seats until 1967.

departures.how: Swaziland became independent under Sobhuza II with a Westminster constitution he had never wanted; five years later he repealed it, banned political parties and ruled by decree.

led.name: Sobhuza II
led.role: king from 1899 to 1982, the longest documented reign of any monarch; led the country to independence and then abolished its constitution in 1973

led.name: Ambrose Zwane
led.role: leader of the Ngwane National Liberatory Congress, the main party opposing royal control

led.name: Prince Makhosini Dlamini
led.role: first prime minister, leading the king's Imbokodvo National Movement

departures.movement: Imbokodvo National Movement

cost.note: No deaths at independence. The cost was land: the Swazi entered independence owning less than half their country, and buying the rest back took another thirty years.

departures.borders: The boundaries were those the Transvaal and Portugal had drawn in the 1880s and 1890s, leaving a large Swazi-speaking population inside South Africa and Mozambique and cutting the kingdom off from the sea by 60 kilometres.

commonwealth.note: A monarchy in its own right; the head of state is the Ngwenyama, the King of Eswatini.

consequences.economicLegacy: The concessions signed in the 1880s and confirmed by Britain in 1907 put the best land and all the minerals in foreign hands; sugar estates on that land are still the country's largest export earner.
consequences.borderLegacy: Eswatini has never accepted the borders. Its claim to Swazi-populated districts of South Africa and to a corridor to the sea has been raised with Pretoria repeatedly since 1968.
consequences.languageAndLaw: A dual system Britain built and independence kept: Roman-Dutch law and a modern court structure alongside Swazi law and custom administered by chiefs under the king.

peak.populationNote: 1966 census, the last before independence.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Swaziland’s largest recorded population: 374,697 people, counted in 1966.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Philip Bonner
evidence.work: Kings, Commoners and Concessionaires: The Evolution and Dissolution of the Nineteenth-Century Swazi State
evidence.supports: The concessions, the Transvaal administration and the loss of the land.

evidence.author: Hilda Kuper
evidence.work: Sobhuza II, Ngwenyama and King of Swaziland
evidence.supports: Sobhuza's long reign, the Privy Council case and the road to independence.

pedagogy.hook: By 1907 white concession-holders held about two thirds of Swaziland, and a British court later ruled that a protecting power could give away land in a protectorate as it pleased.

misconception.belief: A protectorate meant Britain protected a country and left it alone.
misconception.correction: In Swaziland, protection meant Britain confirmed the concessions its own settlers had extracted from Swazi kings in the 1880s, allotted about a third of the country to the Swazi in 1907, and in 1926 the Privy Council held in Sobhuza II v Miller that the Crown's power in a protectorate was unlimited by treaty. Protection was a legal form, not a promise.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Swaziland is the clearest case of the empire making, breaking and remaking promises to the same kingdom: independence guaranteed by treaty in 1881 and 1884, handed to the Transvaal in 1894, taken back in 1903, and its land given away in 1907.

keyDates.what: Britain and the Transvaal guarantee Swazi independence by convention
Britain lets the Transvaal take over the administration of Swaziland
Britain assumes the administration after the South African War
The land partition proclamation leaves the Swazi about a third of the country
Swaziland becomes independent under Sobhuza II
The country is renamed Eswatini

territories.name: Southern Rhodesia
territories.subregion: The Zimbabwean plateau between the Zambezi and the Limpopo

from.note: A rough marker: Mzilikazi's Ndebele state was established on the plateau in the late 1830s.

namesOverTime.name: Rhodesia
namesOverTime.note: Named by the British South Africa Company after its founder, Cecil Rhodes - the only country in modern history named after a living businessman.

namesOverTime.name: Zimbabwe
namesOverTime.note: From dzimba dza mabwe, houses of stone: the medieval city of Great Zimbabwe, which Rhodesian officials spent decades insisting Africans could not have built.

geoCoverage.label: Mashonaland only
geoCoverage.change: The Pioneer Column raised the flag at Fort Salisbury; the Ndebele kingdom west of it was still independent.

geoCoverage.label: Mashonaland and Matabeleland
geoCoverage.change: After the war of 1893 the company took Matabeleland too, and an Order in Council of July 1894 set up its administration.

acquisitions.how: Cecil Rhodes's agents got Lobengula to sign away mineral rights in 1888 for 1,000 rifles, 100,000 rounds, 100 pounds a month and a gunboat; Rhodes turned that document into a royal charter and marched 500 men in to occupy the country.

counterparties.name: Ndebele kingdom under Lobengula
counterparties.lost: Everything, in stages. Lobengula repudiated the Rudd Concession in writing to Queen Victoria within months, saying he had been told it covered one hole; the company occupied his neighbours' land anyway and destroyed his kingdom five years later.

counterparties.name: Shona chieftaincies of the plateau
counterparties.lost: Their land, their cattle and their labour: the company had no revenue but land and forced work, so it took both.

instrument.name: Royal Charter of the British South Africa Company
instrument.note: The charter rested on the Rudd Concession of 30 October 1888, which Lobengula denied having understood and formally repudiated in January 1889.

people.name: Lobengula
people.role: king of the Ndebele; signed the Rudd Concession, repudiated it, fought in 1893 and died in flight early in 1894

people.name: Cecil Rhodes
people.role: founder of the company, prime minister of the Cape and the man the country was named after

people.name: Charles Rudd
people.role: negotiated the 1888 concession with Rochfort Maguire and Francis Thompson

people.name: Leander Starr Jameson
people.role: company administrator; provoked the 1893 war and then invaded the Transvaal in 1895

acquisitions.resistance: Lobengula tried law and diplomacy first, sending envoys to Queen Victoria in 1889; when that failed his regiments fought the Maxim guns at the Shangani and Bembesi in 1893 and lost about 1,500 men in two engagements.

evidence.author: Terence Ranger
evidence.work: Revolt in Southern Rhodesia 1896-7: A Study in African Resistance
evidence.supports: The company occupation and the risings that followed.

acquisitions.how: The company started a war in October 1893, burned Lobengula's capital at Bulawayo, took his cattle and his land, and had its rule over Matabeleland confirmed by an Order in Council nine months later.

counterparties.name: Ndebele nation
counterparties.lost: Their king, roughly 200,000 head of cattle seized as loot, and the fertile highveld, which was cut into farms for company volunteers at 3,000 acres each.

acquisitions.resistance: Three years later the Ndebele and the Shona rose together in the war they call the First Chimurenga and Umvukela, killing about 450 settlers - a tenth of the white population - before artillery and dynamite in the Matopos ended it.

cost.note: Terence Ranger's estimate of African deaths in the 1896-97 risings is about 8,000, against roughly 450 settlers killed. Neither side counted properly and the African figure is a scholarly reconstruction.

warrant.author: Terence Ranger
warrant.work: Revolt in Southern Rhodesia 1896-7: A Study in African Resistance
warrant.supports: Terence Ranger's estimate of African deaths in the 1896-97 risings is about 8,000, against roughly 450 settlers killed.
warrant.check: Heinemann, 1967. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

acquisitions.how: The white electorate voted in October 1922 to become a self-governing colony rather than join South Africa, by 8,774 votes to 5,989; Britain then annexed the territory from the company and handed it to those voters.

counterparties.name: British South Africa Company
counterparties.lost: Administration of the territory, but not its land or minerals: Britain paid the company 3,750,000 pounds for its claims, a debt charged to Southern Rhodesia's own budget.

counterparties.name: The African majority of Southern Rhodesia
counterparties.lost: Any chance of imperial protection. Britain kept a formal veto over laws discriminating against Africans and never once used it in 42 years.

instrument.name: Southern Rhodesia (Annexation) Order in Council, 1923
instrument.note: Responsible government followed on 1 October 1923. About 33,000 white people were now governing about a million Africans.

statusPeriods.label: Ruled by a company with a private army
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A London-registered company, not the Crown, made the laws, collected the taxes, distributed the land and ran the police; a British Resident watched and rarely intervened.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Salisbury, under a company administrator and the High Commissioner at Cape Town
statusPeriods.franchise: A property and income qualification, colour-blind on paper and set high enough to keep almost every African off the roll. The Legislative Council had elected settler members from 1899.
statusPeriods.note: The Privy Council ruled in 1918 that unalienated land belonged to the Crown, not the company - so the company had spent 28 years selling farms it did not own.

statusPeriods.label: Self-government for 33,000 settlers
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Southern Rhodesia had its own prime minister, army and civil service and was treated at imperial conferences almost like a dominion, though Britain kept a reserve power over African affairs it never used.
statusPeriods.franchise: Qualified and racially coded: by 1939 fewer than 100 Africans were on a roll of about 25,000.
statusPeriods.note: The Land Apportionment Act of 1930 divided the country by race: about 50 per cent to roughly 50,000 whites, 30 per cent as reserves for over a million Africans, and the towns closed to African ownership entirely.

statusPeriods.label: Inside the Central African Federation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Southern Rhodesia kept its own government and gained a federal one at Salisbury that ran the Copperbelt's revenue as well; Africans in all three territories opposed the federation from the start and Britain imposed it anyway.
statusPeriods.franchise: Two rolls from 1957, an upper and a lower, designed so that African voters could never outweigh European ones.

statusPeriods.label: After the federation broke
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The federation dissolved, Zambia and Malawi went to independence under African majority rule, and Southern Rhodesia's white government demanded the same independence for itself.
statusPeriods.franchise: Unchanged. Britain's condition, no independence before majority rule, is what the settler government refused.

statusPeriods.label: Unilateral Declaration of Independence
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Zero, not the self-governing default of 2: Britain claimed sovereignty throughout and exercised none. The Governor was ignored, the UN imposed sanctions, and the Smith regime governed for fourteen years.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Ian Smith's cabinet declared independence in a document echoing the American Declaration, was declared illegal by Britain and the United Nations, and ran the country anyway with South African and Portuguese help.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Salisbury, by a regime no state ever recognised
statusPeriods.franchise: The 1969 constitution capped African representation and the Land Tenure Act split the country half and half between 250,000 whites and five million Africans.
statusPeriods.note: From 1972 the war for the country was fought in earnest; by 1979 the regime was conscripting white men to 50 and had lost control of most of the countryside at night.

statusPeriods.label: Britain governs again, for four months
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Lord Soames arrived as Governor with a Commonwealth monitoring force, took legal control of a country that had been in rebellion for fourteen years, ran a ceasefire and an election, and handed over.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage for the February 1980 election, the first in the country's history.

departures.how: A fifteen-year guerrilla war, sanctions, and the collapse of Portuguese Mozambique brought the Smith regime to Lancaster House in London; ZANU won 57 of 80 African seats in February 1980 and Robert Mugabe became prime minister of Zimbabwe.

led.name: Robert Mugabe
led.role: ZANU leader; prime minister from 1980, president from 1987 to 2017

led.name: Joshua Nkomo
led.role: ZAPU leader and the older of the two nationalist chiefs; his ZIPRA forces fought from Zambia

led.name: Josiah Tongogara
led.role: ZANLA commander who pushed hardest for the Lancaster House settlement and died in a car crash in Mozambique days after it

led.name: Ian Smith
led.role: prime minister who declared UDI in 1965 and said there would be no majority rule in a thousand years

led.name: Peter Carington
led.role: British foreign secretary who chaired the Lancaster House conference

led.name: Christopher Soames
led.role: the last Governor, who ran the country for four months and supervised the election

departures.movement: ZANU and ZAPU, fighting as ZANLA and ZIPRA under the Patriotic Front

cost.note: Deaths in the war of 1972-79 are usually put between 20,000 and 30,000, the great majority of them African civilians. There was no counting authority; the Rhodesian security forces published their own totals and had reason to shape them.

departures.borders: No border moved, and that was the point of the settlement. What Lancaster House did fix was land: white farmers keeping the best half of the country could only be bought out by willing sale for ten years, which pushed the land question to 2000 and the violent seizures that followed.

instrument.name: Lancaster House Agreement
instrument.note: Signed after fourteen weeks of talks; it also reserved 20 of 100 parliamentary seats for white voters until 1987.

evidence.author: Luise White
evidence.work: Unpopular Sovereignty: Rhodesian Independence and African Decolonization
evidence.supports: UDI, its legal claims and its collapse.

violence.note: Three wars in ninety years: the conquest of 1893-97, the liberation war of 1972-79, and then the Gukurahundi killings in Matabeleland in 1983-87, carried out by the government that independence produced.

toll.note: Figures here are for the liberation war of 1972-79. The Catholic Commission for Justice and Peace estimated a further 10,000 to 20,000 killed in Matabeleland after independence; that killing was Zimbabwean, not British, and is recorded because a student who reads only to 1980 will not understand the country.

populationTransfer.note: The Land Apportionment Act of 1930 and the Native Land Husbandry Act of 1951 moved hundreds of thousands of African families off land declared European, into reserves that could not feed them.

commonwealth.note: Zimbabwe joined at independence and withdrew in 2003 after its suspension over the 2002 election was extended.

consequences.economicLegacy: Zimbabwe inherited the best-developed farming and manufacturing economy in Africa after South Africa - and a land distribution in which 6,000 white farmers held about 15 million hectares and a million African families held rather less.
consequences.borderLegacy: Rhodes's company drew the Zambezi border to keep the Victoria Falls and the coal at Wankie on his side; the line still splits Tonga communities between Zimbabwe and Zambia.

peak.populationNote: 1969 census: about 4,846,000 Africans and 228,000 Europeans - the peak white population, roughly 4.5 per cent of the total.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Southern Rhodesia’s largest recorded population: 5,090,000 people, counted in 1969.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Terence Ranger
evidence.work: Revolt in Southern Rhodesia 1896-7: A Study in African Resistance
evidence.supports: The company conquest and the risings of 1896-97.

evidence.author: Luise White
evidence.work: Unpopular Sovereignty: Rhodesian Independence and African Decolonization
evidence.supports: UDI, the legal argument about it, and the settler state's collapse.

evidence.author: David Martin and Phyllis Johnson
evidence.work: The Struggle for Zimbabwe: The Chimurenga War
evidence.supports: The liberation war, ZANLA and ZIPRA, and Lancaster House.

pedagogy.hook: A country was named after a living businessman, occupied by his company's private army, and 75 years later declared independence from Britain to stop black people voting.

misconception.belief: Rhodesia's 1965 declaration of independence was like other colonies breaking free from Britain.
misconception.correction: It was the opposite. Britain's condition for independence was majority rule; Ian Smith's government declared independence to prevent it, on behalf of about 220,000 white people ruling four million Africans. No country in the world recognised it, and the war that followed killed at least 20,000 people before Britain briefly resumed direct rule in 1979.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Southern Rhodesia is the case where settler self-government and African majority rule met head on. It also shows Britain's limits: a colony it legally owned defied it for fourteen years, and it took a guerrilla war, not a British decision, to end that.
