The Pioneer Column raises the flag at Fort Salisbury
The First Chimurenga and Umvukela: Shona and Ndebele rise together
Self-government for the white electorate
Ian Smith declares independence unilaterally
Zimbabwe becomes independent under Robert Mugabe

territories.name: Northern Rhodesia
territories.subregion: The Copperbelt, Barotseland and the central plateau

namesOverTime.name: Barotziland-North-Western Rhodesia and North-Eastern Rhodesia
namesOverTime.note: Two separate company administrations, joined in 1911.

namesOverTime.name: Zambia
namesOverTime.note: Named after the Zambezi, deliberately rejecting the name of Cecil Rhodes.

geoCoverage.label: Company concessions, then a protectorate
geoCoverage.change: Lewanika of Barotseland signed a concession with the British South Africa Company in 1890, and the company extended similar claims north and east over the next decade.

acquisitions.how: Lewanika of Barotseland asked for British protection against Ndebele raids and got a company instead: the Lochner Concession of June 1890 gave the British South Africa Company mineral and trading rights over a kingdom the size of France for 2,000 pounds a year.

counterparties.name: Lozi kingdom of Barotseland under Lewanika
counterparties.lost: Its minerals, its trade and eventually its autonomy. Lewanika believed he was dealing with Queen Victoria's government; the missionary who interpreted, Frank Lochner, let him think so.
counterparties.note: Lewanika complained about the deception for the rest of his life and travelled to London for Edward VII's coronation in 1902 to press his case.

counterparties.name: Bemba, Ngoni, Lunda and Tonga polities
counterparties.lost: Their independence over the following decade, taken by company columns and treaties signed under the threat of them; the Bemba submitted in 1898 and the Ngoni were defeated in 1898.

instrument.name: Lochner Concession
instrument.note: The BSAC's royal charter of 1889 covered territory north of the Zambezi, so the same company ruled both Rhodesias for a generation.

people.name: Lewanika
people.role: litunga of the Lozi; sought British protection, was given a company, and spent thirty years trying to get the deal changed

people.name: Frank Lochner
people.role: company agent who negotiated the concession, accompanied by a missionary the Lozi trusted

people.name: Robert Codrington
people.role: administrator who broke the Bemba and Ngoni and set up the tax system that forced men into wage labour

acquisitions.resistance: The Ngoni fought the company in 1898 and lost; the Bemba submitted after their paramount died; the Lozi resisted on paper, in petitions, appeals and delegations, for seventy years.

evidence.author: Andrew Roberts
evidence.work: A History of Zambia
evidence.supports: The concessions, company rule and the making of Northern Rhodesia.

acquisitions.how: The Colonial Office took the administration off the company in 1924 - but let it keep the mineral royalties, so for the next forty years the copper under Zambia paid dividends to shareholders in London.

counterparties.name: British South Africa Company
counterparties.lost: The cost of administering a territory that never paid; it kept the minerals, which paid enormously from 1930.

counterparties.name: The peoples of Northern Rhodesia
counterparties.lost: The change of ruler brought no vote and no royalty income; between 1930 and 1964 the company took an estimated 82 million pounds in mineral royalties out of the country.

instrument.name: Northern Rhodesia Order in Council, 1924
instrument.note: Took effect on 1 April 1924. The mineral rights stayed with the company until the eve of independence.

statusPeriods.label: Ruled by the British South Africa Company
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Company administrators collected a hut tax in cash, which forced men to walk to the mines of Southern Rhodesia and Katanga to earn it - which was the point of the tax.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Livingstone, under the company and the High Commissioner
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The Barotse kept a treaty-protected internal autonomy under their litunga, alone among the peoples of the territory.

statusPeriods.label: Colonial Office protectorate over a copper colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor ruled through district officers and recognised chiefs, while four huge copper mines opened between 1928 and 1932 and built a wage economy the administration barely controlled.
statusPeriods.franchise: A Legislative Council with elected European members from 1926; the first two African members were nominated in 1948.
statusPeriods.note: African mineworkers struck on the Copperbelt in 1935 and 1940. Police shot six dead at Roan Antelope in 1935 and seventeen at Mufulira in 1940; both strikes produced commissions of inquiry and no African trade union until 1949.

statusPeriods.label: Inside the Central African Federation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Copperbelt revenue was pooled in a federation run from Salisbury, and about two thirds of the money it spent on development went south of the Zambezi.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Lusaka, under a federal government in Salisbury
statusPeriods.franchise: Two-roll system from 1958, weighted so that a few thousand European voters counted for as much as the whole African electorate.
statusPeriods.note: Kenneth Kaunda's UNIP ran the Cha-cha-cha campaign of mass defiance in 1961; about 50 people were killed and thousands arrested.

statusPeriods.label: Self-government under Kaunda
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Lower than the protectorate default of 3: UNIP won the January 1964 election under universal suffrage and formed a government running everything but defence and external affairs.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Kenneth Kaunda became prime minister in January 1964 and negotiated the buy-out of the company's mineral rights before independence.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage from January 1964.

departures.how: Zambia became independent by agreement after mass civil disobedience rather than war, and on its last day as a colony had to pay the British South Africa Company 4 million pounds to get back the minerals under its own ground.

led.name: Kenneth Kaunda
led.role: UNIP leader and first president; jailed twice before independence

led.name: Harry Nkumbula
led.role: leader of the African National Congress of Northern Rhodesia, who led the anti-federation campaign in the 1950s and was overtaken by Kaunda

led.name: Simon Kapwepwe
led.role: UNIP organiser and Kaunda's closest colleague in the independence campaign

led.name: Mwanawina Lewanika III
led.role: litunga of Barotseland, who signed a separate agreement in May 1964 to bring his kingdom into Zambia with guaranteed autonomy

departures.movement: United National Independence Party (UNIP)

cost.note: About 50 people were killed during the Cha-cha-cha civil disobedience campaign of July to October 1961, on figures collected at the time; there was no war of independence here.

departures.borders: The borders were the company's: the Zambezi line drawn to give Rhodes the Victoria Falls, the Katanga pedicle carved out for Belgium in 1894, and the Caprivi Strip for Germany in 1890. Zambia has eight neighbours and was landlocked among hostile white-ruled states for a decade.

instrument.name: Zambia Independence Act 1964
instrument.note: The Barotseland Agreement of 18 May 1964 promised the Lozi kingdom special status; Zambia abolished it in 1969, and the grievance is still alive.

evidence.author: Andrew Roberts
evidence.work: A History of Zambia
evidence.supports: The nationalist campaign, the federation and independence.

commonwealth.note: A republic from independence day, with Kaunda as president.

consequences.economicLegacy: Copper was 90 per cent of Zambia's exports at independence and the country had two African university graduates in its own civil service; when the copper price collapsed in 1975 there was nothing underneath it.
consequences.borderLegacy: The Barotseland Agreement of 1964, which brought the Lozi kingdom into Zambia on promises of autonomy, was abrogated in 1969 and remains a live secessionist grievance.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English is the official language of a country with more than seventy others, chosen at independence precisely because it belonged to none of them.

peak.populationNote: 1963 census: about 3.4 million, including roughly 75,000 Europeans, most of them on the Copperbelt.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Northern Rhodesia’s largest recorded population: 3,409,110 people, counted in 1963.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Andrew Roberts
evidence.work: A History of Zambia
evidence.supports: Company rule, the Copperbelt, the federation and independence.

evidence.author: Charles Perrings
evidence.work: Black Mineworkers in Central Africa
evidence.supports: The Copperbelt labour system and the strikes of 1935 and 1940.

pedagogy.hook: On the day Zambia became independent it had to pay a London company 4 million pounds to buy back the rights to the copper under its own soil.

misconception.belief: Colonies were run by the British government from beginning to end.
misconception.correction: Northern Rhodesia was governed by the British South Africa Company, a private firm with a royal charter, from 1890 until 1924 - and the company kept the mineral royalties for forty years after it stopped governing. Between 1930 and 1964 it drew an estimated 82 million pounds out of a territory it no longer administered.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Zambia shows the economics of empire at its plainest: a hut tax designed to drive men into mines, a company drawing royalties from another continent, and a federation that moved copper revenue south to build white Rhodesia.

keyDates.what: Lewanika signs the Lochner Concession with Rhodes's company
The Colonial Office takes over; the company keeps the minerals
The first Copperbelt strike; police kill six at Roan Antelope
The Central African Federation is imposed against African opposition
The Cha-cha-cha campaign of mass defiance
Zambia becomes independent under Kenneth Kaunda

territories.name: Nyasaland
territories.subregion: The Shire highlands and the western shore of Lake Malawi

namesOverTime.name: Nyasaland
namesOverTime.note: From nyasa, the Yao word for lake - so the colony was called Lakeland, and the lake was called Lake Lake.

namesOverTime.name: Malawi
namesOverTime.note: Chosen by Hastings Banda from an old name for the Maravi state that once dominated the region.

geoCoverage.label: The lake shore and the Shire valley
geoCoverage.change: Britain declared a protectorate to keep Portugal out of the Shire highlands, where Scottish missionaries had settled after David Livingstone.

acquisitions.how: Britain declared a protectorate over the Shire highlands and the lake to shut out Portugal, whose claim to a belt across Africa it had killed with an ultimatum in January 1890, and to satisfy Scottish churches campaigning against the slave trade.

counterparties.name: Yao chiefs of the southern lake
counterparties.lost: Their trade. The Yao ran the slave and ivory route to the Indian Ocean, and Harry Johnston's forces spent the 1890s destroying their stockades one by one.
counterparties.note: The anti-slavery justification was real and was also useful: crushing the Yao removed the only organised power that could resist a protectorate.

counterparties.name: Portugal
counterparties.lost: The Pink Map - its claim to a continuous territory from Angola to Mozambique - abandoned under British threat of war in January 1890.

counterparties.name: Ngoni and Chewa communities
counterparties.lost: Their land in the Shire highlands to about 15 per cent freehold estates owned by planters, on which they were required to work in exchange for living there.

instrument.name: Proclamation of the British Central Africa Protectorate
instrument.note: The Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 11 June 1891 fixed the borders with Mozambique.

people.name: Harry Johnston
people.role: first commissioner; fought the Yao chiefs and wrote the administrative rules copied elsewhere in British Africa

people.name: Mlozi bin Kazbadema
people.role: Swahili-Arab trader at Karonga who fought the British for eight years and was hanged in 1895

people.name: Gomani I
people.role: Ngoni paramount, shot in 1896 after resisting the protectorate's authority

acquisitions.resistance: The Yao chiefs and the Karonga traders fought a decade of small wars against Johnston's Sikh troops and Maxim guns; the last independent Ngoni submitted in 1904.

evidence.author: John McCracken
evidence.work: A History of Malawi, 1859-1966
evidence.supports: The protectorate's foundation, the wars of the 1890s and the estate economy.

statusPeriods.label: British Central Africa
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A commissioner with a few hundred Sikh and African soldiers imposed a hut tax, and men who could not pay in cash worked it off on planters' estates for a month a year.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: The empire's labour reserve
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor and a district administration ran a territory with almost no exportable wealth; its main product was men, who walked south to work in Rhodesian and South African mines.
statusPeriods.franchise: None; a Legislative Council of officials and nominated settlers from 1907, with the first two African members nominated in 1949.
statusPeriods.note: The thangata system on the southern estates required tenants to work for the landowner in place of rent, and it is the grievance behind John Chilembwe's rising in 1915.

statusPeriods.label: Inside a federation nobody there wanted
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain federated Nyasaland with the two Rhodesias against the near-unanimous opposition of its African population, then declared a state of emergency in 1959 when that opposition became unmanageable.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Zomba, under a federal government in Salisbury
statusPeriods.franchise: Almost nobody. On the eve of the emergency the territory had a few hundred African voters in a population of nearly three million.
statusPeriods.note: In the emergency of 3 March 1959 police and troops killed 51 people, 20 of them at Nkhata Bay, and detained over 1,300. The Devlin Commission reported in July 1959 that Nyasaland was, no doubt temporarily, a police state - and the government rejected the report.

statusPeriods.label: Self-government under Banda
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Lower than the protectorate default of 3: from February 1963 Hastings Banda was prime minister with full internal self-government, and took Nyasaland out of the federation in December.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Banda's Malawi Congress Party had won every elected seat in August 1961; as prime minister he negotiated secession from the federation and then independence.
statusPeriods.franchise: A broad qualified franchise from 1961, universal adult suffrage from 1964.

departures.how: Nyasaland's population had refused the federation for ten years by boycott, protest and prison; Britain conceded first the right to secede and then independence, and Malawi took its name from a pre-colonial state.

led.name: Hastings Kamuzu Banda
led.role: doctor who practised in Britain and Ghana for forty years, returned in 1958 to lead the campaign, was detained in 1959, and ruled Malawi as a one-party state until 1994

led.name: Henry Chipembere
led.role: young nationalist who invited Banda home and led the militants; broke with him within months of independence

led.name: Orton Chirwa
led.role: founder of the Malawi Congress Party and first justice minister; later died in Banda's prison

led.name: Patrick Devlin
led.role: British judge whose 1959 commission called the protectorate a police state and undermined the case for the federation

departures.movement: Malawi Congress Party

cost.note: The Devlin Commission recorded 51 Africans killed by security forces during the emergency of March 1959, 20 of them shot at Nkhata Bay. The figure is from a British judicial inquiry and is not seriously disputed.

warrant.author: Sir Patrick Devlin and the Nyasaland Commission of Inquiry
warrant.work: Report of the Nyasaland Commission of Inquiry (Cmnd. 814)
warrant.supports: 51 Africans killed by the security forces in the Nyasaland emergency of March 1959, 20 of them shot at Nkhata Bay.
warrant.check: Command Paper Cmnd. 814, HMSO, July 1959; British Parliamentary Papers 1958–59.

departures.borders: The borders were drawn by the Anglo-Portuguese treaty of 1891 and follow the lake and the Portuguese claim, not any African polity; Malawi is 900 kilometres long and 90 wide, and still disputes ownership of the lake with Tanzania.

violence.note: John Chilembwe's rising of January 1915 against forced estate labour and the conscription of Africans into a European war was crushed in days, and Chilembwe was shot on 3 February.

toll.note: The rising killed three Europeans; about 40 of Chilembwe's followers were executed and some 300 imprisoned. Figures come from the colonial commission of inquiry of 1916.

populationTransfer.note: Nyasaland exported labour: by the 1950s something like 150,000 to 200,000 Malawian men were working in Southern Rhodesia and South Africa at any one time, roughly a third of the adult male population.

commonwealth.note: A republic from 6 July 1966; Banda was made president for life in 1971 and was voted out in 1994.

consequences.economicLegacy: Britain left a country with tea and tobacco estates, no minerals, no railway to the sea it controlled, and an economy built on selling its own men to the mines of richer colonies.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Scottish missions built the schools: the Livingstonia and Blantyre missions produced the clerks, teachers and ministers who founded the nationalist movement, including Chilembwe's own teachers.

peak.populationNote: 1966 census, the first full count, taken two years after independence; the 1945 census had recorded about 2.05 million.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Nyasaland’s largest recorded population: 4,039,583 people, counted in 1966.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: John McCracken
evidence.work: A History of Malawi, 1859-1966
evidence.supports: The protectorate, thangata, Chilembwe, the federation and independence.

evidence.author: George Shepperson and Thomas Price
evidence.work: Independent African: John Chilembwe and the Origins, Setting and Significance of the Nyasaland Native Rising of 1915
evidence.supports: Chilembwe, his mission and the 1915 rising.

pedagogy.hook: In November 1914 a Malawian pastor asked in a newspaper why Africans should die in a European war for a country that gave them nothing; ten weeks later he led a rising, and was shot.

misconception.belief: Africans accepted colonial rule until nationalist parties appeared after the Second World War.
misconception.correction: John Chilembwe rose in Nyasaland in January 1915, and he did it with an argument, published in the Nyasaland Times, about conscription and unpaid estate labour. Resistance ran continuously from the wars of the 1890s through Chilembwe to the federation boycotts of the 1950s. What changed after 1945 was organisation and scale, not the fact of opposition.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Nyasaland is the poorest kind of colony: no minerals, no settler bonanza, useful to the empire mainly as a source of men for other colonies' mines. It also shows a British judicial inquiry, the Devlin Report, doing more damage to a colonial policy than any rebellion.

keyDates.what: Britain declares the British Central Africa Protectorate
John Chilembwe's rising begins in the Shire highlands
Nyasaland is federated with the Rhodesias against its people's wishes
State of emergency; 51 killed, Banda and 1,300 others detained
The federation dissolves after Nyasaland secedes
Malawi becomes independent

territories.name: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland
territories.formalName: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland (the Central African Federation)
territories.subregion: Central Africa

namesOverTime.name: Central African Federation
namesOverTime.note: The everyday name, used by supporters and opponents alike.

geoCoverage.label: One federal state over a self-governing colony and two protectorates
geoCoverage.change: Southern Rhodesia, Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland kept their separate governments and their separate legal statuses, and gained a federal parliament in Salisbury above all three.

acquisitions.how: Britain welded three of its own possessions into one federal state by Order in Council, after a referendum in which only Southern Rhodesia's mostly white electorate voted. Africans in all three territories opposed it and were not asked.

counterparties.name: African National Congresses of Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland
counterparties.note: Both bodies petitioned against federation from 1949 onwards and boycotted the federal parliament.
counterparties.lost: the promise, given in the 1890s protectorate treaties, that Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia would not be handed to settler rule from the south

counterparties.name: Southern Rhodesian settler government
counterparties.lost: nothing; it gained the federal capital, the federal civil service and the larger share of federal spending

instrument.name: Rhodesia and Nyasaland Federation Order in Council 1953
instrument.note: Made under the Rhodesia and Nyasaland Federation Act 1953. The Southern Rhodesian referendum of 9 April 1953 approved federation by 25,570 to 14,729 on a roll of about 50,000 voters, of whom fewer than 500 were African.

people.name: Godfrey Huggins
people.role: prime minister of Southern Rhodesia, then first federal prime minister; called the partnership of black and white 'that of the horse and its rider'

people.name: Roy Welensky
people.role: Northern Rhodesian trade unionist turned federal prime minister 1956-63, the federation's last defender

people.name: Hastings Kamuzu Banda
people.role: Nyasaland doctor who returned from Britain and Ghana in July 1958 to lead the campaign to break the federation

people.name: Harry Nkumbula
people.role: president of the Northern Rhodesian African National Congress, who burned the federation white paper in public in 1951

acquisitions.resistance: Continuous and organised from before it began. The Nyasaland emergency of March 1960 saw 51 Africans shot dead by police and over 1,300 detained, including Banda.

statusPeriods.label: Federal parliament in Salisbury, three territories underneath
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A federal parliament in Salisbury ran defence, external affairs, the economy, railways and European education for all three territories. Britain kept African affairs in the two northern protectorates and the power to disallow federal laws, and used it almost never.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Britain had reserved powers and hardly used them. Real power sat with a settler electorate of roughly 100,000 Europeans governing about 8 million Africans.
statusPeriods.franchise: A property and income franchise that put almost all Africans off the roll. Of 59 federal parliamentary seats in 1958, six were reserved for Africans and two for Europeans charged with representing African interests.
statusPeriods.note: Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia remained protectorates in law throughout; the federation never made them colonies, which is why they could leave.

departures.how: Britain dissolved the federation at midnight on 31 December 1963 after conceding that Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia could secede. Nyasaland became Malawi on 6 July 1964 and Northern Rhodesia became Zambia on 24 October 1964. Southern Rhodesia was refused independence, kept the federal army's aircraft and armoured cars, and declared independence unilaterally on 11 November 1965.

led.name: Hastings Kamuzu Banda
led.role: led the Nyasaland campaign that broke the federation; first prime minister and later president of Malawi

led.name: Kenneth Kaunda
led.role: founded the Zambian African National Congress in 1958 and led Northern Rhodesia out; first president of Zambia

led.name: Iain Macleod
led.role: British colonial secretary 1959-61 who accepted African majority rule in the north and so ended the federation

led.name: Patrick Devlin
led.role: judge whose 1959 report on the Nyasaland emergency called the country 'a police state', which destroyed the federation's case in Britain

departures.movement: The Nyasaland African Congress and the Zambian African National Congress, and the Nyasaland emergency of 1959-60

cost.note: Fifty-one Africans were shot dead by police and soldiers during the Nyasaland emergency of March 1959 and its aftermath, and about 1,300 were detained without trial. The Devlin Commission of July 1959 found there had been no massacre plot.

warrant.author: Sir Patrick Devlin and the Nyasaland Commission of Inquiry
warrant.work: Report of the Nyasaland Commission of Inquiry (Cmnd. 814)
warrant.supports: 51 Africans killed by the security forces in the Nyasaland emergency of March 1959, 20 of them shot at Nkhata Bay.
warrant.check: Command Paper Cmnd. 814, HMSO, July 1959; British Parliamentary Papers 1958–59.

departures.borders: No border moved. The three internal boundaries drawn in the 1890s became three international ones, which is why Malawi and Zambia inherited frontiers no African had drawn.

instrument.name: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland (Dissolution) Order in Council 1963
instrument.note: Made under the Rhodesia and Nyasaland Act 1963, which took effect at midnight on 31 December 1963.

contested.note: Was the federation an economic project that racial politics wrecked, or a device to extend settler rule northwards over the Copperbelt? Both readings are argued from the same record: the federation did build the Kariba dam and did raise output, and it was also designed by men who said in public that Africans were not ready to govern.

positions.claim: Federation was a rational economic union that could have worked and was destroyed by nationalist politics and British nerve.
positions.heldBy: Roy Welensky's memoirs and a strand of Rhodesian historiography

positions.claim: Federation was settler self-government by another name, whose purpose was to attach Northern Rhodesian copper revenue to Southern Rhodesian white politics.
positions.heldBy: Most later scholarship, following the Devlin Report and the archival work of the 1980s onwards

partition.note: One federal state became three countries. Two were independent within a year; the third spent fifteen more years under white minority rule and a war.
partition.lineDrawnBy: Nobody redrew anything: the three internal boundaries of 1891-1911 simply became international frontiers.

violence.note: During the Nyasaland emergency of March 1959 police and soldiers shot dead 51 Africans and over 1,300 people were detained without trial.

toll.note: The Devlin Commission counted 51 dead by July 1959 and found there had been no massacre plot to justify the emergency.

warrant.author: Sir Patrick Devlin and the Nyasaland Commission of Inquiry
warrant.work: Report of the Nyasaland Commission of Inquiry (Cmnd. 814)
warrant.supports: 51 Africans killed by the security forces in the Nyasaland emergency of March 1959, 20 of them shot at Nkhata Bay.
warrant.check: Command Paper Cmnd. 814, HMSO, July 1959; British Parliamentary Papers 1958–59.

consequences.borderLegacy: Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe still use the boundaries drawn between 1891 and 1911 by the British South Africa Company and the Foreign Office.
consequences.economicLegacy: The Kariba dam on the Zambezi, built 1955-59, displaced about 57,000 Gwembe Tonga people. It still supplies both Zambia and Zimbabwe, and is the federation's one durable joint asset.

commonwealth.note: The federation itself was never a Commonwealth member. Malawi and Zambia joined on independence in 1964; Rhodesia never did.

peak.populationNote: About 8.5 million people, of whom roughly 310,000 were European and about 100,000 of those had the vote.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland’s greatest extent, 1,256,000 km² in 1960: the 3 map units this atlas draws it holding that year measure 1,265,108 km², within 0.7% of it.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Robert I. Rotberg
evidence.work: The Rise of Nationalism in Central Africa: The Making of Malawi and Zambia, 1873-1964
evidence.supports: The African political campaigns that made the federation ungovernable.

evidence.author: Patrick Devlin (chair)
evidence.work: Report of the Nyasaland Commission of Inquiry, Cmnd 814
evidence.supports: The 51 deaths, the mass detentions, and the finding that Nyasaland was 'no doubt temporarily, a police state'.

evidence.author: Andrew Cohen
evidence.work: The Politics and Economics of Decolonization in Africa: The Failed Experiment of the Central African Federation
evidence.supports: The economic case for federation and why it did not hold.

pedagogy.hook: A country that existed for ten years and five months, had its own parliament, flag and air force, and appears on no modern map: the Central African Federation.

misconception.belief: The British Empire only ever broke countries up; it did not build them.
misconception.correction: In 1953 Britain welded three of its own territories into one new state, and in 1963 it unwelded them. Federation was tried in central Africa, the West Indies, Malaya, Nigeria and Aden. Only Malaya's and Nigeria's survived.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The federation is the clearest case of the empire's late contradiction: London wanted economically viable successor states, and the only people willing to build them locally were settlers who would not share power. When Britain finally chose African majority rule in the north, Southern Rhodesia's government declared independence rather than accept it.

keyDates.what: Southern Rhodesia's mostly white electorate votes for federation
The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland comes into being
State of emergency in Nyasaland; Banda detained, 51 Africans killed
The Devlin Report calls Nyasaland a police state
The federation is dissolved at midnight

territories.name: Egypt
territories.formalName: Occupied Egypt, then the Sultanate and Kingdom of Egypt under British protection
territories.subregion: The Nile valley, the Delta and the Suez Canal

namesOverTime.name: Khedivate of Egypt
namesOverTime.note: Legally an autonomous province of the Ottoman Empire throughout the first 32 years of the British occupation.

namesOverTime.name: Sultanate of Egypt
namesOverTime.note: Britain cut the Ottoman tie by making the Khedive's uncle Sultan, under a British protectorate.

modernSuccessors.name: Egypt
modernSuccessors.note: Nominally independent from 1922, genuinely so from 1956.

geoCoverage.label: The whole country under occupation
geoCoverage.change: British troops entered Cairo on 14 September 1882 after destroying Ahmad Urabi's army at Tel el-Kebir, and did not leave for 74 years.

geoCoverage.label: Independent on paper, garrisoned everywhere
geoCoverage.change: Britain declared Egypt independent but reserved four subjects to itself, including imperial communications and defence, and kept troops in Cairo, Alexandria and the Canal.

geoCoverage.label: The Canal Zone base only
geoCoverage.change: The Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936 pulled British forces back to the Suez Canal Zone, where the base grew to hold about 80,000 troops - the largest military installation in the world.

geoCoverage.label: Seven weeks back, at Port Said
geoCoverage.change: Five months after the last British soldier left, Britain and France invaded, took Port Said and about 40 kilometres of the canal, and were out again by Christmas.

acquisitions.how: Britain bombarded Alexandria in July 1882 to protect the bondholders who owned Egypt's debt, beat Ahmad Urabi's nationalist army at Tel el-Kebir on 13 September, and entered Cairo the next day promising to leave as soon as order was restored.

counterparties.name: Egypt under Ahmad Urabi's nationalist government
counterparties.lost: The first Egyptian government in centuries led by an Egyptian-born officer rather than a Turco-Circassian elite. Urabi was tried for rebellion and exiled to Ceylon for nineteen years.

counterparties.name: Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: Effective sovereignty over its richest province, though the legal fiction of Ottoman Egypt was kept up until 1914 because it suited everyone.

counterparties.name: Egyptian taxpayers
counterparties.lost: Their revenue was pledged to European bondholders: by 1880 debt service took roughly half of all government income, and the occupation existed to keep it flowing.

people.name: Ahmad Urabi
people.role: Egyptian colonel who led the movement demanding a constitution and an end to European financial control; defeated at Tel el-Kebir and exiled

people.name: Garnet Wolseley
people.role: commanded the invasion and the night attack at Tel el-Kebir

people.name: Evelyn Baring, Lord Cromer
people.role: Consul-General from 1883 to 1907; ran Egypt without ever holding an Egyptian office

people.name: William Ewart Gladstone
people.role: prime minister who ordered an invasion he had spent his career arguing against

acquisitions.resistance: Urabi's army fought at Kafr el-Dawwar and Tel el-Kebir; about 2,000 Egyptian soldiers were killed at Tel el-Kebir against 57 British dead, in a battle that lasted under an hour.

cost.note: Egyptian dead at Tel el-Kebir are usually put at around 2,000, counted by the victors. British and Indian dead were 57. Casualties in the Alexandria bombardment and the riots that preceded it are not reliably known.

warrant.author: The British expeditionary force, in its own returns
warrant.work: British returns of the Egyptian campaign of 1882
warrant.supports: Egyptian dead at Tel el-Kebir are usually put at around 2,000, counted by the victors. British and Indian dead were 57. Casualties in the Alexandria bombardment and the riots that preceded it are not reliably known.
warrant.check: Campaign returns and casualty states are in the WO, ADM and CO series at The National Archives, Kew, and were printed in the London Gazette and in British Parliamentary Papers.
warrant.note: Fifty-seven British and Indian dead, counted man by man; about 2,000 Egyptian dead, counted by the victors.

contested.note: Why Britain invaded is one of the oldest arguments in imperial history. Robinson and Gallagher's Africa and the Victorians (1961) argued strategic panic about the route to India and a local crisis Britain did not control; others, following Hobson and Cain and Hopkins, emphasise the bondholders and the City of London. Both readings use the same cabinet papers.

evidence.author: Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher
evidence.work: Africa and the Victorians: The Official Mind of Imperialism
evidence.supports: The strategic and political reasoning behind the 1882 occupation.

acquisitions.how: When the Ottoman Empire joined Germany, Britain ended the legal fiction it had maintained for 32 years, declared a protectorate, deposed the Khedive Abbas Hilmi II while he was abroad, and put his uncle on the throne as Sultan.

counterparties.name: Ottoman Empire
counterparties.lost: Its last claim to Egypt, severed by proclamation while its army was fighting Britain in Sinai.

counterparties.name: Abbas Hilmi II
counterparties.lost: His throne, deposed in absentia and never allowed back.

counterparties.name: The Egyptian population
counterparties.lost: Martial law, censorship and requisitioning for four years; hundreds of thousands of Egyptians were conscripted into the Labour Corps and Camel Transport Corps, and their animals and grain were taken for the army.

instrument.name: Proclamation of the British Protectorate over Egypt

acquisitions.resistance: Wartime requisitioning and conscription produced the anger that exploded in March 1919, when the arrest of Saad Zaghlul set off a nationwide rising of students, peasants, railway workers and, for the first time in Egyptian politics, large demonstrations of women.

statusPeriods.label: The veiled protectorate
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the occupation default of 5 because British power was exercised through Egyptian ministers under nominal Ottoman sovereignty: Cromer gave orders as an adviser and Egyptians signed them.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Evelyn Baring, Lord Cromer, held no Egyptian office and ruled anyway: British advisers sat in every ministry, the army was commanded by a British sirdar, and any minister who refused was removed.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cairo, through the Khedive's ministers, under a British Consul-General
statusPeriods.franchise: A Legislative Council and General Assembly with limited elected membership existed from 1883 and could advise, not decide.
statusPeriods.note: Britain issued 66 separate declarations of its intention to withdraw from Egypt between 1882 and 1914. It withdrew in 1956.

statusPeriods.label: Formal protectorate and martial law
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above the protectorate default of 3: Egypt was under martial law and effectively under military government from 1914 to 1922, with the High Commissioner able to deport ministers.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British High Commissioner replaced the Consul-General, martial law ran from 1914 to 1923, and Egypt became the base and the supply depot for the campaigns in Gallipoli, Sinai and Palestine.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cairo, under a British High Commissioner
statusPeriods.franchise: Suspended in practice under martial law.

statusPeriods.label: Independent, with four reserved points
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above the informal-sphere default of 0: Britain reserved defence, imperial communications, the protection of foreigners and the Sudan to itself, kept a garrison, and in 1924 and 1942 used force to change Egyptian governments.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Egypt had a king, a constitution and elections; Britain had the army, the Canal, the Sudan and a High Commissioner who could and did dictate to the palace.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cairo, with a British High Commissioner and garrison
statusPeriods.franchise: Men over 21 voted for a parliament under the 1923 constitution. The Wafd won almost every free election and was dismissed by the king or the British almost every time.
statusPeriods.note: On 4 February 1942 British tanks surrounded the Abdeen Palace and the ambassador, Miles Lampson, forced King Farouk to appoint a government of British choice. Egyptian officers who watched it, including Gamal Abdel Nasser and Anwar Sadat, said afterwards that it decided them.

statusPeriods.label: The Suez Canal Zone base
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: By treaty Britain kept a garrison in a strip beside the canal; by 1951 that strip held about 80,000 troops, ten airfields, its own railway and a port, on Egyptian soil against the Egyptian government's wishes.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Ismailia and Fayid, under British military command
statusPeriods.franchise: Not applicable: this was a military base, and the Egyptian workers in it were employees, not citizens of it.
statusPeriods.note: Egypt abrogated the treaty in October 1951. A guerrilla campaign against the base followed, and on 25 January 1952 British troops attacked the police barracks at Ismailia, killing about 50 Egyptian policemen. Cairo burned the next day, and the monarchy fell six months later.

statusPeriods.label: Suez: seven weeks at Port Said
statusPeriods.gapReason: Between 13 June and 5 November 1956 there were no British forces in Egypt at all. The occupation had ended; the invasion of November was a new and separate act.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British and French paratroops and marines took Port Said and pushed about 40 kilometres down the canal, in collusion with an Israeli attack agreed in secret at Sevres, before a ceasefire stopped them 100 kilometres short of Suez.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Said, under Anglo-French military command
statusPeriods.franchise: Not applicable.

departures.how: After the revolution of 1919 and the failure of the Milner mission to buy the Wafd off, Britain unilaterally declared Egypt an independent kingdom while reserving four subjects to itself - which meant the parts that mattered.

led.name: Saad Zaghlul
led.role: leader of the Wafd; his deportation to Malta in March 1919 set off the revolution, and he became prime minister in 1924

led.name: Safiyya Zaghlul
led.role: his wife, called Mother of the Egyptians; helped organise the women's demonstrations of March 1919

led.name: Huda Sharawi
led.role: led the women's march of 16 March 1919 and founded the Egyptian Feminist Union in 1923

led.name: Alfred Milner
led.role: led the 1919-20 mission that concluded Britain could not hold Egypt by force, and was overruled

departures.movement: The Wafd

cost.note: British official figures record about 800 Egyptians killed in the 1919 revolution; Egyptian accounts give higher numbers. Around 30 British soldiers and officials were killed.

warrant.author: The British administration in Egypt, in its official figures
warrant.work: British official figures for the deaths of the 1919 revolution
warrant.supports: British official figures record about 800 Egyptians killed in the 1919 revolution; Egyptian accounts give higher numbers. Around 30 British soldiers and officials were killed.
warrant.check: FO 141 and FO 371 at The National Archives, Kew; summarised in the Milner mission report, Cmd. 1131 (1921).
warrant.note: Egyptian accounts give higher numbers, and there was no count that both sides accepted.

departures.borders: No borders moved. Britain kept the Sudan out of the deal entirely, which is why Egypt spent the next 34 years demanding unity of the Nile valley and got a separate Sudanese state instead.

instrument.name: Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence
instrument.note: Not a treaty: Britain wrote it alone after negotiations collapsed, and reserved imperial communications, defence, the protection of foreign interests and minorities, and the Sudan.

contested.note: Whether 1922 counts as independence at all is genuinely argued. Britain kept troops, the Canal, the Sudan and a veto; Egyptian nationalists called it a fraud at the time. This atlas records 1922 as a real but partial departure, and 1956 as the end.

departures.how: With Italy in Ethiopia and war coming, Britain and the Wafd signed a twenty-year alliance: British forces pulled out of Cairo, Alexandria and the Delta into a defined zone beside the canal, and Egypt entered the League of Nations.

led.name: Mustafa el-Nahas
led.role: Wafd leader and prime minister who signed the 1936 treaty and spent the next fifteen years being attacked for it

led.name: Miles Lampson
led.role: British High Commissioner, then ambassador; negotiated the treaty and in 1942 surrounded the king's palace with tanks

cost.note: No deaths in the treaty itself. It was signed by a Wafd government under pressure from the Italian invasion of Ethiopia, and Egyptian students burned copies of it within four years.

departures.borders: The treaty drew a line around the canal and called what was inside it a base: 10,000 British troops in peacetime, unlimited in war, on the territory of a sovereign ally.

instrument.name: Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936
instrument.note: Egypt abrogated it unilaterally in October 1951.

departures.how: Under the agreement Nasser's government signed in October 1954, the last British soldier walked out of the Canal Zone on 13 June 1956, ending 74 years of British troops in Egypt.

led.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser
led.role: Free Officer who took power after the 1952 coup and negotiated the British evacuation

led.name: Mohamed Naguib
led.role: figurehead leader of the 1952 revolution, removed by Nasser in 1954

led.name: Anthony Eden
led.role: British foreign secretary who agreed the withdrawal in 1954, and as prime minister invaded two years later

departures.movement: The Free Officers, after four years of guerrilla attacks on the base

cost.note: The campaign that forced the negotiation killed Egyptians and Britons: about 50 Egyptian police died at Ismailia on 25 January 1952, and British service deaths in the Canal Zone between 1951 and 1954 ran to several dozen.

departures.borders: Nothing moved on the map. What ended was a base larger than some countries, and with it Britain's ability to act in the Middle East without asking.

instrument.name: Anglo-Egyptian Agreement of 1954
instrument.note: Set a twenty-month timetable for withdrawal, with a right of re-entry if an outside power attacked an Arab state or Turkey.

departures.how: Britain, France and Israel attacked Egypt in secret collusion after Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company; a run on sterling, an American refusal to help and a United Nations emergency force forced Britain out within seven weeks.

led.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser
led.role: nationalised the canal company on 26 July 1956 and emerged from military defeat as the political victor of the Arab world

led.name: Anthony Eden
led.role: British prime minister; denied collusion with Israel in the House of Commons and resigned on 9 January 1957

led.name: Dwight Eisenhower
led.role: American president who refused to support sterling until Britain announced a withdrawal

led.name: Dag Hammarskjold
led.role: UN Secretary-General who assembled the first UN peacekeeping force to replace the invaders

departures.movement: Egyptian national resistance, backed by the United Nations General Assembly

cost.note: Egyptian deaths, military and civilian, are usually given between 1,000 and 3,000, with several hundred civilians killed at Port Said; there was no impartial count. British losses were 22 killed, French 10, Israeli about 190.

warrant.author: Three defence ministries for their own dead; contemporary estimates for Egypt’s
warrant.work: Casualty returns of the Suez–Sinai war of 1956
warrant.supports: Egyptian deaths, military and civilian, are usually given between 1,000 and 3,000, with several hundred civilians killed at Port Said; there was no impartial count. British losses were 22 killed, French 10, Israeli about 190.
warrant.check: Campaign returns and casualty states are in the WO, ADM and CO series at The National Archives, Kew, and were printed in the London Gazette and in British Parliamentary Papers.
warrant.note: Britain lost 22, France 10, Israel about 190, and each government counted its own precisely. Nobody counted Port Said.

departures.borders: No border changed, and that is the point: the first war Britain lost without losing a battle. The canal stayed Egyptian, and every remaining British colony learned that London could be stopped by Washington.

instrument.name: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 997 and the ceasefire of 6-7 November 1956
instrument.note: The withdrawal was completed on 22 December 1956, supervised by the United Nations Emergency Force.

evidence.author: Keith Kyle
evidence.work: Suez: Britain's End of Empire in the Middle East
evidence.supports: The Sevres protocol, the collusion and the collapse of the operation.

violence.note: Two moments define British force in Egypt: the hanging of four villagers after the Denshawai pigeon-shooting affair in 1906, and the shelling of the police barracks at Ismailia in January 1952.

toll.note: Denshawai killed one British officer of heatstroke and cost four Egyptian villagers their lives on the gallows, with others flogged; the disproportion is why the affair is remembered in Egypt and forgotten in Britain.

commonwealth.note: Egypt was never a colony in law and never joined the Commonwealth, which is a useful reminder that British power did not require British sovereignty.

consequences.economicLegacy: Britain bought 44 per cent of the Suez Canal Company in 1875 for just under 4 million pounds, borrowed from the Rothschilds; that stake, and the debt Egypt had run up building the canal, is the thread running from 1875 to 1956.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain kept the Sudan out of every Egyptian settlement from 1899 to 1956, and the result is that Egypt's southern border ends at a line drawn by British officials rather than at the Nile's headwaters.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Egypt's legal system stayed French in inspiration and its administration Ottoman in structure: 74 years of British control changed the government's language of business hardly at all.

peak.populationNote: 1917 census. Egypt was by far the most populous territory Britain controlled in Africa.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Egypt’s largest recorded population: 12,750,918 people, counted in 1917.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Keith Kyle
evidence.work: Suez: Britain's End of Empire in the Middle East
evidence.supports: The 1956 crisis, the collusion at Sevres and the withdrawal.

evidence.author: Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher
evidence.work: Africa and the Victorians: The Official Mind of Imperialism
evidence.supports: The 1882 occupation and its place in the partition of Africa.

evidence.author: Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot
evidence.work: A History of Egypt: From the Arab Conquest to the Present
evidence.supports: Egyptian politics under occupation, 1919, the Wafd and 1952.

contested.note: Egypt is the hardest case in this atlas for the question 'when did Britain take a place, and when did it leave?' It was occupied in 1882 but never annexed; a protectorate only from 1914 to 1922; formally independent from 1922 with British troops throughout; and finally free of them in 1956. Different textbooks give 1882, 1914, 1922 and 1956 as the key date. All four are defensible, which is why all four are recorded here.

pedagogy.hook: Between 1882 and 1914 Britain promised 66 separate times to leave Egypt. It left in 1956, and only after the Americans threatened to let the pound collapse.

misconception.belief: Egypt was a British colony.
misconception.correction: It never was. Egypt was legally Ottoman until 1914, a protectorate for eight years, and a nominally independent kingdom from 1922. Britain ran it anyway, through advisers, an army and a veto. Empire did not need a pink patch on the map: informal control by debt, garrison and gunboat covered more of the world than formal rule ever did.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Egypt shows both ends of the story. In 1882 Britain took a country to protect bondholders and a canal, and the occupation triggered the scramble for the rest of Africa. In 1956 the same canal showed that Britain could no longer act without American consent, and every colonial nationalist movement in the world noticed.

keyDates.what: Britain buys Egypt's 44 per cent stake in the Suez Canal Company
British troops enter Cairo after Tel el-Kebir
The 1919 revolution begins with Zaghlul's deportation
Britain declares Egypt independent, with four reserved subjects
The Anglo-Egyptian Treaty pulls British troops out of Cairo and the Delta into the Canal Zone
The last British troops leave the Canal Zone; Britain comes back by force at Port Said on 5 November and is out again by 22 December

territories.name: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan
territories.formalName: The Anglo-Egyptian Condominium of the Sudan
territories.subregion: The Nile from Wadi Halfa to the Uganda border

namesOverTime.name: Turkiyya
namesOverTime.note: Sudanese name for the Turco-Egyptian regime of Muhammad Ali and his successors, which British officers such as Charles Gordon served.

namesOverTime.name: The Mahdiyya
namesOverTime.note: The independent Islamic state founded by Muhammad Ahmad, the Mahdi, and ruled after his death by the Khalifa Abdallahi.

modernSuccessors.name: South Sudan
modernSuccessors.note: Seceded after a referendum in which 98.83 per cent voted to separate, along a line that was a British provincial boundary in 1956.

geoCoverage.label: The largest country in Africa
geoCoverage.change: Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army destroyed the Mahdist state at Omdurman; the southern provinces were not brought under real administration for another twenty-five years.

acquisitions.how: Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army, backed by a railway built across the desert as it advanced, destroyed the Khalifa's army outside Omdurman on 2 September 1898: about 11,000 Sudanese dead in five hours against 48 on Kitchener's side.

counterparties.name: The Mahdist state under the Khalifa Abdallahi
counterparties.lost: An independent state that had held the Sudan for thirteen years after driving out the Turco-Egyptian regime and killing Charles Gordon at Khartoum in 1885.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: The upper Nile. Marchand's expedition reached Fashoda in July 1898 and was faced down by Kitchener in September; France withdrew in November and gave up the Nile basin by declaration in March 1899.

counterparties.name: The southern Sudanese peoples
counterparties.lost: They had fought the Mahdists and now got a new conqueror: Dinka, Nuer and Azande country was subdued by patrols, punitive expeditions and, from the 1920s, aerial bombing.

people.name: Herbert Kitchener
people.role: sirdar of the Egyptian army; commanded the reconquest and had the Mahdi's tomb destroyed and his body thrown in the Nile

people.name: Abdallahi ibn Muhammad, the Khalifa
people.role: ruler of the Mahdist state; defeated at Omdurman and killed at Umm Diwaykarat in November 1899

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.role: took part in the 21st Lancers' charge at Omdurman and then published a book criticising Kitchener's treatment of the wounded

people.name: Jean-Baptiste Marchand
people.role: French commander who reached Fashoda first and was ordered home

acquisitions.resistance: The Ansar charged massed rifle and Maxim fire in the open. Churchill, who was there, wrote that it was not a battle but the destruction of an army, and that the wounded were left where they fell.

cost.note: About 11,000 Sudanese killed and 16,000 wounded at Omdurman on 2 September 1898, against 48 dead on Kitchener's side. The Sudanese figures are British estimates made by burial parties.

warrant.author: Kitchener’s burial parties, in the British returns from Omdurman
warrant.work: British despatches and returns of the Sudan campaign of 1896–98
warrant.supports: About 11,000 Sudanese killed and 16,000 wounded at Omdurman on 2 September 1898, against 48 dead on Kitchener's side. The Sudanese figures are British estimates made by burial parties.
warrant.check: Campaign returns, casualty states and despatches are in the WO, ADM and CO series at The National Archives, Kew; the despatches were printed in the London Gazette and the totals in British Parliamentary Papers.
warrant.note: The side doing the killing counted its own dead precisely and the other side’s by estimate. That asymmetry is in the figure, not just in the footnote.

evidence.author: Peter Malcolm Holt and Martin Daly
evidence.work: A History of the Sudan: From the Coming of Islam to the Present Day
evidence.supports: The Mahdiyya, the reconquest and the condominium.

acquisitions.how: Britain invented a legal form to keep the Sudan out of everyone else's hands: two flags, joint Anglo-Egyptian sovereignty, and a Governor-General appointed by Egypt on British nomination and removable only with British consent.

counterparties.name: Egypt
counterparties.lost: Everything but the flag and the bill. Egypt had conquered the Sudan in 1821 and paid most of the reconquest's cost; it got nominal co-sovereignty and no say.
counterparties.note: The unity of the Nile valley was an Egyptian demand in every negotiation from 1922 to 1953, and Britain refused it every time.

counterparties.name: The Ottoman Sultan
counterparties.lost: The last theoretical claim, since Egypt had held the Sudan as an Ottoman viceroyalty.

instrument.name: Anglo-Egyptian Condominium Agreement, 1899
instrument.note: Drafted in Cromer's office in Cairo. It gave the Governor-General supreme military and civil command, and excluded the Egyptian legal codes and the Ottoman capitulations.

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Kitchener governed by military order between Omdurman and the signing of the condominium agreement, while columns hunted the Khalifa in Kordofan.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Two flags, one government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Governor-General in Khartoum ruled through the Sudan Political Service - about 125 British officials, mostly Oxford and Cambridge sportsmen, for a territory of a million square miles - and through Egyptian army officers and Sudanese sheikhs beneath them.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.note: The service was nicknamed the country of blacks ruled by blues, after the sporting blues its recruits held. It was probably the thinnest administration in the empire: roughly one British official for every 80,000 people.

statusPeriods.label: British alone, after Stack's murder
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above the condominium default of 3: after 1924 the condominium was a fiction. Britain expelled the Egyptian army and officials and governed the Sudan by itself for nearly thirty years.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: When the Governor-General Lee Stack was assassinated in Cairo in November 1924, Britain used it to expel Egyptian troops and officials from the Sudan and to crush the Sudanese officers of the White Flag League who had mutinied in support of them.
statusPeriods.franchise: An Advisory Council for the Northern Sudan from 1944 and a Legislative Assembly from 1948, boycotted by the pro-Egyptian parties.
statusPeriods.note: In 1922 the Passports and Permits Ordinance, and from 1930 the formal Southern Policy, closed the three southern provinces to northern traders, banned Arabic and Islam from official use there and handed education to Christian missions. It was reversed in 1946, nine years before independence.

statusPeriods.label: Self-government and self-determination
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the condominium default of 3: from the 1953 agreement Sudanese ministers ran the government, with British and Egyptian governors reduced to supervising a three-year transition.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain and Egypt agreed to let Sudanese voters choose between union with Egypt and independence; Ismail al-Azhari's pro-Egyptian party won the election and then chose independence anyway.
statusPeriods.franchise: Elections to a House of Representatives in November-December 1953, on a wide but not universal male franchise.

departures.how: The Sudanese parliament declared independence unanimously on 19 December 1955 and both condominium powers accepted it; the two flags came down in Khartoum on 1 January 1956 and Sudan became the first British-ruled African territory to go.

led.name: Ismail al-Azhari
led.role: leader of the National Unionist Party, elected on a platform of union with Egypt, and the man who declared independence instead

led.name: Abd al-Rahman al-Mahdi
led.role: posthumous son of the Mahdi and patron of the Umma Party, which campaigned for independence from both Britain and Egypt

led.name: Ali Abd al-Latif
led.role: founder of the White Flag League, whose 1924 rising was the first modern Sudanese nationalist movement; he died in an Egyptian asylum

led.name: Robert Howe
led.role: the last British Governor-General, who handed over to a five-man Sudanese council

departures.movement: The Umma Party and the National Unionist Party

cost.note: Independence itself was peaceful in Khartoum. Four months earlier the Equatoria Corps mutinied at Torit on 18 August 1955 and several hundred people were killed, most of them northern officials and traders in the south; that mutiny began a civil war that ran, with one pause, until 2005.

departures.borders: Britain handed over a state stitched from a Muslim, Arabic-speaking north that it had governed since 1899 and a Nilotic and Equatorial south it had deliberately kept separate until 1946. The southern provincial boundary of 1956 is the international border of today.

instrument.name: Anglo-Egyptian Agreement on Self-Government and Self-Determination for the Sudan, 1953
instrument.note: It set a three-year timetable; the Sudanese parliament shortened it by declaring independence unilaterally, and both powers accepted.

partition.note: Sudan split in two on 9 July 2011, along the provincial line British administrators had drawn between north and south, after two civil wars and a referendum in which 98.83 per cent voted to separate.
partition.lineDrawnBy: British provincial boundaries of 1956, confirmed by the 2005 peace agreement and the 2011 referendum

violence.note: Sudan has been at war with itself for most of its independent life: 1955-1972, 1983-2005, Darfur from 2003, and again from 2023.

toll.note: The second civil war of 1983-2005 is usually estimated to have killed between 1.5 and 2 million people, mostly through war-induced famine and displacement. These are modelled estimates, not counts; the first war of 1955-72 is generally put at around 500,000.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 1956 boundary between the northern and southern provinces became an international border in 2011 with Abyei still disputed, and the Halayib triangle on the Red Sea remains contested with Egypt because Britain drew an administrative line in 1902 that did not match the treaty line of 1899.
consequences.economicLegacy: The Gezira scheme, opened in 1925 between the Blue and White Niles, was the largest irrigated cotton farm in the world under a single management, and tied Sudan's economy to one crop for half a century.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Britain governed the north in Arabic and the south in English through mission schools, and the language question was the first thing the two halves fought about after 1956.

peak.populationNote: The 1955-56 census, Sudan's first, taken in the year of independence.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan’s largest recorded population: 10,262,536 people, counted in 1956.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Peter Malcolm Holt and Martin Daly
evidence.work: A History of the Sudan: From the Coming of Islam to the Present Day
evidence.supports: The Mahdiyya, the reconquest, the condominium and independence.

evidence.author: Martin Daly
evidence.work: Empire on the Nile: The Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, 1898-1934
evidence.supports: How the condominium was governed and the Sudan Political Service.

evidence.author: Douglas H. Johnson
evidence.work: The Root Causes of Sudan's Civil Wars
evidence.supports: Southern Policy, the 1955 mutiny and the origins of the civil wars.

pedagogy.hook: About 125 British officials governed a million square miles of Sudan - roughly one man for every 80,000 people, in the largest country in Africa.

misconception.belief: The empire ruled its colonies with large numbers of British administrators.
misconception.correction: The Sudan Political Service never had more than about 400 members at once and usually far fewer, in a territory the size of western Europe. Rule worked because it recruited existing authority: sheikhs, clan and village heads, Egyptian officers and later Sudanese clerks. When those intermediaries withdrew their cooperation, as in 1924, the whole structure shook.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Sudan is the clearest case of a border made by an administrative decision. Britain governed north and south as separate countries from 1922 to 1946, then joined them for independence in 1956 with no time to build anything common. Two civil wars and roughly two million deaths later, the line it had drawn became a border in 2011.

Omdurman: about 11,000 Sudanese killed in five hours
