territories.name: The Southern Sudan
territories.formalName: The Southern Provinces of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan (Bahr al-Ghazal, Upper Nile, Equatoria)
territories.subregion: The Sudd, the Bahr al-Ghazal and Equatoria

modernSuccessors.name: South Sudan
modernSuccessors.note: The world's newest recognised state, and one of its poorest; civil war broke out within two and a half years of independence.

geoCoverage.label: Claimed on paper, patrolled on foot
geoCoverage.change: The condominium claimed the south from 1899, but real administration reached the Nuer and Dinka only in the 1920s, and some areas not until the 1930s.

geoCoverage.label: Closed districts under the Southern Policy
geoCoverage.change: The Passports and Permits Ordinance of 1922 sealed the southern provinces off from the north; from 1930 the Southern Policy governed them as a separate country.

geoCoverage.label: Reattached to the north
geoCoverage.change: Britain reversed the Southern Policy in 1946 and decided the south's future lay with the north, leaving nine years to undo twenty-four years of separation.

date.note: Administration was extended piecemeal by patrols over thirty years; there is no single date of conquest.

acquisitions.how: The condominium claimed the southern provinces in 1899 and then spent three decades taking them: punitive patrols against the Dinka and Azande, the killing of the Nuer prophet Guek Ngundeng in 1929, and RAF bombing of Nuer cattle camps in the Nuer Settlement of 1927-30.

counterparties.name: Nuer, Dinka, Shilluk and Azande peoples
counterparties.lost: Their independence, their cattle in punitive seizures, and their prophets and leaders. The Anuak, Nuer and Dinka fought government patrols for a generation.

counterparties.name: The Zande kingdom
counterparties.lost: Its cohesion: Britain moved Zande communities onto roadsides in the 1940s for a cotton scheme, breaking up settlements that had stood for generations.

people.name: Guek Ngundeng Bong
people.role: Nuer prophet who led resistance in the Lou Nuer country and was killed by a government patrol in 1929

people.name: E.E. Evans-Pritchard
people.role: anthropologist whose fieldwork among the Nuer in the 1930s was conducted in the aftermath of the government's punitive campaigns, a fact he acknowledged

acquisitions.resistance: The Nuer fought the administration for over twenty years; the government answered with the Nuer Settlement of 1927-30, in which aircraft bombed cattle camps and villages, and the prophet Guek was killed and his pyramid at Dengkur partly demolished.

cost.note: No reliable death toll exists for the southern patrols. Government reports counted casualties in individual operations and not across the campaign; the loss of cattle, which meant famine, was not counted at all.

evidence.author: Douglas H. Johnson
evidence.work: Nuer Prophets: A History of Prophecy from the Upper Nile in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
evidence.supports: The Nuer Settlement, Guek Ngundeng and the campaigns that broke Nuer resistance on the Upper Nile.

statusPeriods.label: Barely governed at all
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the condominium default of 3: for two decades British authority in the far south was a handful of district commissioners and an occasional patrol, with much of the Nuer and Anuak country outside any administration.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A few district commissioners, a company of troops and a steamer on the Nile; taxes were collected in cattle where they could be collected at all.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Khartoum, through provincial headquarters at Malakal, Wau and Mongalla
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: The Southern Policy: a country sealed off
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Northern traders needed permits to enter, Arabic was discouraged and Islam excluded from official use, English became the language of administration and Christian missions were given the schools, each denomination its own zone.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Khartoum, but deliberately separately from the north
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.note: The 1930 memorandum on Southern Policy set out the intention in its own words: to build up 'a series of self-contained racial or tribal units', with a view to eventual union with East Africa rather than with the Arab north.

statusPeriods.label: Reversal, and the Juba Conference
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Sudan Administration Conference of 1946 decided the south's future was with the north; at Juba in June 1947 southern chiefs were persuaded, in one day, to accept a single legislature in Khartoum.
statusPeriods.franchise: Southern representation in the 1948 Legislative Assembly and the 1953 parliament was small and largely nominated or indirectly chosen.
statusPeriods.note: By 1955 only 6 of about 800 senior posts vacated by the British in the Sudanisation of the civil service went to southerners. That figure is the immediate trigger of the Torit mutiny.

departures.how: The three southern provinces became part of an independent Sudan governed from Khartoum, having been administered as a separate country for the previous 24 years and given nine to prepare.

led.name: Buth Diu
led.role: one of the few southern politicians in the 1948 Legislative Assembly; argued for a federal constitution and was refused

led.name: Stanislaus Paysama
led.role: southern leader at the Juba Conference of 1947 who pressed for guarantees before union

led.name: James Robertson
led.role: Civil Secretary who reversed the Southern Policy in 1946 and later said the south had been given too little time

cost.note: The Torit mutiny of 18 August 1955 and the reprisals that followed killed several hundred people. Estimates vary and no impartial count was made; the mutiny is the start of a war that would kill vastly more.

departures.borders: The provincial line Britain drew between north and south became first a fault line and then, in 2011, an international border - with Abyei, the Nuba mountains and Blue Nile left on the northern side and still fighting about it.

instrument.name: Sudanisation of the administration and the 1953 self-government statute
instrument.note: Southern members voted for independence in December 1955 on a promise that federation would be considered. It never was.

contested.note: Historians argue about how far the Southern Policy caused Sudan's civil wars. Douglas Johnson stresses that the policy left the south without administrators, schools or a share of power, but insists the wars were driven by post-independence decisions in Khartoum as much as by British ones. Blaming the map alone lets later governments off.

partition.note: South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 after 98.83 per cent of voters chose separation, ending a struggle that had run since before Sudan's own independence.
partition.lineDrawnBy: The 1956 boundary of the southern provinces, as drawn by British administrators

violence.note: The south fought two long civil wars against Khartoum, from 1955 to 1972 and from 1983 to 2005, and then a civil war of its own from 2013.

toll.note: Combined estimates for both Sudanese civil wars, mostly deaths from war-induced famine and displacement rather than combat. These are demographic reconstructions with wide margins, not counts.

consequences.economicLegacy: Britain built almost nothing in the south: at independence in 1956 the three provinces had a few dozen kilometres of tarred road, three secondary schools and hardly any southern graduates, and most of the oil later found there straddles the 1956 line.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English, taught by missionaries under the Southern Policy, is the official language of South Sudan today - the direct legacy of a policy designed to keep the south out of the Arabic-speaking north.

peak.populationNote: The 1955-56 census recorded about 2.78 million people in the three southern provinces, roughly 27 per cent of Sudan's population; enumeration in the Sudd was acknowledged to be incomplete.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.work: The 1956 census of The Southern Sudan
populationWarrant.supports: The Southern Sudan’s largest recorded population: 2,783,000 people, counted in 1956.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Douglas H. Johnson
evidence.work: The Root Causes of Sudan's Civil Wars
evidence.supports: The Southern Policy, its reversal, the 1955 mutiny and the wars that followed.

evidence.author: Douglas H. Johnson
evidence.work: Nuer Prophets: A History of Prophecy from the Upper Nile in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries
evidence.supports: Resistance in the Upper Nile and the Nuer Settlement.

evidence.author: Martin Daly
evidence.work: Imperial Sudan: The Anglo-Egyptian Condominium 1934-1956
evidence.supports: The reversal of the Southern Policy, the Juba Conference and Sudanisation.

pedagogy.hook: For 24 years Britain ran southern Sudan as a separate country - permits to enter, English not Arabic, missions instead of mosques - then in 1946 changed its mind and gave it nine years to join the north.

misconception.belief: Sudan's civil wars are an ancient religious quarrel between Arab Muslims and African Christians.
misconception.correction: The division was administered into existence. Between 1922 and 1946 Britain sealed the three southern provinces off from the north, banned northern traders, replaced Arabic with English and handed the schools to Christian missions. When the policy was reversed, southerners got 6 of about 800 senior posts at independence. Old differences existed; the border between them was drawn by a government.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the atlas's sharpest lesson in how a colonial administrative decision becomes a border, a war and eventually a new country - and also in why blaming the map alone is too easy, since Khartoum's own choices after 1956 did the rest.

keyDates.what: The Passports and Permits Ordinance closes the south to northerners
The Southern Policy memorandum formalises separate government
Britain reverses the policy and ties the south to the north
The Juba Conference: southern chiefs accept a single legislature
The Torit mutiny: civil war begins before independence
South Sudan becomes independent

territories.name: Kenya
territories.subregion: The Rift Valley highlands, the Indian Ocean coast and the northern deserts

namesOverTime.name: Imperial British East Africa Company territory
Kenya
namesOverTime.note: From Kirinyaga, the Kikuyu name for the mountain; the British spelling and pronunciation stuck.

geoCoverage.label: Company concessions on the coast and inland
geoCoverage.change: The Imperial British East Africa Company held a royal charter, a lease of the Sultan of Zanzibar's coastal strip and almost no presence beyond the caravan routes.

geoCoverage.label: The East Africa Protectorate, then Kenya Colony
geoCoverage.change: The Foreign Office bought the bankrupt company out for 250,000 pounds and declared a protectorate, in order to protect the railway it was about to build to Lake Victoria.

acquisitions.how: Britain and Germany divided the Sultan of Zanzibar's mainland between themselves in 1886, and William Mackinnon's Imperial British East Africa Company took a royal charter over the northern half with a lease of the Sultan's coastal strip.

counterparties.name: Sultanate of Zanzibar under Barghash bin Said, and Khalifa bin Said after him
counterparties.lost: Its mainland empire. The Sultan's authority over the coast and the caravan trade to the lakes was partitioned by two European governments in 1886 in an agreement Barghash was told about, not consulted on; he died on 27 March 1888, and it was his successor Khalifa bin Said who leased the coastal strip to Mackinnon's company that October.

counterparties.name: Kikuyu, Kamba, Maasai, Nandi and Mijikenda peoples
counterparties.lost: Nothing yet in 1888 - the company barely reached them - and then everything: land, cattle, and the right to grow the crops that would earn money.

instrument.name: Royal Charter of the Imperial British East Africa Company

people.name: William Mackinnon
people.role: Glasgow shipowner who founded the company and lost his fortune on it

people.name: Barghash bin Said
people.role: Sultan of Zanzibar, whose mainland dominions were partitioned by the Anglo-German agreement of 1886

acquisitions.resistance: The company's caravans were resisted from the start: the Kamba and the Kikuyu of Dagoretti fought its stations, and the company never controlled more than a strip either side of the road to Uganda.

acquisitions.how: The company went broke, the Foreign Office bought it out for 250,000 pounds, and Britain declared the East Africa Protectorate - chiefly to protect the railway it was about to build from Mombasa to Lake Victoria.

counterparties.name: Imperial British East Africa Company
counterparties.lost: The territory, sold to the government it had been meant to save the expense of.

counterparties.name: The Nandi
counterparties.lost: Ten years of war and then their land. Their leader Koitalel arap Samoei was shot in 1905 by Richard Meinertzhagen at a meeting arranged under a flag of truce.
counterparties.note: The Nandi fought five British expeditions between 1895 and 1905, the longest resistance to the railway.

counterparties.name: The Maasai
counterparties.lost: Their best grazing. The Maasai agreements of 1904 and 1911 moved them twice, off the Rift Valley floor into the southern reserve; they sued in 1913 and the court held that it had no jurisdiction over an act of state.

instrument.name: Declaration of the East Africa Protectorate

people.name: Koitalel arap Samoei
people.role: orkoiyot of the Nandi; led resistance to the railway from 1895 and was killed at a truce meeting in October 1905

people.name: Mekatilili wa Menza
people.role: Giriama woman who led the coastal rising of 1913-14 against forced labour and conscription, and was twice deported

people.name: Hugh Cholmondeley, Lord Delamere
people.role: settler leader from 1903; the chief architect of the White Highlands

acquisitions.resistance: The Nandi fought for a decade, the Giriama rose in 1913-14 under Mekatilili wa Menza, and the Kikuyu of Murang'a and Kiambu fought a series of punitive expeditions between 1900 and 1906.

cost.note: The Uganda Railway, 931 kilometres from Mombasa to Kisumu, was built between 1896 and 1901 by about 32,000 indentured labourers brought from India. Around 2,500 died, and roughly 6,700 were invalided home.

evidence.author: Bethwell A. Ogot and William R. Ochieng
evidence.work: Decolonization and Independence in Kenya, 1940-93
evidence.supports: The protectorate, settler land policy and the road to independence.

acquisitions.how: The interior was annexed outright as Kenya Colony so that land could be sold freehold to European settlers; the ten-mile coastal strip stayed a protectorate, because it belonged to the Sultan of Zanzibar and Britain only leased it.

counterparties.name: The African population of the highlands
counterparties.lost: Annexation made all land Crown land. The Crown Lands Ordinance of 1915 offered Europeans 999-year leases, and by the 1930s roughly 7.5 million acres of the best land was reserved for about 2,000 European farms.

counterparties.name: Kenya's Indian population
counterparties.lost: Their claim to equal rights. Indians outnumbered Europeans and had built the railway and the towns; the 1923 Devonshire White Paper refused them a common roll and the Highlands.

instrument.name: Kenya (Annexation) Order in Council, 1920
instrument.note: Took effect 23 July 1920. The coastal strip remained legally the Sultan of Zanzibar's until 1963.

acquisitions.resistance: Harry Thuku's East African Association organised against the pass and the hut tax; when he was arrested on 14 March 1922 a crowd gathered outside Nairobi police station and at least 21 people were shot dead.

statusPeriods.label: The company on the road to Uganda
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A private company with a charter and no money ran stations along the caravan route, hired Swahili and Sudanese soldiers, and gave up after seven years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Mombasa, under the company's court in London
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Protectorate built around a railway
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Foreign Office, then the Colonial Office from 1905, governed through commissioners and punitive expeditions while the railway ran up the Rift and settlers followed it.
statusPeriods.franchise: European settlers got elected seats on the Legislative Council in 1920. Africans got none for another twenty-four years.

statusPeriods.label: Settler colony under the Devonshire formula
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor ruled with a Legislative Council dominated by European settlers, while a white-only Highlands policy, a hut tax payable in cash and a pass system pushed Kikuyu families into wage labour on farms carved out of land they had used.
statusPeriods.franchise: Elected European seats from 1920, Indian seats from 1927, the first nominated African member in 1944 and the first African elections in 1957.
statusPeriods.note: The Devonshire White Paper of July 1923 declared that Kenya was primarily an African territory and that African interests must be paramount. It was written to stop Indian claims to equality, and the settlers kept the Highlands anyway.

statusPeriods.label: State of emergency
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor Evelyn Baring declared an emergency, arrested the nationalist leadership overnight, and over eight years detained tens of thousands of Kikuyu without trial, hanged over a thousand people and moved about a million into guarded villages.
statusPeriods.franchise: The first African elections to the Legislative Council were held in March 1957, during the emergency, on a qualified franchise designed to keep the electorate small.
statusPeriods.note: The official death toll was 11,503 Mau Mau fighters killed, 1,090 hanged, 32 European civilians and about 1,800 African civilians killed by Mau Mau. Caroline Elkins argues the real figures are far higher; David Anderson and demographers dispute her upper estimates. What is not disputed is that Britain removed and later hid the files.

statusPeriods.label: Lancaster House and majority rule
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The emergency ended in January 1960 and the first Lancaster House conference the same month conceded an African majority in the legislature; Britain then spent three years arranging the transfer and buying out settler farms.
statusPeriods.franchise: A common roll with a broad franchise from 1961; KANU won the 1961 and 1963 elections.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government under Kenyatta
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Jomo Kenyatta, jailed as a Mau Mau manager in 1953 on evidence a judge was later shown to have been paid to accept, became prime minister of the colony that had jailed him.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage from May 1963.

departures.how: Kenya became independent eight years after the Mau Mau forests were cleared and three years after the emergency ended, under a leader Britain had imprisoned for seven years and then negotiated with.

led.name: Jomo Kenyatta
led.role: KANU leader; convicted in 1953 of managing Mau Mau, imprisoned and restricted until 1961, then prime minister and first president

led.name: Dedan Kimathi
led.role: field marshal of the Kenya Land and Freedom Army; captured on 21 October 1956 and hanged on 18 February 1957

led.name: Muthoni Kirima
led.role: field marshal of the forest fighters, one of the very few women to hold that rank, who stayed in the forest until 1963

led.name: Tom Mboya
led.role: trade unionist and KANU organiser who did much of the negotiating at Lancaster House; assassinated in 1969

led.name: Oginga Odinga
led.role: nationalist leader who insisted that no settlement was acceptable while Kenyatta was in prison

led.name: Evelyn Baring
led.role: governor who declared the emergency in 1952 and authorised the detention system

departures.movement: KANU, after the Kenya Land and Freedom Army (Mau Mau)

cost.note: Official figures for 1952-60: 11,503 Mau Mau killed, 1,090 hanged, 32 European settlers and about 1,800 African civilians killed by Mau Mau. Caroline Elkins's Britain's Gulag (2005) argues for far higher totals and mass unrecorded deaths; John Blacker's demographic study puts excess deaths at around 50,000, about half of them children. David Anderson accepts the system was vast and questions the highest numbers. The scale is disputed; the system is not.

warrant.author: David Anderson
warrant.work: Histories of the Hanged: Britain's Dirty War in Kenya and the End of Empire
warrant.supports: Official figures for 1952-60: 11,503 Mau Mau killed, 1,090 hanged, 32 European settlers and about 1,800 African civilians killed by Mau Mau.
warrant.check: Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 2005. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

warrant.author: Caroline Elkins
warrant.work: Britain's Gulag: The Brutal End of Empire in Kenya
warrant.supports: Official figures for 1952-60: 11,503 Mau Mau killed, 1,090 hanged, 32 European settlers and about 1,800 African civilians killed by Mau Mau.
warrant.check: Jonathan Cape, 2005. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

departures.borders: Two borders were unfinished business. The Sultan of Zanzibar gave up the ten-mile coastal strip in October 1963 so that Kenya would not begin life leasing its own coast; and the Somali-inhabited Northern Frontier District voted to join Somalia in a British-run referendum in 1962, was kept in Kenya anyway, and fought the Shifta War until 1967.

instrument.name: Kenya Independence Act 1963
instrument.note: The Act received royal assent on 3 December 1963. Section 1 ended the United Kingdom government's responsibility for governing Kenya from 12 December 1963.

evidence.author: David Anderson
evidence.work: Histories of the Hanged: Britain's Dirty War in Kenya and the End of Empire
evidence.supports: The emergency, the hangings and the courts.

evidence.author: Caroline Elkins
evidence.work: Britain's Gulag: The Brutal End of Empire in Kenya
evidence.supports: The detention camps and villagisation; her scale estimates are contested and the contest is recorded here.

evidence.author: UK Parliament
evidence.work: Kenya Independence Act 1963 (1963 c. 54)
evidence.supports: Royal assent on 3 December 1963; section 1 ended the United Kingdom government's responsibility for governing Kenya from 12 December 1963.

violence.note: Between 1952 and 1960 the colonial government detained tens of thousands of Kikuyu without trial, hanged 1,090 people, and moved about a million into guarded villages; in 2013 Britain paid 19.9 million pounds to 5,228 survivors and expressed regret.

toll.note: Ranges cover official counts at the low end and scholarly reconstructions at the high end. Elkins argues for a far larger death toll; Blacker's demographic estimate is about 50,000 excess deaths; Anderson works from the court records of the 1,090 hangings. Records were destroyed at independence and thousands more were removed to Britain and concealed until 2011.

warrant.author: David Anderson
warrant.work: Histories of the Hanged: Britain's Dirty War in Kenya and the End of Empire
warrant.supports: Elkins argues for a far larger death toll; Blacker's demographic estimate is about 50,000 excess deaths; Anderson works from the court records of the 1,090 hangings.
warrant.check: Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 2005. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

warrant.author: Caroline Elkins
warrant.work: Britain's Gulag: The Brutal End of Empire in Kenya
warrant.supports: Elkins argues for a far larger death toll; Blacker's demographic estimate is about 50,000 excess deaths; Anderson works from the court records of the 1,090 hangings.
warrant.check: Jonathan Cape, 2005. This atlas names it here because the figure’s own note names this historian.

populationTransfer.note: Villagisation moved roughly one million Kikuyu into 800 or more guarded villages between 1954 and 1956, and the Highlands policy had already pushed a quarter of a million people into squatting on European farms.

commonwealth.note: A realm for one year; a republic from 12 December 1964 with Kenyatta as president.

retainedTerritory.note: Nothing was retained, but Britain kept a training agreement: British Army units have trained in Kenya continuously since independence, an arrangement renewed by treaty and repeatedly controversial.

consequences.economicLegacy: Independence transferred the White Highlands by purchase, not seizure: British loans funded the Million-Acre Settlement Scheme, and much of the best land passed to a new Kenyan elite rather than to the landless who had fought for it.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain's Northern Frontier District was drawn to hold Somali pastoralists inside Kenya; they voted to leave in 1962, were kept, and the region has been marginal and militarised ever since.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English and Swahili are both official; the Kenyan legal system, the provincial administration and the chief's office all descend directly from colonial statutes.

peak.populationNote: 1962 census, the last colonial count: about 55,000 Europeans, 177,000 Asians and 8.4 million Africans.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Kenya’s largest recorded population: 8,636,263 people, counted in 1962.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: Kenya’s greatest extent, 582,646 km² in 1963: the 1 map unit this atlas draws it holding that year measure 588,320 km², within 1.0% of it.

areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: David Anderson
evidence.work: Histories of the Hanged: Britain's Dirty War in Kenya and the End of Empire
evidence.supports: The emergency, the courts and the hangings.

evidence.author: Caroline Elkins
evidence.work: Britain's Gulag: The Brutal End of Empire in Kenya
evidence.supports: The detention camps and villagisation.

evidence.author: Bethwell A. Ogot and William R. Ochieng
evidence.work: Decolonization and Independence in Kenya, 1940-93
evidence.supports: Kenyan politics, land and the transfer of power.

contested.note: The scale of the Mau Mau emergency is genuinely contested. Elkins argues for a very large number of unrecorded deaths; Blacker's demography suggests around 50,000 excess deaths; Anderson works from documented executions and detentions. The disagreement is about magnitude, not about whether mass detention, forced villagisation and systematic beatings happened - the British government conceded those in court in 2013.

pedagogy.hook: In 2011 the Foreign Office admitted it had been hiding 1,500 Kenyan colonial files in a warehouse at Hanslope Park; two years later Britain paid 19.9 million pounds to 5,228 people it had detained.

misconception.belief: Britain left its colonies peacefully once they were ready for independence.
misconception.correction: Kenya was fought over. Between 1952 and 1960 the colonial government hanged 1,090 people, held tens of thousands without trial in camps where beatings were routine, and moved about a million Kikuyu into guarded villages. It then destroyed or removed the records. Independence came in 1963 because holding Kenya had become impossible, not because Britain judged Kenyans ready.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Kenya is where the end of empire is best documented, because the documents were hidden and then found. It also shows the settler problem in miniature: 4,000 European farmers holding 7.5 million acres of the best land in a country of eight million people.

keyDates.what: The Uganda Railway reaches Lake Victoria; about 2,500 Indian labourers have died building it
At least 21 people shot outside Nairobi police station after Harry Thuku's arrest
The Devonshire White Paper declares African interests paramount, and changes nothing
State of emergency declared; Kenyatta and 180 others arrested
Eleven detainees beaten to death at Hola camp
Kenya becomes independent

territories.name: Uganda
territories.subregion: The kingdoms of the Great Lakes and the northern Nile districts

namesOverTime.name: Buganda

from.note: A rough marker; the kingdom is much older and its foundation date is not fixed.

namesOverTime.note: Uganda is the Swahili form of Buganda: the country is named after the one kingdom the British dealt with first.

geoCoverage.label: Buganda and the neighbouring kingdoms
geoCoverage.change: Frederick Lugard arrived in Buganda for the Imperial British East Africa Company in December 1890 and signed a treaty with Kabaka Mwanga II.

geoCoverage.label: Uganda after the boundary changes
geoCoverage.change: The Eastern Province, including the whole railway line to the coast, was transferred to the East Africa Protectorate in 1902, and Rudolf Province followed in 1926 - so Uganda's borders were set by railway administration, not by any local polity.

acquisitions.how: Frederick Lugard marched into Buganda for the Imperial British East Africa Company with a Maxim gun, signed a treaty with Kabaka Mwanga II, and then used the gun in 1892 to decide a civil war between Protestant and Catholic converts in the Protestants' favour.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of Buganda under Mwanga II
counterparties.lost: Control of its own succession and its own religious politics; Mwanga was deposed in 1897, fought a two-year war, and was captured and exiled to the Seychelles in 1899.

counterparties.name: The Catholic party of Buganda
counterparties.lost: The 1892 battle at Mengo and, with it, the chieftaincies. The winners of a fight decided by a British machine gun became the chiefs Britain then ruled through for seventy years.

instrument.name: Lugard's treaty with Kabaka Mwanga II

people.name: Mwanga II
people.role: Kabaka of Buganda; signed with Lugard, rebelled in 1897, was captured in 1899 and died in exile in the Seychelles

people.name: Frederick Lugard
people.role: company agent, later the theorist of indirect rule in The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa (1922)

people.name: Apolo Kagwa
people.role: katikkiro (chief minister) of Buganda for thirty years; co-signed the 1900 Agreement and became the most powerful African official in the protectorate

acquisitions.resistance: Bunyoro fought hardest: Omukama Kabalega resisted from 1893 to 1899, and Britain destroyed his kingdom, gave six of its counties to Buganda as a reward for help, and exiled him to the Seychelles with Mwanga.

evidence.author: A. Adu Boahen (ed.)
evidence.work: General History of Africa, Volume VII: Africa under Colonial Domination 1880-1935
evidence.supports: The imposition of colonial rule on the Great Lakes kingdoms.

acquisitions.how: The company could not pay for Uganda and proposed to withdraw; a campaign by missionary societies and the Uganda Company's supporters persuaded Gladstone's government to declare a protectorate over Buganda instead, extended to the neighbouring kingdoms by 1896.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of Bunyoro under Kabalega
counterparties.lost: Independence, half its territory and its king. Bunyoro was declared conquered territory, and the lost counties were only returned after a referendum in 1964.

counterparties.name: The kingdoms of Toro, Ankole and Busoga
counterparties.lost: External sovereignty, in exchange for agreements that guaranteed their kings, courts and land - the bargain that made indirect rule work here.

acquisitions.how: The Buganda Agreement fixed the terms of British rule for sixty years: Buganda kept its Kabaka, its parliament and its courts, and about 8,000 square miles of land was handed as private freehold to roughly a thousand chiefs and the royal family.

counterparties.name: The Baganda peasantry
counterparties.lost: Their customary land rights. Mailo tenure turned chiefs into landlords overnight and peasants into rent-paying tenants - a land system Uganda is still arguing about.

counterparties.name: The Kabaka's court
counterparties.lost: Sovereignty, in exchange for wealth and survival: Buganda became a privileged sub-government inside a protectorate, resented by everyone else in it.

instrument.name: Uganda Agreement (Buganda Agreement), 1900
instrument.note: Negotiated by Harry Johnston with Apolo Kagwa on behalf of the infant Kabaka Daudi Chwa. It is the model text of indirect rule in British Africa.

statusPeriods.label: The company in Buganda
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Lugard and a few dozen Sudanese soldiers held a fort on Kampala hill and took sides in Buganda's religious civil wars.
statusPeriods.franchise: None; Buganda's own Lukiiko continued to meet.

statusPeriods.label: Protectorate declared, kingdoms subdued
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A commissioner with Sudanese and Indian troops fought Bunyoro and Mwanga's rebellion, and put down a mutiny of his own Sudanese soldiers in 1897-98.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Indirect rule through the kingdoms
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: About 300 British officials supervised African kings, chiefs and courts that did the actual governing; cotton grown by African smallholders from 1903 paid for it, and no white settlement was permitted.
statusPeriods.franchise: A Legislative Council from 1921 with no African member until 1945. Buganda's Lukiiko was the real political forum.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1900 and 1920 sleeping sickness killed something like 250,000 people around the northern shore of Lake Victoria, and the administration forcibly cleared the lakeshore and islands to break the transmission cycle.

statusPeriods.label: After the Kabaka crisis
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor Andrew Cohen had deported Kabaka Mutesa II to London in 1953 for refusing to cooperate with a unitary Uganda; two years of Baganda protest and a court defeat forced Britain to bring him back and rewrite the constitution.
statusPeriods.franchise: Direct elections to the Legislative Council in 1958 and 1961, boycotted in Buganda in 1961.
statusPeriods.note: The Kabaka crisis of 1953-55 is a rare case of a colonial power losing in its own courts and having to reverse a deportation.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the protectorate default of 3: from March 1962 Milton Obote was prime minister with full internal self-government and Britain retained only external affairs and defence.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Obote's Uganda People's Congress governed in coalition with Buganda's royalist Kabaka Yekka party, an alliance that lasted four years and then broke violently.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage in the April 1962 election, except in Buganda, where the Lukiiko chose the members.

departures.how: Uganda became independent by agreement with no war and no settler problem to solve, under a federal constitution that gave Buganda special status and left everyone else resenting it.

led.name: Milton Obote
led.role: leader of the Uganda People's Congress and first prime minister; abolished the kingdoms in 1966 and was overthrown by Idi Amin in 1971

led.name: Edward Mutesa II
led.role: Kabaka of Buganda, deported by Britain in 1953 and returned in triumph in 1955; first president of Uganda and driven into exile by Obote in 1966

led.name: Benedicto Kiwanuka
led.role: first Ugandan chief minister and prime minister in 1961-62, leader of the Democratic Party; murdered under Amin in 1972

led.name: Ignatius Musaazi
led.role: founder of the Uganda National Congress in 1952, the country's first nationalist party

departures.movement: Uganda People's Congress and the Democratic Party

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. Uganda's violence came afterwards: the storming of the Kabaka's palace in 1966, Amin's dictatorship from 1971 to 1979, and the wars that followed.

departures.borders: Britain drew Uganda's borders to suit administration, not people: the Eastern Province went to Kenya in 1902 to keep the railway under one government, Rudolf Province followed in 1926, and the boundary in the north cut the Acholi and Karamojong communities in half.

violence.note: Britain's wars here were fought early: the destruction of Bunyoro from 1893 to 1899, the Sudanese mutiny of 1897, and punitive expeditions in the north into the 1920s.

toll.note: No reliable totals exist for the Bunyoro campaigns. Bunyoro's population is thought to have fallen sharply between 1890 and 1910 through war, famine and disease, but the figures are estimates from missionary and administrative reports.

commonwealth.note: A realm for one year; a republic from 1963 with Mutesa II as the first president.

consequences.borderLegacy: The lost counties taken from Bunyoro and given to Buganda in 1900 were returned only after a referendum in 1964, and the Uganda-Kenya boundary still follows the administrative convenience of a railway built in 1901.
consequences.economicLegacy: Cotton and later coffee were grown by African smallholders, not on settler estates - so Uganda kept its land and got a prosperous peasantry, and Asian traders and ginners took the profit until Amin expelled them in 1972.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The Buganda Agreement's mailo land tenure still governs much of central Uganda, and the kingdoms Britain ruled through, abolished in 1967, were restored in 1993.

peak.populationNote: 1959 census, the last before independence; about 11,000 Europeans and 72,000 Asians.

evidence.author: Frederick Lugard
evidence.work: The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa
evidence.supports: The doctrine of indirect rule, written by the man who began the British presence in Uganda.

evidence.author: Phares Mutibwa
evidence.work: Uganda since Independence: A Story of Unfulfilled Hopes
evidence.supports: The independence settlement, Buganda's special status and its collapse.

evidence.author: Holly Hanson
evidence.work: Landed Obligation: The Practice of Power in Buganda
evidence.supports: The 1900 Agreement, mailo land and the transformation of Buganda's chiefs into landlords.

pedagogy.hook: Britain ruled Uganda with about 300 officials for seven million people, because it governed through kings and chiefs who did the work - and paid them in land taken from their own peasants.

misconception.belief: All African colonies were the same: settlers took the land and Africans worked it.
misconception.correction: Uganda had almost no white settlement and no alienated highlands. Africans grew the cotton and coffee on their own land and kept the farms. That is why Uganda's independence was peaceful and Kenya's was not - and it is also why Uganda's conflicts after 1962 were between Ugandans, over a constitution Britain had designed to keep one kingdom happy.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Uganda is the textbook case of indirect rule: the 1900 Buganda Agreement is the document Lugard generalised into a doctrine that was then applied from Nigeria to Tanganyika. It also shows the cost - a state built on one privileged region cracked apart within four years of the British leaving.

territories.name: Zanzibar
territories.formalName: Sultanate of Zanzibar under British protection
territories.subregion: Unguja and Pemba, off the Swahili coast

from.note: A rough marker for the Swahili city-states of the island; the name is much older than any date we can fix.

namesOverTime.name: Sultanate of Zanzibar
namesOverTime.note: Separated from Oman on the death of Said bin Sultan, by an arbitration that Britain conducted.

namesOverTime.name: Zanzibar
namesOverTime.note: A semi-autonomous part of Tanzania with its own president, parliament and courts.

modernSuccessors.name: Tanzania
modernSuccessors.note: Zanzibar joined Tanganyika three months after its revolution; the union kept Zanzibar's own government and is still argued about on the islands.

geoCoverage.label: A sultanate run by a British consul
geoCoverage.change: From the 1873 anti-slave-trade treaty the Sultan governed and the British consul decided; the sultanate still claimed the coast from Somalia to Mozambique, which no unit on this map can show.

geoCoverage.label: The islands of Unguja and Pemba
geoCoverage.change: Britain declared a protectorate over the sultanate after trading its claims in Zanzibar with Germany for the North Sea island of Heligoland.

acquisitions.how: Sir Bartle Frere arrived with a squadron and a draft treaty; when Sultan Barghash refused to close the slave market, the Royal Navy prepared to blockade the island, and he signed within weeks.

counterparties.name: Sultan Barghash bin Said
counterparties.lost: The revenue of the largest slave market in East Africa, and any illusion that he could refuse a British request.
counterparties.note: The Anglican cathedral at Stone Town was built on the site of the market; its altar stands where the whipping post had been.

counterparties.name: The Omani and Swahili plantation economy
counterparties.lost: Its labour supply, though not at once: the clove plantations of Pemba ran on enslaved labour until legal status was abolished in 1897, and concubinage was not ended until 1909.

instrument.name: Anglo-Zanzibari Treaty for the Suppression of the Slave Trade, 1873

people.name: Barghash bin Said
people.role: Sultan of Zanzibar; closed the slave market under naval threat and spent his reign losing his mainland empire

people.name: Bartle Frere
people.role: British envoy who forced the 1873 treaty; six years later, as High Commissioner in South Africa, he started the Anglo-Zulu War

people.name: John Kirk
people.role: British consul from 1866 to 1887; the most powerful man in Zanzibar without ever holding office there

acquisitions.resistance: Barghash refused for six weeks and gave way only when told the island would be blockaded. Slave trading continued illegally for two decades, and the Navy's anti-slavery patrol seized ships and freed captives who were then indentured on Christian mission stations.

acquisitions.how: Britain and Germany swapped colonial claims in July 1890 - Germany recognised a British Zanzibar, Britain handed Germany the North Sea island of Heligoland - and four months later Britain declared the protectorate.

counterparties.name: Sultanate of Zanzibar
counterparties.lost: External sovereignty and the last of the mainland: the sultanate had ruled the Swahili coast from Somalia to Mozambique and was reduced to two islands and a ten-mile strip leased to Britain.

counterparties.name: German Empire
counterparties.lost: Nothing it minded losing: it took Heligoland, the coast of Tanganyika, and a free hand there.

instrument.name: Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty (Anglo-German Agreement), 1890
instrument.note: Britain's protectorate over Zanzibar was proclaimed on 4 November 1890 and accepted by France in a separate deal that gave France a free hand in Madagascar.

evidence.author: Abdul Sheriff
evidence.work: Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar: Integration of an East African Commercial Empire into the World Economy, 1770-1873
evidence.supports: The Zanzibari commercial empire and its subordination to British power.

statusPeriods.label: Ruled by a consul without an office
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above the informal-sphere default of 0: John Kirk, the British consul, chose ministers, vetoed treaties and settled successions in a state Britain did not own.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Sultan reigned and the British consul decided: Kirk arranged the succession of 1870 and 1888, controlled the customs concessions, and told the Sultan which Europeans to deal with.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Zanzibar Town, through the Sultan's court
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Protectorate under the Foreign Office
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British agent and consul-general supervised the Sultan's government; the Sultan kept his flag, his court and his revenues, and lost the ability to say no.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: After the shortest war in history
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above the protectorate default of 3: after 1896 Britain chose the sultan. The shelling of the palace settled the point that the succession required British approval.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: On 27 August 1896 the Royal Navy shelled the palace for about 38 minutes after Khalid bin Barghash seized the throne without British consent, killed roughly 500 of his supporters, and installed the sultan Britain wanted.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.note: Legal slavery was abolished in 1897, but only on application by each enslaved person to a court, with compensation to the owner. Freeing about 12,000 people took years; concubinage remained lawful until 1909.

statusPeriods.label: Colonial Office rule through the Sultan
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above the protectorate default of 3: a British Resident held executive power, appointed and dismissed ministers, and legislated by decree in the Sultan's name.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Resident under the Colonial Office ran the islands; the Sultan signed the decrees, Arab landowners held the clove plantations, Indian merchants financed them, and African labourers, most of them descended from enslaved people, cut the cloves.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Zanzibar Town, under a British Resident
statusPeriods.franchise: A Legislative Council from 1926, nominated; the first elections were held in 1957 on a restricted roll.

statusPeriods.label: Self-government, on a disputed count
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the protectorate default of 3: from June 1963 a Zanzibari cabinet governed internally while Britain kept external affairs for six months.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Zanzibar Nationalist Party and its allies formed a government having won 18 of 31 seats with 46 per cent of the vote, while the Afro-Shirazi Party won 54 per cent and 13 seats.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage in July 1963, on constituencies that gave the loser of the popular vote the government.

departures.how: Britain handed Zanzibar to a constitutional monarchy under Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah, on an electoral system that had given power to a party which had lost the popular vote; the government lasted 33 days.

led.name: Abeid Amani Karume
led.role: leader of the Afro-Shirazi Party, which won the popular vote and not the seats; president of Zanzibar after the revolution

led.name: Ali Muhsin al-Barwani
led.role: leader of the Zanzibar Nationalist Party and foreign minister of the 33-day independent state

led.name: Jamshid bin Abdullah
led.role: last Sultan of Zanzibar; deposed on 12 January 1964 and exiled to Britain, where he lived for 56 years

led.name: John Okello
led.role: Ugandan-born labourer who led the armed insurrection of 12 January 1964 and was pushed aside within weeks

departures.movement: Zanzibar Nationalist Party in government, Afro-Shirazi Party in opposition

cost.note: Independence itself was peaceful. The revolution five weeks later killed somewhere between about 2,000 and 20,000 people, overwhelmingly Arab and South Asian Zanzibaris; no count was made, the range in the literature is enormous, and the lower estimates come from contemporary diplomats while the higher come from later accounts.

departures.borders: Zanzibar had already given up its last mainland territory two months earlier: the ten-mile Kenyan coastal strip, leased to Britain since 1895, was ceded outright in October 1963 so that Kenya would not start life as the Sultan's tenant.

contested.note: The death toll of the January 1964 revolution is one of the least settled figures in modern African history. Estimates run from around 2,000 to 20,000. There was no functioning administration to count, foreign journalists were excluded, and both the new government and its enemies had reasons to shape the number.

slavery.note: Zanzibar was the hub of the East African slave trade: something like 600,000 to 800,000 captives passed through its market in the nineteenth century, and Britain both profited from the sultanate's trade and then shut the market down.

abolitionDate.note: The 1873 treaty closed the market and banned seaborne trading; it did not free anyone.

emancipationDate.note: The 1897 decree abolished the legal status of slavery, but freedom had to be claimed person by person in court, with compensation paid to owners.

toll.note: Estimates of captives passing through Zanzibar in the nineteenth century, reconstructed from customs records and naval reports; the trade was partly clandestine after 1873, so the figures are ranges, not counts.

warrant.note: The trade went clandestine after the 1873 treaty, so the later the year the worse the count — the opposite of what a reader expects.

commonwealth.note: Zanzibar's Commonwealth membership passed to Tanzania on the union of April 1964.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Anglo-German treaty of 1890 fixed the coast of East Africa in a single afternoon in Europe, and the Kenya-Tanzania border still runs where it was drawn, straight past Kilimanjaro.
consequences.economicLegacy: Cloves and the plantation society that grew them left Zanzibar with land owned by one community and worked by another - and that division, entrenched under a British protectorate, is what exploded in January 1964.

evidence.author: Abdul Sheriff
evidence.work: Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar: Integration of an East African Commercial Empire into the World Economy, 1770-1873
evidence.supports: The sultanate's economy and its subordination to Britain.

evidence.author: Jonathon Glassman
evidence.work: War of Words, War of Stones: Racial Thought and Violence in Colonial Zanzibar
evidence.supports: How colonial racial categories shaped the politics that ended in the 1964 revolution.

pedagogy.hook: The shortest war in recorded history lasted about 38 minutes: on 27 August 1896 the Royal Navy shelled the Sultan's palace at Zanzibar until the man Britain had not chosen ran away.

misconception.belief: Britain colonised East Africa to stop the slave trade.
misconception.correction: Britain did force Zanzibar to close its slave market in 1873, under naval threat, and the Navy's patrols freed thousands of captives. But legal slavery survived on the clove plantations of a British protectorate until 1897 and concubinage until 1909, and owners were compensated while the freed were not. Anti-slavery was a real motive, and it was also the argument that justified taking the coast.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Zanzibar shows empire at its most indirect: no annexation, no British governor for decades, just a consul who decided who would be sultan. It also shows what happens when a colonial power hardens social categories into racial ones and then leaves.

territories.name: Tanganyika
territories.subregion: From the Indian Ocean to the great lakes

namesOverTime.name: Deutsch-Ostafrika
namesOverTime.note: German East Africa also included Rwanda and Burundi, which went to Belgium in 1919.

namesOverTime.name: Tanganyika Territory
namesOverTime.note: Named after the lake, deliberately avoiding any German or dynastic name.

namesOverTime.name: Tanzania
namesOverTime.note: A word made from Tanganyika and Zanzibar.

geoCoverage.label: German East Africa without Ruanda-Urundi
geoCoverage.change: British and South African forces took Dar es Salaam in September 1916; Belgium kept Ruanda-Urundi in the west and Portugal took the Kionga triangle in the south.

acquisitions.how: Britain invaded German East Africa in 1914, was beaten at Tanga, brought in Indian, South African, Nigerian and Gold Coast troops, took Dar es Salaam in September 1916, and never caught Lettow-Vorbeck, who surrendered two weeks after the armistice.

counterparties.name: German Empire
counterparties.lost: Its largest colony, stripped by the Treaty of Versailles and divided between Britain, Belgium and Portugal.

counterparties.name: The peoples of German East Africa
counterparties.lost: More than either army. The British and German commands both conscripted porters: over a million Africans were pressed into carrier service across the East African campaign, and famine followed the armies everywhere they went.

people.name: Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck
people.role: German commander who kept about 300,000 Allied troops busy with a force never larger than 15,000, and surrendered undefeated on 25 November 1918

people.name: Jan Smuts
people.role: commanded the Allied forces in East Africa in 1916, with South African, Indian and African troops

people.name: Effendi Juma Mursal
people.role: one of the African askari of the German Schutztruppe whose loyalty and skill kept the campaign going for four years

acquisitions.resistance: The German force was overwhelmingly African: its askari fought for four years across four modern countries, and the campaign only ended when Germany surrendered in Europe.

cost.note: Recorded deaths among carriers recruited by the British in East Africa are usually given as about 95,000 to 100,000, and that figure counts only those on the British registers. Including African civilians who died in the famine and influenza that followed the armies, estimates for the region run to several hundred thousand. Nobody counted the porters properly, which is itself the point.

warrant.author: Edward Paice
warrant.work: Tip and Run: The Untold Tragedy of the Great War in Africa
warrant.supports: The East African campaign and the carrier corps death toll.
warrant.check: Weidenfeld and Nicolson

evidence.author: Edward Paice
evidence.work: Tip and Run: The Untold Tragedy of the Great War in Africa
evidence.supports: The East African campaign and the carrier corps death toll.

acquisitions.how: The League of Nations gave Britain a Class B mandate: it could administer Tanganyika but not annex it, not raise African troops for anything but local defence, and had to report to Geneva every year.

counterparties.name: German Empire
counterparties.lost: Title, by the Treaty of Versailles; German settlers were deported in 1920 and their estates sold, and many came back in the 1920s and bought them again.

counterparties.name: The people of Tanganyika
counterparties.lost: Nothing they had not already lost - and they gained something unusual: a legal status that said the territory could never be British property, which the nationalists used against Britain in the 1950s.

instrument.name: League of Nations mandate for East Africa (Tanganyika)
instrument.note: Confirmed by the League Council in July 1922, backdated in effect to the peace settlement of 1919.

acquisitions.how: The League's mandate became a United Nations trusteeship, which added something the mandate never had: a visiting mission every three years and a right for Tanganyikans to petition the UN directly.

counterparties.name: The British colonial administration
counterparties.lost: Privacy. Julius Nyerere addressed the UN Trusteeship Council in 1955 and 1956, and the visiting missions gave the nationalists an international platform no ordinary colony had.

instrument.name: United Nations Trusteeship Agreement for Tanganyika

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation and famine
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military administration governed a country stripped bare by four years of campaigning, where famine and the 1918 influenza pandemic killed far more people than the fighting had.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Dar es Salaam, under the military
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: League of Nations mandate
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Governor Donald Cameron introduced indirect rule on the Uganda and Nigerian model in 1926, governing through native authorities, and blocked settler demands to join Tanganyika to Kenya.
statusPeriods.franchise: A Legislative Council from 1926 with nominated Europeans and Asians; the first African members were nominated in 1945.
statusPeriods.note: Because Tanganyika was a mandate and not a colony, the campaign in the 1920s and 1930s to merge it into a settler-dominated East African federation with Kenya could always be answered with the mandate's terms. Legal status protected it.

statusPeriods.label: United Nations trust territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain administered under UN supervision, with visiting missions and a right of petition; the Groundnut Scheme of 1947-51 spent about 36 million pounds clearing bush for a crop that failed.
statusPeriods.franchise: Elections from 1958-59 on a common roll with parity of European, Asian and African seats; TANU won every seat it contested and swept the 1960 election with 70 of 71.
statusPeriods.note: The Groundnut Scheme is the standard example of late-colonial development done badly: 3.2 million acres planned, about 50,000 cleared, machinery destroyed by the bush, and the whole thing abandoned.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government under Nyerere
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the trusteeship default of 4: from May 1961 Julius Nyerere was chief minister with responsibility for everything except defence and external affairs.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nyerere formed a government seven months before independence, with the outgoing governor Richard Turnbull working openly to hand over quickly and quietly.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage from the August 1960 election.

departures.how: Tanganyika became independent without a shot fired, six years after Julius Nyerere first put the case to the United Nations Trusteeship Council in New York, and TANU won the last colonial election with 70 seats out of 71.

led.name: Julius Nyerere
led.role: founder of TANU in 1954, teacher, translator of Shakespeare into Swahili, first prime minister and president

led.name: Bibi Titi Mohamed
led.role: led TANU's women's section, which recruited more members than the men's; the single most effective organiser of the independence campaign

led.name: Rashidi Kawawa
led.role: trade unionist, TANU organiser and the country's second prime minister

led.name: Richard Turnbull
led.role: the last governor, who accelerated the transfer rather than resist it

departures.movement: Tanganyika African National Union (TANU)

cost.note: Nobody died. Tanganyika is the clearest counter-example to the idea that all decolonisation was violent - and it had no settled highlands to fight over, a legal status that forbade annexation, and a leader who insisted on the constitutional route.

departures.borders: Britain handed over German borders drawn in the 1880s and 1890s: the straight line past Kilimanjaro to Kenya, the Ruvuma to Mozambique, and a western frontier that separates Swahili-speaking Tanzania from Rwanda and Burundi, which Belgium took in 1919.

violence.note: The great killing in Tanganyika was German, not British: the Maji Maji war of 1905-07 and the scorched-earth famine that ended it destroyed the southern districts, and the First World War then emptied them again.

toll.note: Estimates of African deaths in the Maji Maji war of 1905-07, most from the famine German forces deliberately created, range from about 75,000 to 300,000. There was no census before or after; the range reflects competing reconstructions.

commonwealth.note: A realm for one year, then a republic from 9 December 1962; the union with Zanzibar followed on 26 April 1964.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Groundnut Scheme lost about 36 million pounds of British taxpayers' money between 1947 and 1951 and produced almost no groundnuts; it is the standard warning about development planned in London for soil nobody had tested.
consequences.borderLegacy: Tanzania's borders are German, its official language is Swahili rather than English, and its western neighbours Rwanda and Burundi are francophone because Belgium took them from the same colony in 1919.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Nyerere made Swahili the national language of government and school, so Tanzania is one of the few African states not governed in the coloniser's language.

peak.populationNote: 1957 census: about 22,000 Europeans and 76,000 Asians in a population of nearly nine million.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Tanganyika’s largest recorded population: 8,788,466 people, counted in 1957.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: John Iliffe
evidence.work: A Modern History of Tanganyika
evidence.supports: German rule, Maji Maji, the mandate, the trusteeship and independence.

evidence.author: Edward Paice
evidence.work: Tip and Run: The Untold Tragedy of the Great War in Africa
evidence.supports: The East African campaign and the carriers who died in it.

pedagogy.hook: More than a million Africans were forced to carry supplies for the armies in East Africa in the First World War, and at least 95,000 of them died - more than all the soldiers killed in the campaign.

misconception.belief: The First World War was a European war that the colonies watched from a distance.
misconception.correction: The longest campaign of the war was fought in East Africa, from 1914 until two weeks after the armistice. Britain and Germany both fought it with African soldiers and moved everything on African backs: over a million people were conscripted as carriers, and at least 95,000 of those on the British registers died. Famine followed the armies through what is now Tanzania, Kenya, Malawi and Mozambique.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Tanganyika shows that legal status mattered. Because it was a mandate and then a trust territory, it could not be annexed, could not be merged into settler Kenya, and had a platform at the UN. That is a large part of why it left the empire first in East Africa, and peacefully.

keyDates.what: The Maji Maji war against German rule begins; famine follows
British and South African forces take Dar es Salaam
Britain receives a League of Nations mandate
The mandate becomes a UN trusteeship
TANU founded; Nyerere petitions the UN the following year
Tanganyika becomes independent

territories.name: British Somaliland
territories.subregion: The Gulf of Aden coast and the Ogo highlands

namesOverTime.name: Somaliland
namesOverTime.note: A self-declared republic within the borders of the former British protectorate; no state recognises it.

modernSuccessors.name: Somalia
modernSuccessors.note: The protectorate united with Italian Somaliland five days after independence.

modernSuccessors.name: Somaliland (unrecognised)
modernSuccessors.note: Declared independence again in 1991 in exactly the old British borders; it holds elections and issues passports, and no country recognises it.

geoCoverage.label: Treaty protectorate on the Aden coast
geoCoverage.change: Britain signed protection treaties with Somali clans after Egypt withdrew its garrisons from the coast in 1884, chiefly to secure meat for the garrison at Aden.

geoCoverage.label: Retaken from Italy
geoCoverage.change: Italy conquered the protectorate in August 1940, the only British territory in Africa fully overrun by the Axis; British and Commonwealth forces retook it in March 1941.

acquisitions.how: When Egypt pulled its garrisons off the Somali coast to fight the Mahdi, Britain moved in from Aden and signed treaties of protection with the Habr Awal, Gadabuursi, Habr Toljaala and other clans, mostly to keep the meat supply for Aden out of French hands.

counterparties.name: Somali clans of the northern coast
counterparties.lost: Their external relations, in treaties they understood as alliances against Egypt and France. Britain read them as sovereignty and never conceded the difference.

counterparties.name: Egypt
counterparties.lost: The garrisons at Berbera and Zeila, abandoned in 1884 because the Mahdist revolt had swallowed the Sudan.

counterparties.name: France and Italy
counterparties.lost: The chance to take the whole Somali coast; they got Djibouti and the eastern coast instead, and the Somali people were divided into five.

instrument.name: Anglo-Somali protection treaties, 1884-1886
instrument.note: The protectorate was administered from Aden by the Government of India until 1898, then by the Foreign Office, then by the Colonial Office from 1905.

people.name: Frederick Mercer Hunter
people.role: Political Resident at Aden who negotiated the treaties to secure the meat supply

acquisitions.resistance: The treaties were not resisted; the protectorate was. From 1899 Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan's Dervish movement fought Britain, Italy and Ethiopia for twenty-one years.

evidence.author: I. M. Lewis
evidence.work: A Modern History of the Somali: Nation and State in the Horn of Africa
evidence.supports: The protection treaties, the Dervish wars and Somali unification.

acquisitions.how: Italy overran the protectorate in a fortnight in August 1940 and Britain evacuated to Aden; seven months later British, Indian and African troops landed at Berbera and took it back in four days.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of Italy
counterparties.lost: Its seven-month conquest, and then its own East African empire: Eritrea, Italian Somaliland and occupied Ethiopia all fell in 1941.

acquisitions.resistance: The 1940 defence was fought by a small force at Tug Argan against overwhelming odds; Britain then held the protectorate under military administration until 1948.

statusPeriods.label: Aden's butcher's shop, and twenty years of war
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A handful of officials on the coast, supplied from Aden, who for two decades could not travel inland: Britain withdrew to the coastal towns entirely between 1910 and 1914 and left the interior to the Dervishes.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Berbera, under Aden and the Government of India, then the Colonial Office from 1905
statusPeriods.franchise: None.
statusPeriods.note: Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, whom the British called the Mad Mullah, led the Dervish state from 1899. Four expeditions between 1900 and 1904 failed to beat him. In January 1920 the Royal Air Force bombed his fort at Taleh in the first use of air power to end a colonial war; he died of influenza in December.

statusPeriods.label: Peace, and almost no government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: After the Dervish defeat the protectorate was administered as cheaply as any territory in the empire: a few district commissioners, no railway, one secondary school opened in 1953.
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: British Military Administration
statusPeriods.gapReason: Italy conquered and occupied the protectorate from 19 August 1940 until 16 March 1941. For seven months it was not British at all - the only British African territory the Axis took whole.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A military administration ran the protectorate, and until 1948 it also governed Italian Somaliland and the Ethiopian Ogaden, so for seven years most Somalis were under one government for the only time in their history.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Hargeisa, under the East Africa Command
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

statusPeriods.label: Civil rule, and the loss of the Haud
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Civil administration returned under the Colonial Office, and Britain handed the Ogaden back to Ethiopia in 1948 and the Haud grazing lands in 1954 - pastures Somali herders had used for centuries and to which Britain had guaranteed them access in 1897.
statusPeriods.franchise: A Legislative Council with elected members from 1957; the first full elections were held in February 1960.
statusPeriods.note: The transfer of the Haud in 1954 caused the largest political mobilisation in the protectorate's history and made unification with Italian Somaliland the central Somali demand.

departures.how: British Somaliland became independent on 26 June 1960, was recognised by more than thirty states, and five days later voluntarily merged with Italian Somaliland to make the Somali Republic.

led.name: Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal
led.role: prime minister of the five-day independent state; later prime minister of Somalia and, from 1993, president of self-declared Somaliland

led.name: Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan
led.role: leader of the Dervish state from 1899 to 1920, the first and longest armed resistance to British rule in the Horn

led.name: Michael Hall
led.role: the last governor, who handed over on 26 June 1960

departures.movement: Somali National League and the Somali Youth League

cost.note: Independence itself was peaceful. The great cost had been paid earlier: estimates that as much as a third of the population of northern Somalia died in the wars, raids and famines between 1900 and 1920 are widely repeated but rest on very thin evidence and should be treated as an order of magnitude, not a count.

departures.borders: Britain left five Somalilands: British, Italian, French Djibouti, the Ethiopian Ogaden and the Northern Frontier District of Kenya. Two united in 1960; the five points of the star on Somalia's flag stand for all of them, and the attempt to gather them caused the Ogaden war of 1977.

instrument.name: Somaliland Order in Council, 1960, and the Union of Somaliland and Somalia Law
instrument.note: The two territories rushed the union through with two differently worded acts of union, a legal muddle that Somaliland cited in 1991.

contested.note: Whether the 1960 union was legally completed is disputed and politically live: the two territories passed different union laws and a proper Act of Union was only signed in January 1961, after a referendum that the north largely boycotted. Somaliland's case for its 1991 secession rests partly on that.

violence.note: Britain fought the Dervish state for twenty-one years, from 1899 to 1920, and finished it with aerial bombing - the first time air power was used to end a colonial war.

toll.note: No reliable count exists for the Dervish wars. The often-quoted claim that a third of northern Somalia's population died between 1900 and 1920 comes from colonial estimates of famine and warfare and cannot be verified.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Haud and Reserved Area, transferred to Ethiopia by Britain in 1954, and the Northern Frontier District, kept in Kenya in 1963, are the two British decisions behind Somali irredentism and the wars of 1963-67 and 1977-78.
consequences.economicLegacy: The protectorate existed to supply meat to Aden and Britain invested almost nothing else: at independence it had no railway, one secondary school and a hospital budget smaller than a single district's in Kenya.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Somali was not written officially until 1972; Britain administered in English and Arabic, and the northern legal system still differs from the south's because one was British and the other Italian.

peak.populationNote: Estimate at independence: no census was ever taken of a largely pastoral, mobile population, and the figure is a British administrative guess.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: British Somaliland’s largest recorded population: 640,000 people, counted in 1960.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: I. M. Lewis
evidence.work: A Modern History of the Somali: Nation and State in the Horn of Africa
evidence.supports: The protectorate, the Dervish wars, the Haud transfer and the 1960 union.

evidence.author: Mark Bradbury
evidence.work: Becoming Somaliland
evidence.supports: The 1960 union, its legal muddle and the 1991 re-declaration of independence.

contested.note: Two things here are unsettled: the human cost of the 1900-1920 Dervish wars, for which no serious count exists, and the legal status of the 1960 union, on which Somaliland's claim to statehood since 1991 partly depends.

pedagogy.hook: British Somaliland was independent for five days in 1960 - and used them to give its independence away, joining Italian Somaliland to make a single Somali state.

misconception.belief: African countries were held together by colonial borders that nobody wanted.
misconception.correction: Here the opposite happened. Somalis wanted one state and the colonial borders had given them five: British, Italian, French, Ethiopian and Kenyan. In 1960 two of the five joined voluntarily. The union then went badly for the north, and in 1991 Somaliland seceded back into exactly its old British boundaries - which no country has recognised.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Somaliland is the sharpest case of the empire dividing a people, and of what happens next. It also holds the first use of aerial bombing to finish a colonial war, at Taleh in January 1920 - a tactic Britain then took to Iraq and Afghanistan.

keyDates.what: Britain signs protection treaties on the Somali coast
Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan begins twenty-one years of war
The RAF bombs Taleh: air power ends a colonial war for the first time
Italy conquers the protectorate; Britain retakes it in March 1941
Britain transfers the Haud grazing lands to Ethiopia
Independence, and union with Italian Somaliland five days later

territories.name: Italian Somaliland (British administration)
territories.subregion: The Indian Ocean coast of the Horn, from Mogadishu to the Juba

namesOverTime.name: Trust Territory of Somaliland under Italian administration

geoCoverage.label: Conquered from Italy, held for nine years
geoCoverage.change: British, Indian, South African, Nigerian and Gold Coast troops took Mogadishu on 25 February 1941 in a campaign that destroyed Italy's East African empire in three months.

acquisitions.how: In a three-month campaign from Kenya and the Sudan, Commonwealth forces drove the Italians out of Somalia, Eritrea and Ethiopia; Mogadishu fell on 25 February 1941 and Britain governed it for the next nine years.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of Italy
counterparties.lost: Its whole East African empire in ninety days, and with it the colonies it had taken from 1889 and the Ethiopia it had invaded in 1935.

counterparties.name: Somali clans of the south
counterparties.lost: One occupier for another - though for the first time most Somalis were under a single administration, which is where the demand for one Somali state came from.

people.name: Alan Cunningham
people.role: commanded the advance from Kenya that took Mogadishu and then Addis Ababa

people.name: Abdulkadir Sakhawadin
people.role: a founder of the Somali Youth Club in Mogadishu in 1943, the first modern Somali political party, formed under the British administration

acquisitions.resistance: There was little Somali resistance to the British arrival, and considerable Somali political organisation under it: the Somali Youth Club, founded in Mogadishu in 1943, became the Somali Youth League and led the country to independence.

evidence.author: I. M. Lewis
evidence.work: A Modern History of the Somali: Nation and State in the Horn of Africa
evidence.supports: The British Military Administration, the Bevin plan and the return to Italy.

statusPeriods.label: British Military Administration
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An army administration governed under the law of belligerent occupation, kept Italian officials in post because it had no one else, and allowed Somali political parties for the first time.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Mogadishu, under the East Africa Command
statusPeriods.franchise: None, but political association was permitted: the Somali Youth League grew to tens of thousands of members under British rule.
statusPeriods.note: In 1946 the British foreign secretary Ernest Bevin proposed uniting British Somaliland, Italian Somaliland and the Ogaden into one trusteeship - a Greater Somalia. The other great powers rejected it, partly because it looked like Britain enlarging its own empire.

departures.how: The United Nations gave the territory back to Italy, the country that had colonised it and then lost a war, as a ten-year trusteeship with a fixed independence date - the only UN trust territory administered by a defeated power.

becomes.name: Trust Territory of Somaliland under Italian administration

led.name: Ernest Bevin
led.role: British foreign secretary who proposed a united Somalia in 1946 and was overruled

led.name: Haji Muhammad Hussein
led.role: Somali Youth League president who campaigned against the return of Italian rule and was jailed for it

departures.movement: Somali Youth League, which opposed the handover

cost.note: Rioting in Mogadishu on 11 January 1948, when a UN commission arrived to decide the territory's future, killed 51 Italians and at least 17 Somalis on contemporary counts; figures vary between sources.

departures.borders: The handover locked the Somali partition in place for another decade: the Ogaden had already gone back to Ethiopia in 1948, and Britain kept its own protectorate to the north, so the two halves that united in 1960 did so from different legal systems and different languages of government.

instrument.name: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 289 (IV)
instrument.note: Placed the territory under Italian trusteeship for ten years with independence guaranteed in 1960 - the only case where the UN set an independence date in advance.
