consequences.borderLegacy: Nine years of one administration over most Somalis, followed by their re-division, is the immediate origin of the Greater Somalia project and of the wars fought for it in 1963-67 and 1977-78.
consequences.economicLegacy: The Italian banana plantations on the Juba and Shabelle, worked partly by conscripted labour before 1941, survived the British administration intact and were returned to their owners.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Southern Somalia kept Italian law and Italian as a language of administration; the north kept English. Unifying two legal systems in 1960 was one of the first problems the Somali Republic could not solve.

peak.populationNote: Estimated at roughly 1.3 million in the late 1940s; no census was taken, and the population was largely pastoral and mobile.

evidence.author: I. M. Lewis
evidence.work: A Modern History of the Somali: Nation and State in the Horn of Africa
evidence.supports: The British administration, the Bevin plan, the 1948 riots and the Italian trusteeship.

contested.note: Britain's motives for the Bevin plan of 1946 are argued about: a genuine recognition that Somalis wanted one state, or a bid to keep the Horn under British control. The Soviet Union and the United States both suspected the second, which is why the plan died.

pedagogy.hook: For nine years after 1941 most Somalis lived under one government for the first and only time - a British army administration - and then the United Nations handed half of them back to Italy.

misconception.belief: The Second World War stopped colonial expansion; after 1945 empires only shrank.
misconception.correction: Britain ended the war administering Italian Somaliland, Eritrea, Libya and much of Ethiopia, and in 1946 proposed to keep the Somali territories together under its own trusteeship. The empire's largest territorial extent in Africa was in 1945, not 1919.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the United Nations making a border decision that shaped a country for good: handing a territory back to the colonial power that had lost it, and refusing the unification most of its people wanted.

keyDates.what: Commonwealth forces take Mogadishu from Italy
The Somali Youth Club is founded under British administration
Bevin proposes a united Somalia and is refused
The territory is returned to Italy as a UN trusteeship
Independence and union with the former British protectorate

territories.name: Eritrea (British administration)
territories.subregion: The Red Sea coast and the Asmara highlands

modernSuccessors.name: Eritrea
modernSuccessors.note: Independent after a thirty-year war against Ethiopia, which had annexed it in 1962 by dissolving the federation Britain handed it to.

geoCoverage.label: Eleven years of British administration
geoCoverage.change: British and Indian troops broke the Italian defence at Keren in March 1941 and entered Asmara on 1 April; Britain then governed Eritrea for eleven years while the powers argued about its future.

acquisitions.how: The hardest battle of the East African campaign was fought at Keren in February and March 1941; when the Italian line broke, British and Indian troops entered Asmara and took Italy's oldest colony.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of Italy
counterparties.lost: The colony it had held since 1890 and used as the base for invading Ethiopia in 1935.

counterparties.name: The people of Eritrea
counterparties.lost: One ruler for another, but they gained a decade of political organisation: Britain permitted parties, unions and newspapers, which Italy never had.

people.name: William Platt
people.role: commanded the advance from Sudan that won at Keren

people.name: Woldeab Woldemariam
people.role: Eritrean journalist and union organiser who campaigned for independence, survived seven assassination attempts and lived to see it in 1993

people.name: Sylvia Pankhurst
people.role: British campaigner who publicly attacked her own government for stripping Eritrea's industrial plant and selling it abroad

acquisitions.resistance: Eritrean askari fought on the Italian side at Keren and afterwards formed the core of the political movements. The Muslim League and the Unionist Party divided over whether Eritrea should be independent or join Ethiopia, and Britain never settled it.

cost.note: The battle of Keren cost the Commonwealth forces about 500 dead and several thousand wounded; Italian and Eritrean colonial losses were higher and are not reliably recorded.

evidence.author: Ruth Iyob
evidence.work: The Eritrean Struggle for Independence: Domination, Resistance, Nationalism, 1941-1993
evidence.supports: The British administration, the federation of 1952 and the origins of the independence war.

statusPeriods.label: Eleven years of army government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military administration governed under the law of occupation, allowed political parties and a free-ish press for the first time in Eritrean history, and dismantled and sold off much of the Italian industrial plant.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Asmara, under the East Africa Command and later the Foreign Office
statusPeriods.franchise: None, but political parties were legal from 1941 and an elected Eritrean assembly was established in 1952 as part of the federation.
statusPeriods.note: The removal of Eritrean industrial equipment - port cranes, railway stock, factory plant, sold to buyers as far away as Pakistan - was raised in the House of Commons and defended as the disposal of enemy property. Sylvia Pankhurst campaigned against it for years.

departures.how: Britain handed Eritrea to Ethiopia under a United Nations resolution that made it an autonomous unit federated with the Ethiopian crown, over the objection of the Eritreans who had wanted independence.

led.name: Haile Selassie
led.role: Emperor of Ethiopia, who wanted the Red Sea coast and got it, then abolished the federation in 1962

led.name: Ibrahim Sultan Ali
led.role: leader of the Muslim League, which campaigned for Eritrean independence at the United Nations

led.name: Tedla Bairu
led.role: Unionist leader who became the first chief executive of federated Eritrea and resigned four years later

departures.movement: The Muslim League and the Independence Bloc, which lost; the Unionist Party, which won

cost.note: The federation was handed over peacefully. Ethiopia dissolved it in November 1962 and the thirty-year war that followed is generally estimated to have killed between 150,000 and 250,000 people; there was no impartial count and the estimates are wide.

departures.borders: Britain had proposed in 1949 to partition Eritrea, giving the Muslim western lowlands to Sudan and the Christian highlands to Ethiopia. The Bevin-Sforza plan failed at the UN by one vote, and Eritrea survived whole - which is why it exists as a country today.

instrument.name: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 390 (V)
instrument.note: Federated Eritrea with Ethiopia under the Ethiopian crown from 15 September 1952, with its own constitution, flag, parliament and languages. Ethiopia abolished all of them by 1962.

contested.note: Whether the 1952 federation was a reasonable compromise or a handover of a people to a monarch is argued. American strategic interest in the Kagnew communications station at Asmara is documented in US papers and is generally thought to have weighed heavily; Britain's own preference had been partition.

violence.note: The federation Britain handed over was dissolved by Ethiopia in 1962, and Eritreans then fought for thirty years, one of the longest wars of independence in the twentieth century.

toll.note: Estimates for the Eritrean war of independence, 1961-1991. No agreed count exists; the range is drawn from the wider scholarly literature and is not precise.

consequences.economicLegacy: Eritrea entered the federation with much of its Italian-built industry dismantled and sold by the administering power, and Asmara's factories never recovered.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain's 1949 proposal to partition Eritrea between Sudan and Ethiopia was defeated at the UN by a single vote. Had it passed there would be no Eritrea, and Ethiopia would still have a coast.

peak.populationNote: A British administrative estimate of about a million; no census was taken.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Eritrea (British administration)’s largest recorded population: 1,000,000 people, counted in 1952.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: Eritrea (British administration)’s greatest extent, 121,100 km² in 1952: the 1 map unit this atlas draws it holding that year measure 122,972 km², within 1.5% of it.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Ruth Iyob
evidence.work: The Eritrean Struggle for Independence: Domination, Resistance, Nationalism, 1941-1993
evidence.supports: The British administration, the UN debate and the federation.

evidence.author: G.K.N. Trevaskis
evidence.work: Eritrea: A Colony in Transition, 1941-52
evidence.supports: The British administration written from inside it, by an official who served in it.

pedagogy.hook: A single vote at the United Nations in 1949 stopped Britain cutting Eritrea in half; that vote is why Eritrea is a country and Ethiopia has no coastline.

misconception.belief: Colonial borders were fixed once and for all at the Berlin Conference or the Scramble.
misconception.correction: Borders in the Horn were still being redrawn in the late 1940s, by the United Nations, on British proposals. Britain suggested splitting Eritrea between Sudan and Ethiopia in 1949; the plan failed by one vote. Eritrea was then federated to Ethiopia in 1952, annexed in 1962, and fought for thirty years to become independent in 1993.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Eritrea shows the empire in its last, least familiar phase: not conquering, but administering conquered enemy territory and then arguing at the UN about whose it should be. The decision taken there produced Africa's longest war of independence.

keyDates.what: British forces enter Asmara after the battle of Keren
The Bevin-Sforza plan to partition Eritrea fails at the UN by one vote
The UN votes to federate Eritrea with Ethiopia
Britain hands over; the federation begins
Ethiopia dissolves the federation and annexes Eritrea
Eritrea becomes independent after thirty years of war

territories.name: Ethiopia (British military administration)
territories.formalName: British military administration and reserved areas in Ethiopia, 1941-1954
territories.subregion: Addis Ababa, the Ogaden and the Haud

from.note: A rough marker for the Solomonic dynasty; Ethiopia's statehood long predates any European claim.

namesOverTime.name: Africa Orientale Italiana
namesOverTime.note: Italy's occupation, never recognised by most states and ended by a British-led campaign.

namesOverTime.name: Ethiopian Empire
namesOverTime.note: Haile Selassie re-entered Addis Ababa five years to the day after the Italians had taken it.

namesOverTime.name: Ethiopia
namesOverTime.note: The Derg deposed Haile Selassie on 12 September 1974 and abolished the monarchy the following March. The state has been the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia since 1995.

modernSuccessors.name: Ethiopia
modernSuccessors.note: Never a colony. Ethiopia is the only African state that defeated a European invasion and kept its independence, at Adwa in 1896.

geoCoverage.label: British advisers, British courts, British money
geoCoverage.change: British forces restored Haile Selassie in May 1941 and then kept extensive powers over his government: British advisers, British-run military courts, and control of the railway and the Ogaden.

geoCoverage.label: The Ogaden and the Reserved Area only
geoCoverage.change: The 1944 agreement returned most powers to Ethiopia, but Britain kept administering the Ogaden until 1948 and the Haud and Reserved Area until 1954.

acquisitions.how: British, Indian, Sudanese, Kenyan, Nigerian, South African and Ethiopian forces drove the Italians out in 1941 and put Haile Selassie back on his throne - then governed much of his country as Occupied Enemy Territory for three more years.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of Italy
counterparties.lost: The empire it had proclaimed in 1936, and the revenge it had sought since Ethiopia destroyed an Italian army at Adwa in 1896.

counterparties.name: The Ethiopian state under Haile Selassie
counterparties.lost: Not its independence, which was restored, but its freedom of action: the January 1942 agreement gave Britain the right to appoint advisers, control the currency and administer the Ogaden and a reserved zone along the railway.

counterparties.name: Somali communities of the Ogaden and the Haud
counterparties.lost: Their hope of joining a Somali state: Britain administered them for seven years, proposed uniting them with the Somalilands, then handed them to Ethiopia in 1948 and 1954.

people.name: Haile Selassie
people.role: Emperor, exiled to Bath in England from 1936, restored on 5 May 1941, and determined to get British advisers out again

people.name: Orde Wingate
people.role: commanded Gideon Force, the small Anglo-Sudanese-Ethiopian column that escorted the emperor back

people.name: Belay Zeleke
people.role: leader of the Ethiopian patriot resistance, the arbegnoch, who had fought the Italians for five years before the British arrived

acquisitions.resistance: Ethiopians had been fighting the Italians without help since 1936: the arbegnoch resistance kept large Italian garrisons tied down, and the 1941 campaign succeeded because they were already there.

contested.note: Whether Britain in 1941-44 was liberating an ally or trying to make Ethiopia a client is argued from the same documents. British officials drafted plans for a Greater Somalia that would have taken Ethiopian territory; Haile Selassie treated the advisers as an occupation to be ended, and ended it in three years.

evidence.author: Bahru Zewde
evidence.work: A History of Modern Ethiopia, 1855-1991
evidence.supports: The Italian occupation, the 1941 restoration and the Anglo-Ethiopian agreements.

statusPeriods.label: Occupied Enemy Territory Administration
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Below the occupation default of 5: the emperor had been restored and was governing, while a British administration ran finance, communications and the Somali areas alongside him.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military administration collected the revenue, ran the courts for non-Ethiopians and governed the Somali-inhabited east, while Haile Selassie rebuilt an Ethiopian government beside it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Addis Ababa, under the East Africa Command
statusPeriods.franchise: Not applicable: Ethiopia was an absolute monarchy before, during and after.

statusPeriods.label: The 1942 agreement: advisers and reserved areas
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Above the informal-sphere default of 0: under the first Anglo-Ethiopian agreement Britain appointed advisers to ministries, held military authority, subsidised the budget and administered the Ogaden.
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British advisers sat in Ethiopian ministries, a British general commanded, sterling was the currency, and the Ogaden and the railway corridor were run from outside the emperor's authority.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Addis Ababa, with a British Minister and advisers
statusPeriods.franchise: Not applicable.
statusPeriods.note: Haile Selassie spent the next three years playing Washington against London to get the agreement replaced; the American connection that resulted lasted until 1974.

statusPeriods.label: The Ogaden and the Reserved Area
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British military administration continued over the Somali-inhabited east of Ethiopia after the rest of the country was returned: the Ogaden until 1948, and the Haud and the Reserved Area until November 1954.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Jijiga and Hargeisa, under the administration of British Somaliland
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

departures.how: Haile Selassie negotiated the British advisers, the British courts and the British military authority out of his country in the second Anglo-Ethiopian agreement of December 1944, three and a half years after they arrived.

led.name: Haile Selassie
led.role: Emperor; used American diplomacy and the promise of a US airbase to prise Britain's advisers out

led.name: Robert Howe
led.role: British minister in Addis Ababa who negotiated the 1944 agreement

cost.note: No one died in the negotiation. It is one of the few places in this atlas where a sovereign African state used diplomacy to remove a British presence and succeeded within four years.

departures.borders: Nothing changed in 1944, but two large questions were left open: Britain went on administering the Ogaden until 1948 and the Haud and Reserved Area until 1954, and handed both to Ethiopia rather than to the Somalis living in them.

instrument.name: Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement, 1944
instrument.note: Ended the special position of British advisers and the reserved military authority; it did not return the Somali areas.

departures.how: Britain handed the Haud and the Reserved Area to Ethiopia in 1954, giving away grazing lands used by Somali herders from its own protectorate, to whom it had guaranteed access by treaty in 1897.

led.name: Haile Selassie
led.role: Emperor, who had pressed for the return of the Ogaden and the Haud since 1941

led.name: Michael Mariano
led.role: Somali leader from the British protectorate who led the delegation to London protesting at the transfer

cost.note: No deaths at the transfer. The cost was political and it was large: the Haud protests of 1954-55 built the movement that demanded Somali unification, and the grievance fed the Ogaden wars of 1963-64 and 1977-78.

departures.borders: The 1954 line is the border between Ethiopia and Somaliland today, and it runs through the pastures of people Britain had promised, in an 1897 treaty, would keep their grazing rights.

instrument.name: Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement on the Haud and the Reserved Area, 1954

consequences.borderLegacy: The Ogaden in 1948 and the Haud in 1954 were transferred to Ethiopia by British decision. Somalia went to war over them in 1977, and the Ethiopian-Somali border remains one of the most disputed in Africa.
consequences.economicLegacy: Britain's most durable contribution was the Maria Theresa dollar's replacement by an Ethiopian currency and a modern budget, both drawn up by British advisers in 1942-45.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Ethiopia kept its own law, its own church and its own script throughout. It is the control case: the African state Europe did not colonise, which shows how much of what happened elsewhere was not inevitable.

peak.populationNote: Ethiopia's population in the 1940s is usually estimated between 12 and 16 million; the first census was not taken until 1984.

evidence.author: Bahru Zewde
evidence.work: A History of Modern Ethiopia, 1855-1991
evidence.supports: The Italian occupation, the 1941 restoration and the Anglo-Ethiopian agreements of 1942 and 1944.

evidence.author: Christopher Clapham
evidence.work: Haile-Selassie's Government
evidence.supports: The structure of the imperial government and the removal of the British advisory position.

contested.note: Ethiopia was never a British colony and should not be shown as one. What is recorded here is a real British military administration from 1941, real British powers under the 1942 agreement, and British administration of the Somali-inhabited east until 1954. Historians differ on how far this amounted to control; Ethiopian historians generally treat it as an occupation the emperor outmanoeuvred.

pedagogy.hook: Britain put Haile Selassie back on his throne in 1941 and then spent three years trying to run his country for him; he negotiated the advisers out and kept the Ogaden question open for thirteen more.

misconception.belief: Every part of Africa was colonised by Europeans.
misconception.correction: Ethiopia destroyed an Italian invading army at Adwa in 1896 and stayed independent. Italy occupied it from 1936 to 1941, and a British-led campaign restored the emperor - after which Britain held wide powers for three years and administered the Ogaden until 1948. Ethiopia was invaded, occupied and pressured; it was never a colony, and it shows that colonisation was not inevitable.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Ethiopia is the control case for the whole atlas: an African state that beat a European army, kept its sovereignty, and then dealt with British power as a state rather than a subject. It is also where Britain quietly gave Somali grazing land to a neighbour and set off two wars.

keyDates.what: Ethiopia destroys an Italian army at Adwa and keeps its independence
Italy proclaims its occupation; the emperor goes into exile in England
Haile Selassie returns to Addis Ababa with Gideon Force
The first Anglo-Ethiopian agreement gives Britain advisers and reserved areas
The second agreement removes most British powers
Britain transfers the Haud to Ethiopia

territories.name: Libya (British administration)
territories.formalName: British Military Administration of Cyrenaica and Tripolitania
territories.subregion: Cyrenaica and Tripolitania; the Fezzan was French

namesOverTime.name: Libia Italiana
namesOverTime.note: Italy's conquest cost tens of thousands of Libyan lives, including about 40,000 who died in concentration camps in Cyrenaica between 1929 and 1934.

namesOverTime.name: British Military Administration, Cyrenaica and Tripolitania

geoCoverage.label: Cyrenaica and Tripolitania, not the Fezzan
geoCoverage.change: After the North African campaign Britain administered the two coastal provinces and France administered the Fezzan in the south-west, so Libya had two occupying powers for nine years.

acquisitions.how: The Eighth Army drove the Axis out of Cyrenaica in late 1942 and took Tripoli on 23 January 1943; Britain then governed the two coastal provinces under military administration for nearly nine years.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of Italy
counterparties.lost: The colony it had taken from the Ottomans in 1911 and held down by mass internment: about 100,000 Cyrenaicans were driven into camps in 1929-34 and roughly 40,000 died.

counterparties.name: The Sanusi order and the people of Cyrenaica
counterparties.lost: Nothing to Britain, and much to Italy before it. Sayyid Idris al-Sanusi had allied with Britain in 1940 and raised a Libyan Arab Force; Britain promised in 1942 that Cyrenaica would never return to Italian rule, and kept that promise.

people.name: Idris al-Sanusi
people.role: head of the Sanusi order, ally of Britain from 1940, and king of Libya from 1951 until Gaddafi overthrew him in 1969

people.name: Omar al-Mukhtar
people.role: leader of Cyrenaican resistance to Italy for twenty years; captured and hanged in front of 20,000 internees in 1931

people.name: Adrian Pelt
people.role: the United Nations commissioner who negotiated Libya's federal constitution and independence

acquisitions.resistance: Libyans had fought Italy for twenty years. Under the British administration the politics were about the future: Cyrenaica wanted the Sanusi emir, Tripolitania wanted a republic, and the argument was settled by a federal monarchy.

evidence.author: Dirk Vandewalle
evidence.work: A History of Modern Libya
evidence.supports: The British and French administrations, the UN process and independence in 1951.

statusPeriods.label: Caretaker government under the army
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British Military Administration ran Cyrenaica and Tripolitania on a shoestring under the law of belligerent occupation, keeping Italian municipal staff and Sanusi notables in place, while the powers argued at the United Nations about whose Libya should be.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Benghazi and Tripoli, under the army
statusPeriods.franchise: None until the UN-supervised constitutional process of 1950-51; the National Assembly of 1950 was appointed, not elected.
statusPeriods.note: In 1949 the Bevin-Sforza plan would have given Tripolitania back to Italy under trusteeship, Cyrenaica to Britain and the Fezzan to France. It failed at the UN by one vote - the same vote that saved Eritrea from partition - and the General Assembly then resolved that Libya should be independent by 1952.

departures.how: Libya became the first country to gain independence through the United Nations: the General Assembly resolved in 1949 that it should be independent, a UN commissioner ran the constitutional process, and King Idris proclaimed the kingdom on Christmas Eve 1951.

led.name: Idris I
led.role: first and only king of Libya; had led the Sanusi and allied with Britain in 1940

led.name: Bashir Sadawi
led.role: leader of the Tripolitanian National Congress, who wanted a unitary republic and was deported after the 1952 election

led.name: Adrian Pelt
led.role: UN commissioner who chaired the process that produced the federal constitution

departures.movement: The Sanusi movement in Cyrenaica and the National Congress in Tripolitania

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. The killing had been Italian: about 40,000 Cyrenaicans died in the internment camps of 1929-34, on estimates drawn from Italian records and later Libyan studies.

departures.borders: Libya kept the borders Italy had negotiated with France and Britain, including the Aouzou strip that Chad and Libya later fought over, and a southern frontier drawn across the Sahara with a ruler.

instrument.name: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 289 (IV) and the Libyan Constitution of 1951
instrument.note: The first state created by a UN decision. The Anglo-Libyan Treaty of 29 July 1953 then gave Britain military bases, notably RAF El Adem, until Gaddafi expelled British forces in 1970.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain kept military bases in independent Libya by treaty from 1953: RAF El Adem near Tobruk and an army garrison, in exchange for a subsidy that was most of Libya's budget until oil was found in 1959.

consequences.economicLegacy: Libya was among the poorest countries in the world in 1951, living on British and American base rents and scrap metal from the desert battlefields; oil was struck at Zelten in 1959 and changed everything within a decade.
consequences.borderLegacy: The Italian-drawn southern border left the Aouzou strip disputed with Chad; Libya occupied it in 1973 and the International Court of Justice awarded it to Chad in 1994.

peak.populationNote: The 1954 census, Libya's first, taken three years after independence.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Libya (British administration)’s largest recorded population: 1,091,830 people, counted in 1954.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Dirk Vandewalle
evidence.work: A History of Modern Libya
evidence.supports: The British and French administrations, the UN process and the 1951 kingdom.

evidence.author: E.E. Evans-Pritchard
evidence.work: The Sanusi of Cyrenaica
evidence.supports: The Sanusi order, Italian repression and the British alliance; written by an officer of the administration itself.

pedagogy.hook: Libya is the only country in the world that the United Nations voted into existence, and Britain governed it out of an army headquarters until the vote took effect.

misconception.belief: The British Empire stopped taking territory after the First World War.
misconception.correction: Britain administered Libya, Eritrea, Italian Somaliland and much of Ethiopia after 1941, held them for between three and eleven years, and in 1949 proposed keeping Cyrenaica as a British trusteeship. The proposal failed at the United Nations by one vote. The last British attempt at a new African territory was in 1949, not 1919.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Libya shows a new way of ending empire: not a nationalist party forcing Britain out, but a United Nations vote deciding the question over the administering power's head - and Britain then buying bases back by treaty two years later.

keyDates.what: Italy hangs Omar al-Mukhtar; about 40,000 Cyrenaicans had died in its camps
The Eighth Army takes Tripoli; British administration begins
The Bevin-Sforza plan fails at the UN by one vote
The UN resolves that Libya shall be independent by 1952
The Kingdom of Libya is proclaimed
Gaddafi's government expels British forces from El Adem

territories.name: Madagascar (British occupation)
territories.subregion: The great island of the western Indian Ocean

namesOverTime.name: Kingdom of Madagascar
namesOverTime.note: Britain signed treaties with the Merina monarchy in the 1810s and 1860s, then recognised French supremacy in 1890 in exchange for a free hand in Zanzibar.

modernSuccessors.name: Madagascar
modernSuccessors.note: Independent from France, not Britain; the British occupation of 1942 lasted seven months.

geoCoverage.label: The harbour at Diego Suarez
geoCoverage.change: Britain landed on 5 May 1942 and took the naval base at Diego Suarez two days later, to stop Japan using it after the Indian Ocean raid of April.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: A second campaign in September took Tananarive and the rest of the island; the Vichy governor surrendered on 6 November.

acquisitions.how: Britain invaded a French colony to keep it out of Japanese hands: Operation Ironclad landed near Diego Suarez on 5 May 1942, took the harbour in two days, and then spent five months conquering the rest of the island from Vichy French forces.

counterparties.name: Vichy France
counterparties.lost: The largest island in the Indian Ocean and its naval base, taken by a country France was not formally at war with.

counterparties.name: Malagasy people
counterparties.lost: Nothing they had not already lost to France in 1895-96, and they gained nothing: Britain handed the island to the Free French, whose forces crushed the Malagasy rising of 1947 with tens of thousands of deaths.

instrument.name: Armistice of Ambalavao
instrument.note: Governor-General Armand Leon Annet surrendered on 6 November 1942 after a five-month campaign.

people.name: Robert Sturges
people.role: commanded the Royal Marine and army landing force at Diego Suarez

people.name: Armand Leon Annet
people.role: Vichy governor-general who fought for five months and then surrendered

people.name: Paul Legentilhomme
people.role: Free French general who took over the administration in December 1942

acquisitions.resistance: The Vichy garrison, largely Malagasy and Senegalese troops under French officers, fought a long delaying campaign down the island; British and Vichy French casualties together were in the hundreds rather than the thousands.

cost.note: Reported totals vary. British and Commonwealth losses across the campaign are usually given as around 100 to 150 killed with several hundred wounded, and Vichy losses somewhat higher. No reliable figure exists for Malagasy civilian deaths.

statusPeriods.label: Seven months of British occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British military administration held the ports and the capital, kept the French colonial administration running underneath it, and handed the island over as soon as the Free French could take it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Diego Suarez and Tananarive, under the military
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

departures.how: Britain handed Madagascar to the Free French under General Legentilhomme in December 1942, having taken it to deny it to Japan and never intending to keep it.

led.name: Charles de Gaulle
led.role: Free French leader who insisted the island be handed to France and resented not being told of the invasion in advance

led.name: Paul Legentilhomme
led.role: took over as Free French High Commissioner

cost.note: No deaths at the handover. Five years later the French administration Britain had installed suppressed the Malagasy rising of 1947, in which estimates of Malagasy deaths range from about 11,000 to 90,000 - one of the worst repressions of the era, and almost unknown outside Madagascar.

departures.borders: No border changed. What changed was who held the harbour at Diego Suarez, which is why the operation happened at all.

instrument.name: Anglo-Free French agreement on the transfer of Madagascar

contested.note: Sources give slightly different dates for the transfer: Free French administration began in December 1942, and some accounts date the completion of the handover to early January 1943. This record uses 14 December 1942 and flags the uncertainty.

violence.note: The British campaign killed hundreds; the French administration Britain restored killed on a different scale in 1947, when the Malagasy rising was suppressed.

toll.note: Estimates for Malagasy deaths in the 1947 rising and its suppression by French forces. The low figure is a French official count, the high one an early Malagasy and French press estimate; most historians now work in the range 30,000 to 40,000.

warrant.author: The French colonial administration’s own count, against contemporary Malagasy and French press estimates
warrant.work: French official returns for the rising of 1947 and its suppression
warrant.supports: Estimates for Malagasy deaths in the 1947 rising and its suppression by French forces. The low figure is a French official count, the high one an early Malagasy and French press estimate; most historians now work in the range 30,000 to 40,000.
warrant.check: French colonial records are in the Archives nationales d’outre-mer, Aix-en-Provence.
warrant.note: The low figure is the administration’s; the high one the press of the time. Most historians now work between them, and the record says so.

consequences.borderLegacy: Britain gave up its treaty position in Madagascar in 1890 in exchange for a free hand in Zanzibar - a straight swap of two islands between two European governments, neither of which asked anyone who lived on them.

peak.populationNote: About 4 million in the 1940s, on French colonial estimates.

evidence.author: Ashley Jackson
evidence.work: The British Empire and the Second World War
evidence.supports: Operation Ironclad, its strategic purpose and the handover to the Free French.

pedagogy.hook: In May 1942 Britain invaded a French colony, fought the French for five months, took the whole island, and then gave it to a different set of French people.

misconception.belief: During the Second World War the Allies were on the same side everywhere.
misconception.correction: Britain fought Vichy French forces in Madagascar, Syria, Lebanon, Senegal and Iraq. Madagascar was invaded in May 1942 to stop Japan using the harbour at Diego Suarez after Japanese carriers had raided Ceylon; Britain then handed the island to the Free French in December, and the war between two Frances went on.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is a reminder that imperial maps in wartime moved for strategic reasons that had nothing to do with the people living there, and that empire could be exercised for seven months and then given away.

keyDates.what: Britain recognises French supremacy in Madagascar in exchange for Zanzibar
Operation Ironclad: British forces land near Diego Suarez
The Vichy governor-general surrenders
Britain hands the island to the Free French

territories.name: Bourbon (Reunion)
territories.formalName: British occupation of the Isle of Bourbon, 1810-1815
territories.subregion: The Mascarene Islands

namesOverTime.name: Isle of Bourbon
namesOverTime.note: Britain restored the pre-revolutionary name on capturing the island; France kept it until 1848.

namesOverTime.name: La Reunion
namesOverTime.note: An overseas department of France since 1946, and part of the European Union.

modernSuccessors.name: France (Reunion)
modernSuccessors.note: Never independent: an overseas department of France, so a French island in the Indian Ocean is inside the European Union.

geoCoverage.label: Five years in British hands
geoCoverage.change: A small British and Indian force took the island in July 1810 as a step towards capturing the French naval base on Mauritius.

acquisitions.how: British and Indian troops from the Bombay and Bengal establishments landed on 7 July 1810 and took the island next day, to close the French privateer bases that were preying on East India Company shipping.

counterparties.name: First French Empire
counterparties.lost: One of the two Mascarene bases from which French frigates and privateers had been taking Company ships for twenty years.

counterparties.name: The enslaved population of Bourbon
counterparties.lost: Nothing and gained nothing: Britain did not free them. Slavery continued under British occupation and then under restored French rule until France abolished it in 1848.

people.name: Josias Rowley
people.role: commanded the naval squadron in the Mascarene campaign

people.name: Henry Sheehy Keating
people.role: commanded the landing force at Saint-Denis

acquisitions.resistance: The French garrison capitulated after one day. The campaign's hard fighting came at Grand Port on Mauritius in August 1810, the only naval defeat Britain suffered in the Napoleonic Wars, before Mauritius fell in December.

statusPeriods.label: British military occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British governor ran the island with the existing French colonial officials and planters, kept the slave-based sugar and coffee economy exactly as it was, and waited for the peace settlement.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Saint-Denis, under the Governor of Mauritius and the East India Company
statusPeriods.franchise: None.

departures.how: Britain handed Bourbon back to France at the peace and kept Mauritius, 200 kilometres away, because Mauritius had Port Louis and Bourbon had no natural harbour at all.

becomes.name: Isle of Bourbon, restored to France

led.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
led.role: British foreign secretary who decided which conquests to keep at the peace settlement

led.name: Robert Farquhar
led.role: first British governor of Mauritius, who argued for keeping the harbour and letting the other island go

cost.note: No one died in the handover. The people who paid were the enslaved: Mauritius stayed British and its enslaved population was emancipated in 1835, while Bourbon returned to France and its enslaved people waited until 1848.

departures.borders: The Mascarenes were split by a decision taken in Europe: Britain kept Mauritius and its dependencies, including Rodrigues and the Chagos Archipelago, and France kept Bourbon. That division is why Mauritius speaks English in its courts and Reunion is part of the European Union.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris, 1814
instrument.note: Britain retained Mauritius, Tobago and Saint Lucia and returned Bourbon and most other French conquests; the actual handover of Bourbon took place in 1815.

contested.note: Accounts differ on the exact date the island was handed back, between December 1814 and April 1815, because the restoration was interrupted by Napoleon's return from Elba. The treaty date of 30 May 1814 is firm; the handover date is not, and is recorded here only as 1815.

slavery.note: Britain occupied a slave colony for five years and changed nothing about it: the sugar and coffee estates ran on enslaved labour throughout, and abolition came only in 1848, from France.

emancipationDate.note: France abolished slavery in its colonies in 1848; about 60,000 people were freed on Reunion.

toll.note: Roughly 60,000 people were freed on Reunion in 1848, on French colonial registers. Numbers enslaved during the British occupation of 1810-15 are not separately recorded.

warrant.author: The French colonial registers of emancipation
warrant.work: Registers of the 1848 emancipation on Bourbon (Réunion)
warrant.supports: Roughly 60,000 people were freed on Reunion in 1848, on French colonial registers. Numbers enslaved during the British occupation of 1810-15 are not separately recorded.
warrant.check: French colonial records are in the Archives nationales d’outre-mer, Aix-en-Provence.
warrant.note: The register counts the people freed in 1848, not the people enslaved during the British occupation of 1810–15, which nobody recorded separately.

consequences.borderLegacy: The 1814 settlement split the Mascarenes and put the Chagos Archipelago into British hands with Mauritius - the chain that leads directly to the Chagossians' expulsion in 1967-73 and to the argument over Diego Garcia today.

peak.populationNote: About 70,000 people in 1810, of whom the great majority were enslaved; the figures come from French colonial returns.

evidence.author: Christopher Alan Bayly
evidence.work: Imperial Meridian: The British Empire and the World 1780-1830
evidence.supports: The Napoleonic-war conquests and which of them Britain chose to keep in 1814-15.

pedagogy.hook: Britain captured two islands in the Indian Ocean in 1810, kept the one with a harbour and gave the other back - and that single choice is why one is now in the European Union.

misconception.belief: The empire kept everything it conquered.
misconception.correction: At the 1814-15 peace Britain handed back most of what it had taken: Bourbon, Java, Guadeloupe, Martinique, the Dutch East Indies. It kept the places with harbours, choke points and sugar: Mauritius, the Cape, Ceylon, Malta, Trinidad and Guyana. Empire was edited, not accumulated.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows how the empire chose. Bourbon had more people and better soil; Mauritius had Port Louis. Britain took the harbour, because the point of the Indian Ocean was the road to India.

keyDates.what: British and Indian troops take the Isle of Bourbon
Mauritius surrenders; Britain keeps it permanently
The Treaty of Paris returns Bourbon to France
France abolishes slavery; about 60,000 people are freed on Reunion

events.title: The Great Trek

date.note: A movement, not an event: parties left in waves over more than a decade, and there is no agreed start or end.

events.summary: Between 1835 and 1846 roughly 15,000 Dutch-speaking farmers and their servants left the Cape Colony with their wagons and herds, to get out from under British law and found republics of their own on the highveld.
events.significance: It exported the Cape frontier north and created the Boer republics that Britain then spent seventy years annexing, abandoning and reconquering; it is also the founding myth of Afrikaner nationalism and the reason South Africa's interior was settled by Europeans at all.

places.name: Blood River (Ncome)
places.note: Where about 470 Voortrekkers with a laager and guns beat a Zulu army on 16 December 1838.

people.name: Piet Retief
people.role: trekker leader who wrote the 1837 manifesto and was killed with his party by Dingane in February 1838

people.name: Dingane kaSenzangakhona
people.role: Zulu king who had Retief's party killed and was defeated at Blood River

people.name: Andries Pretorius
people.role: commanded the Voortrekker force at Blood River

people.name: Anna Steenkamp
people.role: Retief's niece, whose written account named emancipation and racial equality before the law as reasons for leaving

toll.note: Trekker deaths in the wars with the Zulu and Ndebele ran into the hundreds; African deaths were far higher and were not recorded. Blood River is the only engagement with a firm count on one side: three trekkers wounded, and about 3,000 Zulu dead by the trekkers' own estimate.

pedagogy.hook: One trekker wrote that they left the Cape because the British had put enslaved people on an equal footing with Christians, which was, she said, against the laws of God.

misconception.belief: The Voortrekkers left the Cape simply to find free land.
misconception.correction: Land and frontier insecurity mattered, but the trekkers said themselves why they went. Piet Retief's 1837 manifesto complains of losses at emancipation and of the vagrancy laws being relaxed; Anna Steenkamp's account names racial equality before the law as intolerable. The Great Trek is a reaction to British emancipation as well as a land movement.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Everything that follows in South African history - Natal, the republics, the diamond and gold wars, the Union - starts from this movement of about 15,000 people.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: A History of South Africa
evidence.supports: The trek, its causes and its consequences.

contested.note: The number of trekkers is an estimate, usually 12,000 to 15,000 excluding the African servants who went with them and are rarely counted. Whether emancipation or land hunger was the primary cause is a long-running argument in South African historiography.

events.title: The Xhosa cattle-killing

date.note: A movement that spread over about a year; the great disappointment came in February 1857.

events.summary: After eight frontier wars and a lung-sickness epidemic, the Xhosa prophecy of a girl named Nongqawuse said that killing every head of cattle and destroying the grain would raise the ancestors and sweep the British into the sea. Perhaps 400,000 cattle were killed.
events.significance: Roughly 40,000 people starved and about the same number left their land to look for work in the Cape Colony; Xhosa independence west of the Kei ended, and Governor George Grey used the crisis to take the emptied land and recruit the survivors as labour.

places.name: Gxarha River
places.note: Where Nongqawuse said she met the strangers who gave her the prophecy.

people.name: Nongqawuse
people.role: the young woman whose vision began the movement; she survived and lived out her life in the eastern Cape

people.name: Sarhili
people.role: paramount chief of the Gcaleka Xhosa, who believed the prophecy and ordered the killing in his own herds

people.name: George Grey
people.role: Cape governor who refused relief except in return for labour contracts, and settled Europeans on the vacated land

toll.note: Contemporary estimates put deaths from starvation at about 40,000 and the drop in the British Kaffraria population from 105,000 to under 27,000 between 1857 and 1858. The figures come from colonial censuses and are approximations.

pedagogy.hook: In one year the Xhosa killed around 400,000 of their own cattle because a prophecy promised the dead would rise and drive the British out.

misconception.belief: The cattle-killing was mass irrationality, and shows why African societies collapsed before Europeans.
misconception.correction: Lung sickness brought by imported cattle was already destroying the herds, and eight frontier wars had destroyed Xhosa political confidence. Historians such as Jeff Peires read the movement as a millenarian response to catastrophe, of a kind found in societies under extreme pressure everywhere, and note that Governor Grey used it to seize land and recruit labour rather than to relieve the famine.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is where Xhosa independence west of the Kei ended, and where the eastern Cape's supply of migrant labour to colonial farms began.

evidence.author: Jeff Peires
evidence.work: The Dead Will Arise: Nongqawuse and the Great Xhosa Cattle-Killing Movement of 1856-7
evidence.supports: The prophecy, the killing and the famine.

contested.note: Death and depopulation figures come from colonial officials with an interest in the outcome, and the debate over whether Grey encouraged the movement, exploited it, or merely failed to relieve it is unresolved.

events.title: Diamonds and gold: the mineral revolution

date.note: Two discoveries nineteen years apart: diamonds near the Vaal in 1867 and gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886.

events.summary: A diamond found near Hopetown in 1867 and the Witwatersrand gold reef found in 1886 turned southern Africa from a farming backwater into the most valuable ground in the empire, and drew in capital, railways and hundreds of thousands of migrant workers.
events.significance: Everything British in southern Africa after 1870 follows from this: the annexation of the diamond fields in 1871, Rhodes and the British South Africa Company, the Jameson Raid, the South African War, the migrant labour system and the compounds that later became the machinery of apartheid.

places.name: Kimberley
places.note: The Big Hole: about 22 million tonnes of earth moved by hand.

places.name: Johannesburg
places.note: Founded 1886; by 1899 the largest town in southern Africa.

people.name: Cecil Rhodes
people.role: consolidated the Kimberley claims into De Beers by 1888 and used the money to charter a company and take a country

people.name: George Harrison
people.role: prospector credited with the Witwatersrand discovery in 1886, who sold his claim for about ten pounds and vanished

people.name: Barney Barnato
people.role: Rhodes's rival at Kimberley, bought out in the 1888 amalgamation

pedagogy.hook: The man credited with finding the Witwatersrand gold reef sold his claim for about ten pounds and was never heard of again; the reef has since produced roughly a third of all the gold ever mined.

misconception.belief: Britain colonised southern Africa for farmland and living space.
misconception.correction: Before 1867 the interior was of little interest to London and Britain had just given two republics away. Diamonds and gold changed the arithmetic within twenty years: the Cape annexed the diamond fields in 1871, a company took Zimbabwe in 1890, and Britain fought a war costing 22,000 imperial lives for the goldfield in 1899.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains the timing of everything else: why the empire lost interest in the highveld in the 1850s and fought for it in the 1890s.

evidence.author: Robert V. Turrell
evidence.work: Capital and Labour on the Kimberley Diamond Fields, 1871-1890
evidence.supports: The diamond fields, amalgamation and the compound system.

evidence.author: Charles van Onselen
evidence.work: New Babylon, New Nineveh: Everyday Life on the Witwatersrand 1886-1914
evidence.supports: Johannesburg's growth and the society the goldfield made.

events.title: The Anglo-Zulu War
events.summary: Britain invaded the Zulu kingdom on an ultimatum designed to be refused. On 22 January a Zulu army destroyed a British column at Isandlwana; Britain sent reinforcements, burned the royal homestead at Ulundi in July, and cut the kingdom into thirteen pieces.
events.significance: The worst defeat regular British troops ever suffered at the hands of an African army, and the end of the last great independent kingdom in south-eastern Africa. The deliberate partition of Zululand afterwards produced eight years of civil war and made annexation easy.

places.name: Isandlwana
places.note: 22 January 1879: about 1,300 of the 1,800-strong British camp killed.

places.name: Rorke's Drift
places.note: Defended the same night by about 150 men; eleven Victoria Crosses were awarded, the most for a single action.

places.name: Ulundi
places.note: The royal homestead, burned on 4 July 1879.

people.name: Cetshwayo kaMpande
people.role: king of the Zulu; had tried for years to avoid war with Britain

people.name: Ntshingwayo kaMahole
people.role: commanded the Zulu army at Isandlwana

people.name: Henry Bartle Frere
people.role: High Commissioner who sent the ultimatum without London's authority, to force a South African confederation

people.name: Frederic Thesiger, 2nd Baron Chelmsford
people.role: British commander who divided his force and lost the camp

people.name: Garnet Wolseley
people.role: cut Zululand into thirteen chiefdoms designed to keep it divided

toll.note: British and colonial dead about 1,750, of whom roughly 1,300 fell at Isandlwana. Zulu dead are estimated at 8,000 to 12,000 across the war and were never counted; at Ulundi alone about 1,500 died in under an hour against Martini-Henry rifles and Gatling guns.

pedagogy.hook: On 22 January 1879 a Zulu army with spears and a few muskets destroyed a British camp of 1,800 men, and the same evening 150 men at a mission station held out for eleven Victoria Crosses.

misconception.belief: Rorke's Drift was the story of the Zulu war.
misconception.correction: Rorke's Drift was a successful defence of a supply depot by about 150 men on the night after Isandlwana, where roughly 1,300 had just been killed. Eleven Victoria Crosses were awarded, the most ever for one action, and historians have long noted that the honours helped bury the morning's disaster. The war's decisive facts are Isandlwana, Ulundi and the partition that followed.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the standard example of African military capability against a modern European army, and of what a colonial official could start on his own initiative before London could stop him.

evidence.author: John Laband
evidence.work: Rope of Sand: The Rise and Fall of the Zulu Kingdom in the Nineteenth Century
evidence.supports: The war, its causes and the kingdom's destruction.

evidence.author: Jeff Guy
evidence.work: The Destruction of the Zulu Kingdom: The Civil War in Zululand, 1879-1884
evidence.supports: The partition of Zululand and the civil wars it caused.

events.title: The Gun War in Basutoland
events.summary: The Cape Colony tried to disarm the Basotho under its Peace Preservation Act. They refused, fought a mounted war in their own mountains for seven months, and the Cape gave up and let them keep licensed guns.
events.significance: One of very few colonial disarmament campaigns that simply failed. It cost the Cape about three million pounds, ended Cape rule over Basutoland, and led Britain to take the territory back under direct imperial administration in 1884 - which is why Lesotho exists today rather than being part of South Africa.

places.name: Thaba Bosiu
places.note: Moshoeshoe's mountain stronghold, never taken by any attacker.

people.name: Lerotholi Letsie
people.role: Basotho chief who led the resistance to disarmament

people.name: Masupha
people.role: son of Moshoeshoe I and the most determined opponent of surrendering guns

people.name: Gordon Sprigg
people.role: Cape prime minister whose disarmament policy started the war and ended his ministry

toll.note: Casualties were low by colonial-war standards - probably a few hundred Basotho and Cape colonial dead together - because the Basotho fought mounted and avoided pitched battles. The Cape's cost, about three million pounds, is better documented than the deaths.

evidence.author: Elizabeth A. Eldredge
evidence.work: A South African Kingdom: The Pursuit of Security in Nineteenth-Century Lesotho
evidence.supports: The Gun War and its consequences for Basutoland's status.

contested.note: Neither the Basotho nor the Cape recorded the Gun War's casualties properly; the Cape's financial loss is the best-attested measure of its defeat.

events.title: The Rudd Concession
events.summary: Lobengula, king of the Ndebele, signed away all the minerals in his kingdom for 1,000 rifles, 100,000 rounds of ammunition, 100 pounds a month and an armed steamboat on the Zambezi. He repudiated the document within three months.
events.significance: Cecil Rhodes used the concession to obtain a royal charter in 1889 and the charter to occupy Zimbabwe in 1890. A piece of paper that a king said he had not understood became the legal basis for the conquest of a country and for ninety years of settler rule.

places.name: Bulawayo (old)
places.note: Lobengula's capital, where the concession was signed and which he burned in 1893.

people.name: Lobengula
people.role: king of the Ndebele; wrote to Queen Victoria in 1889 saying he had been deceived and withdrew his consent

people.name: Charles Rudd
people.role: Rhodes's partner, who negotiated and carried the document south

people.name: Charles Helm
people.role: missionary who interpreted, and assured Lobengula the concession would bring in no more than ten white men at a time

people.name: Cecil Rhodes
people.role: turned the concession into a royal charter within a year

pedagogy.hook: A whole country was taken on the strength of a document its king said he had been told covered one hole in the ground.

misconception.belief: African rulers signed treaties they did not understand because they were naive.
misconception.correction: Lobengula understood perfectly well that he was being pressed, which is why he sent envoys to Queen Victoria in 1889 and formally repudiated the concession. He was deceived about its contents by a missionary he trusted, and then found that repudiating it made no difference: the charter had already been granted in London.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest single example of how paper, not conquest, was the first instrument of the scramble - and of how little the paper mattered once the guns arrived.

evidence.author: Terence Ranger
evidence.work: Revolt in Southern Rhodesia 1896-7: A Study in African Resistance
evidence.supports: The concession, the occupation and the risings.

events.title: The British Ultimatum to Portugal
events.summary: Britain told Portugal to withdraw its forces from the Shire highlands and Mashonaland within 24 hours or face war. Portugal complied, abandoning its claim to a continuous belt of territory from Angola to Mozambique - the Pink Map.
events.significance: It settled who would take central Africa: Britain got Nyasaland and the Rhodesias and the route from the Cape towards Cairo, and Portugal kept two coasts and nothing between them. In Portugal the humiliation helped bring down the monarchy twenty years later.

people.name: Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, Lord Salisbury
people.role: prime minister and foreign secretary who sent the ultimatum

people.name: Alexandre de Serpa Pinto
people.role: Portuguese explorer whose expedition into the Shire highlands provoked it

people.name: Harry Johnston
people.role: British consul who pressed for the ultimatum and became the first commissioner of the resulting protectorate

evidence.author: John McCracken
evidence.work: A History of Malawi, 1859-1966
evidence.supports: The ultimatum and the founding of the protectorate.

pedagogy.hook: In January 1890 Britain gave Portugal, its oldest ally, 24 hours to get out of central Africa or be fought.

misconception.belief: The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 divided Africa among the European powers.
misconception.correction: Berlin set procedural rules, notably that a claim required effective occupation. The actual borders were fixed afterwards by dozens of bilateral deals and threats: the Anglo-German treaty of 1890, the Anglo-Portuguese treaty of 1891, the Anglo-French declaration of 1899, and ultimatums like this one.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the scramble being decided between European capitals by threat of war, years after the conference that supposedly settled it.

events.title: The Uganda Railway
events.summary: Britain built 931 kilometres of railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria at a cost of about 5.5 million pounds, using roughly 32,000 indentured labourers brought from British India. About 2,500 of them died.
events.significance: The railway is why Kenya became a settler colony: it had to be paid for, so land along it was offered to European farmers, and the White Highlands policy follows directly. It also planted the East African Asian community and fixed the Kenya-Uganda border where administration, not people, required it.

places.name: Tsavo
places.note: Where two lions killed a disputed number of workers in 1898 - contemporary claims of 135, the hunter's own later account fewer.

places.name: Kisumu
places.note: The railhead on Lake Victoria, reached 20 December 1901.

people.name: George Whitehouse
people.role: chief engineer of the railway

people.name: Koitalel arap Samoei
people.role: Nandi leader who fought the railway's advance for ten years and was killed at a truce meeting in 1905

people.name: Charles Eliot
people.role: commissioner who decided the railway could only pay if European farmers were settled along it

toll.note: About 2,500 of the roughly 32,000 indentured Indian workers died and around 6,700 were invalided home, on the railway administration's own returns. African deaths in the fighting along the route were not systematically counted.

pedagogy.hook: British newspapers called it the Lunatic Line: 931 kilometres of railway through a country with no known export, built by 32,000 workers shipped from India, 2,500 of whom died.

misconception.belief: The empire built railways to develop its colonies.
misconception.correction: This one was built for strategy - to reach Uganda and the headwaters of the Nile before anyone else - and then had to be made to pay. Commissioner Charles Eliot's answer was to settle European farmers on the highlands beside it. The railway did not develop Kenya; it created the settler problem that Kenya spent sixty years fighting about.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the single clearest chain of cause and effect in East African history: railway, settlers, land alienation, Mau Mau.

evidence.author: Charles Miller
evidence.work: The Lunatic Express: An Entertainment in Imperialism
evidence.supports: The building of the railway and its costs.

events.title: The Anglo-Zanzibar War
events.summary: When Khalid bin Barghash took the Zanzibar throne without British approval, three Royal Navy ships shelled the palace from about 09:02 until roughly 09:40. It is the shortest war in recorded history.
events.significance: It demonstrated what a protectorate meant in practice: the protected ruler could be chosen, and removed, by the protector. Britain installed its own candidate the same afternoon and no sultan afterwards was in any doubt about the arrangement.

places.name: Stone Town
places.note: The Beit al-Hukm palace was destroyed; the House of Wonders next to it survived.

people.name: Khalid bin Barghash
people.role: claimed the throne on his cousin's death and held it for about two days; escaped to the German consulate and was exiled

people.name: Hamoud bin Mohammed
people.role: installed by Britain the same day; abolished the legal status of slavery the following year

people.name: Basil Cave
people.role: British consul who issued the ultimatum

toll.note: About 500 of the Sultan's defenders and palace servants were killed or wounded; one British sailor was wounded. The figure is a British estimate and no Zanzibari count was made.

pedagogy.hook: The shortest war in history lasted about 38 minutes, killed roughly 500 people on one side and wounded one sailor on the other.

misconception.belief: A protectorate meant Britain protected a country while leaving it to govern itself.
misconception.correction: Zanzibar shows the reality. The Sultan kept his palace, his flag and his title; when one took the throne without British approval, the Royal Navy destroyed the palace in under an hour and Britain named the replacement. Protection meant a veto over everything that mattered, including who ruled.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the fastest, clearest demonstration in the whole atlas of what indirect rule actually rested on.

evidence.author: Abdul Sheriff
evidence.work: Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar: Integration of an East African Commercial Empire into the World Economy, 1770-1873
evidence.supports: The sultanate's subordination to British power.

events.title: The First Chimurenga and Umvukela
events.summary: Eighteen months after the company took their cattle and their land, the Ndebele rose in March 1896 and the Shona in June; together they killed about 450 settlers, a tenth of the white population, and held out for eighteen months.
events.significance: It was the largest armed challenge to company rule anywhere in British Africa, and it failed: Rhodes negotiated with the Ndebele in the Matopos and the Shona were broken by dynamite and starvation. The spirit mediums Nehanda and Kaguvi were hanged in 1898, and their names became the rallying cry of the war that won Zimbabwe in 1980.

places.name: Matopos Hills
places.note: Where Rhodes met the Ndebele leaders unarmed in August 1896 - and where he is buried.

people.name: Charwe Nyakasikana (Mbuya Nehanda)
people.role: medium of the Nehanda spirit; refused Christian conversion and was hanged on 27 April 1898

people.name: Gumboreshumba (Sekuru Kaguvi)
people.role: medium of the Kaguvi spirit; hanged with Nehanda

people.name: Mkwati
people.role: Ndebele-based religious leader who coordinated resistance across both risings

people.name: Cecil Rhodes
people.role: negotiated the Ndebele settlement in person in the Matopos, and refused any settlement with the Shona

toll.note: Terence Ranger's estimate of African deaths is about 8,000, against roughly 450 settlers killed. The African figure is a scholarly reconstruction; nobody counted at the time.

pedagogy.hook: Nehanda's last words, as recorded by the men who hanged her in 1898, were that her bones would rise - and in the 1970s the guerrilla armies fighting for Zimbabwe took her name.

misconception.belief: Colonial conquest was quickly accepted and resistance was sporadic and local.
misconception.correction: In Zimbabwe two peoples with different languages and a recent history of conflict rose together within six years of occupation, coordinated partly through religious mediums, and killed a tenth of the settler population. Britain won by using dynamite in the caves where families were sheltering and by starving out the rest.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Chimurenga means struggle, and Zimbabweans number their wars: 1896 is the first, 1972-79 the second. The naming is the argument.

evidence.author: Terence Ranger
evidence.work: Revolt in Southern Rhodesia 1896-7: A Study in African Resistance
evidence.supports: The risings, their coordination and their suppression.

evidence.author: David Beach
evidence.work: War and Politics in Zimbabwe, 1840-1900
evidence.supports: A revised account of the risings that questions how far they were centrally coordinated.

contested.note: Ranger argued in 1967 that spirit mediums coordinated the risings across both peoples. David Beach and others later argued the risings were more local and less unified than that. The disagreement matters because it is also an argument about whether 1896 was the first stage of a national movement.

events.title: The Jameson Raid
events.summary: About 500 men of the British South Africa Company's police rode into the Transvaal to trigger a rising of foreign miners in Johannesburg against Kruger's government. The rising did not happen and the raiders surrendered at Doornkop after four days.
events.significance: It was a private invasion of a sovereign state, organised with the knowledge of the Colonial Secretary and financed by mining capital. It destroyed trust between Britain and the Transvaal, made Kruger's rearmament programme politically unstoppable, and put the two countries on the road to the war of 1899.

places.name: Doornkop
places.note: Where the raiders surrendered on 2 January 1896.

people.name: Leander Starr Jameson
people.role: led the raid; convicted in London under the Foreign Enlistment Act and served four months

people.name: Cecil Rhodes
people.role: organised and financed it; resigned as prime minister of the Cape in January 1896

people.name: Joseph Chamberlain
people.role: Colonial Secretary; a parliamentary inquiry cleared him in 1897 on evidence that was, at best, incomplete

people.name: Paul Kruger
people.role: president of the Transvaal, who let the raiders be tried in Britain and used the raid to buy German rifles

toll.note: About 30 raiders and roughly the same number of Transvaal burghers were killed. The political cost was out of all proportion to the casualties.

pedagogy.hook: In 1895 a private company's police force invaded a neighbouring country, and the British Colonial Secretary knew about it beforehand.

misconception.belief: Empire was run by governments and armies.
misconception.correction: The Jameson Raid was mounted by a chartered company, financed by mine owners, and launched from a strip of Bechuanaland handed to the company for the purpose. The parliamentary inquiry that followed became known as the Lying-in-State at Westminster, because the telegrams that would have shown ministerial knowledge were not produced.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the fusion of private capital and public power that ran the scramble, and it is the immediate cause of the South African War.

evidence.author: Thomas Pakenham
evidence.work: The Boer War
evidence.supports: The raid, the inquiry and the road to war.

contested.note: How much Joseph Chamberlain knew, and when, is still argued. The 1897 select committee cleared him; the missing telegrams and later archival work have persuaded most historians that he knew a great deal.

events.title: The Battle of Omdurman
events.summary: Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army of about 25,000, with gunboats, Maxim guns and modern artillery, destroyed the Khalifa's army of roughly 50,000 outside Omdurman in about five hours: some 11,000 Sudanese killed against 48 on Kitchener's side.
events.significance: It ended the Mahdist state and returned the Sudan to Anglo-Egyptian rule for 58 years. It is also the standard example of the nineteenth-century firepower gap - and of what Winston Churchill, who was present, called not a battle but the destruction of an army.

places.name: Omdurman
places.note: The Mahdist capital; the Mahdi's tomb was shelled and his body thrown in the Nile afterwards.

people.name: Herbert Kitchener
people.role: sirdar of the Egyptian army; built a railway across the Nubian desert to bring his army south

people.name: Abdallahi ibn Muhammad, the Khalifa
people.role: ruler of the Mahdist state; escaped the field and was killed the following year

people.name: Osman Digna
people.role: Mahdist commander who had beaten British forces in the eastern Sudan in the 1880s

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.role: rode in the 21st Lancers' charge and then published The River War, criticising the treatment of the wounded and the desecration of the Mahdi's tomb

toll.note: About 11,000 Sudanese killed and some 16,000 wounded, against 48 dead on Kitchener's side. The Sudanese numbers are British burial-party estimates; the wounded were largely left on the field, which is what Churchill objected to.

pedagogy.hook: In five hours at Omdurman about 11,000 Sudanese were killed and 48 of Kitchener's men; a 23-year-old cavalry officer named Winston Churchill rode in the charge and then wrote a book attacking his own commander.

misconception.belief: European conquest of Africa succeeded because of better organisation and civilisation.
misconception.correction: At Omdurman the difference was Maxim guns, howitzers, gunboats on the Nile and a purpose-built railway. The Ansar were brave, disciplined and numerous, and they were shot down at ranges from which they could not reply. Where the technology gap was smaller - Isandlwana in 1879, Adwa in 1896 - Europeans lost.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest single measurement of the firepower gap that made the scramble possible, and the moment the Nile became British from the Delta to Uganda.

evidence.author: Peter Malcolm Holt and Martin Daly
evidence.work: A History of the Sudan: From the Coming of Islam to the Present Day
evidence.supports: The Mahdiyya and the reconquest.

evidence.author: Winston S. Churchill
evidence.work: The River War: An Historical Account of the Reconquest of the Soudan
evidence.supports: An eyewitness account, including criticism of the treatment of the wounded.

events.title: Fashoda and the Anglo-French Declaration
events.summary: A French expedition of 132 men under Marchand reached Fashoda on the White Nile in July 1898 and claimed it. Kitchener arrived with gunboats in September. Neither fired; France withdrew in November and gave up the whole Nile basin the following March.
events.significance: It settled the last great question of the scramble - who controlled the Nile - without a shot, and brought Britain and France to the edge of war. The humiliation pushed France towards a settlement of all its colonial disputes with Britain, which became the Entente Cordiale of 1904.

places.name: Fashoda (Kodok)
places.note: A ruined Egyptian fort on the White Nile, in what is now South Sudan.

people.name: Jean-Baptiste Marchand
people.role: led 132 men across Africa from the Congo to the Nile in two years

people.name: Herbert Kitchener
people.role: arrived from Omdurman with five gunboats sixteen days after the battle

people.name: Theophile Delcasse
people.role: French foreign minister who ordered the withdrawal and then built the Entente

evidence.author: Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher
evidence.work: Africa and the Victorians: The Official Mind of Imperialism
evidence.supports: The Nile strategy and the Fashoda crisis.

pedagogy.hook: Two armies met at a ruined fort on the White Nile in 1898, drank each other's champagne and warm beer, and nearly started a European war.

misconception.belief: The scramble for Africa was about land and resources.
misconception.correction: Fashoda was about water. Britain's whole Sudan policy rested on the belief that whoever held the upper Nile could threaten Egypt's water supply, and Egypt was the road to India. The territory itself was swamp and no one in London wanted it for anything it produced.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows imperial strategy as a chain: India needs the canal, the canal needs Egypt, Egypt needs the Nile, so Britain takes the Sudan.

events.title: The Dervish wars in Somaliland
events.summary: Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan built a state in the Somali interior and fought Britain, Italy and Ethiopia for twenty-one years. Four British expeditions between 1900 and 1904 failed; Britain withdrew to the coast in 1910 and left the interior alone for four years.
events.significance: The longest sustained armed resistance to British rule in Africa, and the place where air power was first used to finish a colonial war: in January 1920 RAF bombers attacked the Dervish forts at Taleh, and the movement collapsed within three weeks. The tactic was then used in Iraq, Aden and on the North-West Frontier.

places.name: Taleh
places.note: The Dervish stone fortress, bombed by the RAF's Z Unit in January 1920.

people.name: Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan
people.role: religious leader, poet and founder of the Dervish state; called the Mad Mullah in British writing, a name Somalis reject

people.name: Richard Corfield
people.role: British officer killed at Dul Madoba in August 1913, a defeat commemorated in one of Hassan's best-known poems

people.name: Robert Gordon
people.role: commanded Z Unit, the RAF detachment sent to bomb Taleh in January 1920

toll.note: Colonial estimates that a third of northern Somalia's population died in the wars and the famines that came with them are widely repeated but cannot be verified; no census existed before or after. Treat any figure as an order of magnitude, not a count.

pedagogy.hook: The first time an air force was used to end a colonial war was in Somaliland in January 1920: twelve aircraft finished what four ground expeditions in twenty years had not.

misconception.belief: Britain called Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan the Mad Mullah, so he must have been a fanatic with no political programme.
misconception.correction: He was a religious scholar and one of the great Somali poets, who built a state with forts, taxes and diplomacy, negotiated with the Ottomans and Germany, and fought three empires to a standstill for two decades. The nickname was a British convenience, and Somalis have never used it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is where the twentieth-century technique of controlling territory by bombing it was invented, and it is the longest anti-colonial war in British African history.

evidence.author: I. M. Lewis
evidence.work: A Modern History of the Somali: Nation and State in the Horn of Africa
evidence.supports: The Dervish state and its defeat.

evidence.author: Priya Satia
evidence.work: Spies in Arabia: The Great War and the Cultural Foundations of Britain's Covert Empire in the Middle East
evidence.supports: The origins of air control as a method of imperial policing.

contested.note: The human cost of these wars is genuinely unknown. The often-cited claim that a third of the population died rests on colonial estimates of famine and displacement, not on any count.

events.title: The British occupation of Egypt
events.summary: The Royal Navy bombarded Alexandria on 11 July 1882, and in September a British army destroyed Ahmad Urabi's nationalist forces at Tel el-Kebir in under an hour and occupied Cairo. Britain promised to withdraw as soon as order was restored.
events.significance: Britain stayed 74 years. The occupation secured the Suez Canal and the debt payments to European bondholders, triggered the wider scramble for Africa by making France and Britain rivals across the continent, and made the Nile a British strategic obsession that led to the Sudan.

places.name: Alexandria
places.note: Bombarded for ten and a half hours on 11 July 1882.

places.name: Tel el-Kebir
places.note: Night attack, 13 September 1882: about 2,000 Egyptian dead, 57 British.

people.name: Ahmad Urabi
people.role: Egyptian colonel who led a movement for a constitution and against European financial control; exiled to Ceylon for nineteen years

people.name: Garnet Wolseley
people.role: commanded the invasion

people.name: William Ewart Gladstone
people.role: prime minister who had denounced imperial adventures and ordered this one

people.name: Evelyn Baring, Lord Cromer
people.role: ran Egypt from 1883 to 1907 without holding an Egyptian office

toll.note: Egyptian dead at Tel el-Kebir are usually given as about 2,000, counted by the victors; 57 British and Indian soldiers died. Casualties from the Alexandria bombardment and the riots before it are not reliably known.

pedagogy.hook: Britain invaded Egypt in 1882 to make sure bondholders got paid, promised to leave at once, and left in 1956.
