misconception.belief: Britain occupied Egypt to take it as a colony.
misconception.correction: It never annexed Egypt. The occupation was meant to be temporary, and Britain issued 66 declarations of intent to withdraw before 1914. What kept it there was the canal, the debt and the fear that if Britain left, France would come in. Informal control turned out to be more durable than a colony.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Robinson and Gallagher argued that this occupation set off the scramble for Africa by turning Anglo-French rivalry into a race for territory. Whether or not that is the whole story, everything Britain did on the Nile for the next 74 years starts here.

evidence.author: Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher
evidence.work: Africa and the Victorians: The Official Mind of Imperialism
evidence.supports: The occupation and its place in the partition of Africa.

evidence.author: Juan R. I. Cole
evidence.work: Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East: Social and Cultural Origins of Egypt's Urabi Movement
evidence.supports: The Urabi movement and Egyptian politics before the invasion.

contested.note: Why Britain invaded is one of the oldest arguments in imperial history: strategic panic about the route to India, the interests of bondholders and the City, or a local crisis Britain had helped create and could not control. All three readings use the same cabinet papers.

events.title: The South African War
events.summary: Britain fought the two Boer republics for two years and eight months over the Witwatersrand goldfield and the political rights of foreign miners. It took 448,000 imperial troops to beat about 88,000 Boers, and cost roughly 200 million pounds.
events.significance: The largest and most expensive war Britain fought between 1815 and 1914. It shocked the country into army reform and into worrying about national fitness, exposed Britain's diplomatic isolation, invented the concentration camp system as a tool of counter-insurgency, and produced the peace that made the Union of 1910 on white terms.

places.name: Mafeking
places.note: Besieged 217 days; Sol Plaatje kept a diary of it.

places.name: Spion Kop
places.note: 24 January 1900: a British disaster on a hilltop; Gandhi served as a stretcher-bearer in the campaign.

places.name: Vereeniging
places.note: Where the Boer delegates voted to surrender on 31 May 1902.

people.name: Paul Kruger
people.role: president of the South African Republic; left for Europe in 1900 to seek help that never came

people.name: Christiaan de Wet
people.role: Free State guerrilla commander, never captured

people.name: Jan Smuts
people.role: Transvaal state attorney turned commando leader, who invaded the Cape in 1901

people.name: Horatio Herbert Kitchener
people.role: commander-in-chief from 1900; built 8,000 blockhouses, burned farms and cleared the veld into camps

people.name: Alfred Milner
people.role: High Commissioner who engineered the crisis and wrote the peace

people.name: Sol Plaatje
people.role: court interpreter at Mafeking whose siege diary is the best African account of the war

toll.note: About 22,000 British and imperial dead, roughly two thirds from disease; about 6,000 Boer fighters; 27,927 Boer civilians in the camps; and at least 14,154 recorded African deaths in separate camps, a figure most historians treat as an undercount. Totals vary because African deaths were not included in official counts for eighty years.
toll.source: British official casualty returns; the camp registers for 27,927 Boer deaths; the separately kept African camp returns for 14,154, which Elizabeth van Heyningen and others treat as a floor.

pedagogy.hook: It took 448,000 imperial troops to defeat about 88,000 farmers, and more than half the British dead were killed by typhoid rather than by Boers.

misconception.belief: The Boer War was a white man's war between Britons and Boers.
misconception.correction: At least 100,000 black Africans worked for the British army as scouts, drivers and labourers, some of them armed; Boer commandos had African agterryers with them; about 115,000 Africans were interned in camps of their own where at least 14,154 died. Peter Warwick's work in the 1980s put those camps back into the record after eighty years out of it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The peace of Vereeniging postponed the African franchise until after self-government, and self-government meant white voters. That single clause is the bridge from the war to the Union of 1910 and to apartheid.

evidence.author: Thomas Pakenham
evidence.work: The Boer War
evidence.supports: The military and political course of the war.

evidence.author: Peter Warwick
evidence.work: Black People and the South African War 1899-1902
evidence.supports: African participation and the African camps.

events.title: The concentration camps of the South African War
events.summary: To end a guerrilla war Britain burned about 30,000 farms and moved the civilian population of two republics into camps: roughly 115,000 Boers and 115,000 Africans, in separate systems. About 27,927 Boers died, most of them children, and at least 14,154 Africans.
events.significance: It is where the term concentration camp entered British political language. Emily Hobhouse's report and the resulting Fawcett Commission forced improvements, but the deaths had already done their work: the camps are central to Afrikaner memory of Britain, and they set a template for civilian internment in later counter-insurgencies from Malaya to Kenya.

places.name: Bloemfontein camp
places.note: Where Emily Hobhouse arrived in January 1901 and found children dying of measles and typhoid.

people.name: Emily Hobhouse
people.role: went to South Africa privately, reported what she saw, and was called a hysterical woman in the House of Commons before being proved right

people.name: Millicent Fawcett
people.role: led the official commission of women that confirmed Hobhouse's findings and produced reforms

people.name: Horatio Herbert Kitchener
people.role: ordered the clearances that filled the camps and resisted taking responsibility for them

people.name: Stowell Kessler
people.role: historian whose research from the 1990s established the scale of the separate African camps

toll.note: 27,927 Boer deaths are recorded in the camp registers and about 22,000 of them were children under sixteen. African camp deaths were recorded separately and carelessly; the official 14,154 is generally treated as a floor, with estimates up to about 20,000. The total range reflects that uncertainty.
toll.source: The camp registers for the Boer deaths; the separately kept and less careful African camp returns for 14,154.

pedagogy.hook: Roughly 22,000 of the nearly 28,000 Boer civilians who died in British camps were children under sixteen - and for eighty years the 14,000 Africans who died in separate camps were left out of the count entirely.

misconception.belief: The camps were a wartime accident caused by disease and poor supply.
misconception.correction: They were a policy. Kitchener's clearances emptied the countryside to deny the commandos food and shelter, and the camps were where the people went. Supply and medical care were badly organised, but the decision to move a civilian population into guarded camps was deliberate, and the death rate in some camps exceeded 300 per thousand per year.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the first time Britain interned a civilian population on this scale, and the method reappears in Malaya's New Villages and Kenya's villagisation fifty years later.

evidence.author: Elizabeth van Heyningen
evidence.work: The Concentration Camps of the Anglo-Boer War: A Social History
evidence.supports: Camp administration, mortality and the argument about causes.

evidence.author: Peter Warwick
evidence.work: Black People and the South African War 1899-1902
evidence.supports: The separate African camps and their death toll.

contested.note: Historians agree the Boer death figures and dispute their causes - deliberate cruelty, administrative incompetence, or an epidemiological catastrophe among a population with no immunity to measles. The African camp figures are disputed as to scale, because the records were kept badly and the deaths were excluded from official totals until the 1980s.

events.title: The Buganda Agreement
events.summary: Harry Johnston and the Buganda regents signed an agreement that kept the Kabaka, the Lukiiko parliament and Ganda courts in place, fixed the taxes, and turned about 8,000 square miles of land into private freehold for roughly a thousand chiefs and the royal family.
events.significance: It is the model text of indirect rule. Frederick Lugard generalised the method into a doctrine in The Dual Mandate (1922) and it was applied from Northern Nigeria to Tanganyika. It also made Buganda a privileged region inside Uganda, which is the fault line the country broke along in 1966.

places.name: Mengo
places.note: The Kabaka's capital, beside the British fort on Kampala hill.

people.name: Apolo Kagwa
people.role: katikkiro of Buganda; negotiated for the infant Kabaka and became the most powerful African official in British East Africa

people.name: Harry Johnston
people.role: special commissioner who drafted the agreement and thought he was saving money

people.name: Daudi Chwa II
people.role: Kabaka, aged four when the agreement was signed in his name

pedagogy.hook: One agreement in 1900 turned a thousand Ganda chiefs into private landowners and their neighbours into rent-paying tenants, and the land law it created is still in force.

misconception.belief: Indirect rule meant leaving African societies as they were.
misconception.correction: It transformed them. Before 1900 Ganda chiefs held office and allocated land as a public trust; after it they held freehold estates and the peasants on them paid rent. The chiefs got rich, the Kabaka's authority was underwritten by British power, and customary obligations became property rights - a bigger change than most direct rule produced.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Indirect rule is how a few hundred Britons governed millions. This is the document that shows what it cost the people at the bottom.

evidence.author: Holly Hanson
evidence.work: Landed Obligation: The Practice of Power in Buganda
evidence.supports: The agreement, mailo land and the transformation of chiefship.

evidence.author: Frederick Lugard
evidence.work: The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa
evidence.supports: The doctrine of indirect rule as its architect stated it.

events.title: The Denshawai hangings
events.summary: British officers shot pigeons kept by villagers at Denshawai in the Nile Delta; a fight followed, a barn caught fire, a village woman was wounded and one officer died of heatstroke and concussion while walking for help. A special tribunal hanged four villagers and flogged and imprisoned others.
events.significance: The punishment, carried out in front of the villagers' families, did more damage to British standing in Egypt than any policy of Cromer's twenty-four years. It radicalised a generation of Egyptian nationalists, was denounced in Britain by George Bernard Shaw and Wilfrid Scawen Blunt, and contributed to Cromer's resignation the next year.

places.name: Denshawai
places.note: A village in Minufiyya province in the Delta.

people.name: Mustafa Kamil
people.role: Egyptian nationalist leader who made Denshawai an international scandal

people.name: Evelyn Baring, Lord Cromer
people.role: Consul-General; approved the special tribunal and resigned the following year

people.name: George Bernard Shaw
people.role: wrote a preface attacking the executions as a demonstration of what British justice meant in a subject country

toll.note: Four villagers were hanged and one had already died; one British officer died of heatstroke and concussion. Others were flogged and given hard labour. The court records are clear and the numbers are not disputed.

pedagogy.hook: Four Egyptian villagers were hanged in front of their families because British officers had gone shooting pigeons.

misconception.belief: Colonial rule was harsh only in wars and rebellions.
misconception.correction: Denshawai was a routine day in a village. It ended with a special tribunal, public hangings and floggings, because the punishment was intended as a demonstration. Everyday colonial law was where most people met the empire, and the deterrent principle behind Denshawai was normal practice, not an aberration.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: A pigeon shoot, four gallows built beside the village, and the sentences carried out in front of the villagers' families. Egyptian schoolbooks still teach Denshawai; British ones do not mention it.

evidence.author: Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot
evidence.work: A History of Egypt: From the Arab Conquest to the Present
evidence.supports: Denshawai and its effect on Egyptian nationalism.

events.title: The Union of South Africa
events.summary: Four British colonies became one self-governing dominion under a constitution written by white South Africans at a convention with no black or Indian delegates, and passed at Westminster despite a delegation that came to London to object.
events.significance: It created the modern South African state, entrenched a racial franchise in an Act of the British Parliament, and closed the only non-racial voters' roll in southern Africa to any possibility of extension. The African response was the founding of the South African Native National Congress in 1912, which became the ANC.

places.name: Bloemfontein
places.note: Where the South African Native Convention met in March 1909 and the SANNC was founded in January 1912.

people.name: William Philip Schreiner
people.role: led the 1909 delegation to London against the colour bar

people.name: Abdullah Abdurahman
people.role: president of the African Political Organisation and a member of the delegation

people.name: John Tengo Jabavu
people.role: editor of Imvo Zabantsundu and leading African voice in Cape politics

people.name: John Langalibalele Dube
people.role: first president of the South African Native National Congress, founded in response

people.name: Louis Botha
people.role: first prime minister of the Union

pedagogy.hook: A delegation of South Africans sailed to London in 1909 to ask Parliament not to write a colour bar into their constitution. Parliament wrote it anyway, and the ANC was founded three years later.

misconception.belief: Apartheid was invented in 1948 and had nothing to do with Britain.
misconception.correction: The 1909 South Africa Act was British legislation. It restricted membership of the Union parliament to white men, left the franchise to each province, and blocked the Cape's non-racial roll from spreading. Segregationist law followed at once: the Natives Land Act of 1913 reserved about 7 per cent of the country for Africans. 1948 radicalised a structure Britain had built.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the single clearest case in the atlas of Britain trading the rights of a colonised majority for the loyalty of a settler minority, in writing, in an Act of Parliament.

evidence.author: Leonard Thompson
evidence.work: The Unification of South Africa, 1902-1910
evidence.supports: The National Convention, the franchise question and the 1909 delegation.

events.title: The Natives Land Act
events.summary: The Union parliament reserved about 7 per cent of South Africa for African occupation and made it illegal for Africans to buy or rent land outside it, or for black sharecroppers to farm white-owned land on shares.
events.significance: It converted a productive African peasantry into a labour force, at a stroke: families who had farmed on shares were evicted onto the roads with their stock. The reserves were extended to about 13 per cent in 1936 and stayed there; land is still the most unresolved question in South African politics.

people.name: Sol Plaatje
people.role: travelled the country by bicycle recording the evictions and published Native Life in South Africa in 1916

people.name: Jacobus Wilhelmus Sauer
people.role: minister of native affairs who introduced the Bill

people.name: John Langalibalele Dube
people.role: led the SANNC deputation to London in 1914 to petition against the Act; it was refused

pedagogy.hook: One Act gave 7 per cent of South Africa to two thirds of its people, and made it a crime for them to rent land anywhere else.

misconception.belief: Africans lost their land through conquest in the nineteenth century.
misconception.correction: Much of it was lost by statute in the twentieth. In 1913 there were prosperous African sharecroppers and tenant farmers across the Orange Free State and the Transvaal. The Land Act made their contracts illegal, and Sol Plaatje watched families walking the winter roads with their cattle dying beside them because there was nowhere legal to stop.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the law that made migrant labour compulsory, and the reason the mines and farms always had workers who had no other option.

evidence.author: Sol Plaatje
evidence.work: Native Life in South Africa
evidence.supports: Eyewitness account of the evictions that followed the Act.

evidence.author: Colin Bundy
evidence.work: The Rise and Fall of the South African Peasantry
evidence.supports: How an African commercial peasantry was destroyed by law and market pressure.

events.title: The East African campaign of the First World War
events.summary: The longest campaign of the First World War was fought across what is now Tanzania, Kenya, Malawi, Zambia and Mozambique. The British and German armies both fought mainly with African soldiers and moved everything on African backs: over a million people were conscripted as carriers.
events.significance: Recorded deaths among carriers recruited by the British alone are about 95,000, more than all the soldiers killed in the campaign, and famine and influenza followed the armies through the region. It is the largest single loss of African life in either world war, and it is missing from most textbooks.

places.name: Tanga
places.note: November 1914: a British and Indian landing beaten off, partly by bees.

places.name: Chambeshi
places.note: Where Lettow-Vorbeck surrendered on 25 November 1918, two weeks after the armistice.

people.name: Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck
people.role: German commander who tied down about 300,000 Allied troops with a force never larger than 15,000, most of them African askari

people.name: Jan Smuts
people.role: commanded Allied forces in 1916 with South African, Indian and African troops

people.name: John Chilembwe
people.role: Nyasaland pastor who rose in January 1915 explicitly against the conscription of Africans into this war

toll.note: About 95,000 deaths are recorded among carriers on the British registers of the Carrier Corps; that count excludes those never registered, those recruited by Germany and Belgium, and civilians who died in the famine and influenza that followed the armies. Wider regional estimates run to several hundred thousand.

pedagogy.hook: More African porters died carrying supplies in East Africa than soldiers died fighting there, and the war did not end in Africa until two weeks after the armistice in Europe.

misconception.belief: The First World War was a European war fought in European trenches.
misconception.correction: It was fought in East Africa for four years and three months, longer than anywhere else. Britain and Germany both conscripted African men as carriers because there were no roads; over a million were taken, and at least 95,000 on the British registers died of dysentery and exhaustion. Most were never named: the Imperial War Graves Commission chose not to record African dead individually.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the largest and least-known African death toll of either world war, and it is the direct trigger for the Chilembwe rising in Nyasaland in 1915.

evidence.author: Edward Paice
evidence.work: Tip and Run: The Untold Tragedy of the Great War in Africa
evidence.supports: The campaign and the carrier corps.

evidence.author: Geoffrey Hodges
evidence.work: The Carrier Corps: Military Labor in the East African Campaign, 1914-1918
evidence.supports: The recruitment, conditions and mortality of the carriers.

contested.note: Carrier deaths are certainly undercounted. The 95,000 figure comes from British registers; men recruited informally, and those who died after discharge, were not counted at all. Estimates of total African deaths in the region including famine range far higher and cannot be verified.

events.title: The Chilembwe rising
events.summary: John Chilembwe, a Nyasaland pastor educated in the United States, led an armed rising against forced estate labour and the conscription of Africans into the First World War. Three Europeans were killed; the rising was crushed in ten days and Chilembwe was shot on 3 February.
events.significance: It is the first modern nationalist rising in British central Africa, and it came with a written argument: Chilembwe's letter in the Nyasaland Times in November 1914 asked why Africans should die in a European war for a country that gave them no rights. Malawi's independence movement claimed him as its founder, and his face is on the currency.

places.name: Mbombwe
places.note: Chilembwe's Providence Industrial Mission, dynamited by the government after the rising.

people.name: John Chilembwe
people.role: pastor and founder of the Providence Industrial Mission; led the rising and was shot near the Mozambique border

people.name: William Jervis Livingstone
people.role: manager of the Bruce estates, notorious for burning workers' huts and churches; killed and beheaded on the first night

people.name: Joseph Booth
people.role: radical British missionary who took Chilembwe to America and taught him that African churches should be run by Africans

toll.note: Three Europeans were killed. About 40 of Chilembwe's followers were executed and some 300 imprisoned, on the figures of the colonial commission of inquiry of 1916.

pedagogy.hook: Ten weeks before he led a rising, John Chilembwe published a letter in a colonial newspaper asking why Africans were dying in a war that promised them nothing.

misconception.belief: African resistance to colonial rule was traditional and backward-looking.
misconception.correction: Chilembwe was educated in Virginia, ran a mission with a brick church he had designed, wore a suit, and argued his case in print in English before he took up arms. His grievances were the thangata labour system on the estates and conscription for the First World War. This was a modern political argument, not a revolt against modernity.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It links the First World War directly to African nationalism, and it is why Malawi dates its independence movement from 1915 rather than 1944.

evidence.author: George Shepperson and Thomas Price
evidence.work: Independent African: John Chilembwe and the Origins, Setting and Significance of the Nyasaland Native Rising of 1915
evidence.supports: Chilembwe's life, his letter and the rising.

events.title: The Egyptian revolution of 1919
events.summary: When Britain deported Saad Zaghlul and three colleagues to Malta for asking to put Egypt's case at the Paris peace conference, the country rose: students, lawyers, railway workers, peasants cutting the telegraph lines, and mass demonstrations of women in Cairo.
events.significance: It ended the protectorate. Britain sent Lord Milner to negotiate, could not find terms, and in February 1922 declared Egypt independent unilaterally while reserving defence, imperial communications, foreign interests and the Sudan. The Wafd became Egypt's dominant party for thirty years.

places.name: Cairo
places.note: Where Huda Sharawi led a women's march on 16 March 1919.

people.name: Saad Zaghlul
people.role: leader of the Wafd; his deportation set off the revolution and he became prime minister in 1924

people.name: Huda Sharawi
people.role: led the women's demonstration of 16 March 1919 and founded the Egyptian Feminist Union in 1923

people.name: Safiyya Zaghlul
people.role: called Mother of the Egyptians; her house was the movement's headquarters

people.name: Alfred Milner
people.role: led the 1919-20 mission that concluded the protectorate could not be maintained

toll.note: British official figures record about 800 Egyptians killed; Egyptian accounts give higher totals. Around 30 British soldiers and officials were killed.

pedagogy.hook: The Egyptian revolution of 1919 began because four men asked for passports to go to a peace conference and talk about self-determination.

misconception.belief: Woodrow Wilson's principle of self-determination applied to colonised peoples after 1918.
misconception.correction: Egyptians, Indians, Koreans and Vietnamese all took Wilson at his word in 1919 and were all refused. The United States recognised the British protectorate over Egypt while Zaghlul's delegation was in Paris waiting to be heard. 1919 is the year colonised peoples across the world discovered that self-determination was meant for Europe.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It produced the first negotiated retreat of British power in Africa, and it is the year that made a generation of anti-colonial politics.

evidence.author: Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot
evidence.work: A History of Egypt: From the Arab Conquest to the Present
evidence.supports: The 1919 revolution, the Wafd and the 1922 declaration.

events.title: The Devonshire White Paper
events.summary: Faced with Kenya's European settlers demanding self-government and its Indian population demanding equal voting rights, the Colonial Secretary declared that Kenya was primarily an African territory and that where interests conflicted, African interests must be paramount.
events.significance: The declaration blocked settler self-government in Kenya permanently, which is why Kenya never became a Rhodesia. It also refused Indians the common roll and left the White Highlands untouched, so the principle it announced changed nothing on the ground for another forty years.

people.name: Victor Cavendish, Duke of Devonshire
people.role: Colonial Secretary whose name is on the paper

people.name: Manilal Ambalal Desai
people.role: leader of the Kenyan Indian campaign for a common electoral roll

people.name: Hugh Cholmondeley, Lord Delamere
people.role: settler leader who had threatened to kidnap the governor rather than accept Indian equality

people.name: Harry Thuku
people.role: African leader deported in 1922 after the Nairobi shootings; the African case was not represented in the negotiation at all

pedagogy.hook: In 1923 Britain declared that African interests in Kenya must be paramount, and then left the best land reserved for 2,000 white farmers for another forty years.

misconception.belief: Britain's stated policies tell you what colonial rule was like.
misconception.correction: The Devonshire paper is the most quoted statement of trusteeship in British African policy, and it was written to settle a quarrel between white settlers and Indian traders. Africans were not in the room. The Highlands stayed white, the pass system stayed, and the declaration was used for decades to argue that reform was unnecessary because the principle was already conceded.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the reason Kenya stayed a Crown colony rather than becoming a settler state like Southern Rhodesia - and the reason the settlers still had the land in 1952.

evidence.author: Bethwell A. Ogot and William R. Ochieng
evidence.work: Decolonization and Independence in Kenya, 1940-93
evidence.supports: The paramountcy doctrine and settler politics.

events.title: The East African campaign of 1940-41
events.summary: Italy conquered British Somaliland in a fortnight in August 1940. Six months later Commonwealth forces from Kenya and Sudan destroyed Italian East Africa in three months, restored Haile Selassie to Addis Ababa, and put Eritrea, Italian Somaliland and much of Ethiopia under British administration.
events.significance: It was the first Allied land victory of the Second World War, and it left Britain governing four territories it had not owned in 1939. The British administrations in Eritrea, Somalia and Libya, and the reserved areas in Ethiopia, are the empire's last territorial expansion - and the arguments about their future were settled at the United Nations, not in London.

places.name: Keren
places.note: February-March 1941: the hardest fighting of the campaign, in the Eritrean mountains.

places.name: Addis Ababa
places.note: Haile Selassie re-entered on 5 May 1941, five years to the day after the Italians took it.

people.name: Haile Selassie
people.role: Emperor of Ethiopia, restored with Gideon Force

people.name: Orde Wingate
people.role: led Gideon Force, the small Anglo-Sudanese-Ethiopian column that escorted the emperor home

people.name: Alan Cunningham
people.role: commanded the advance from Kenya through Somalia to Addis Ababa

people.name: William Platt
people.role: commanded the advance from Sudan and won at Keren

toll.note: Commonwealth losses across the campaign were comparatively light - a few thousand killed and wounded - and Italian and colonial losses considerably higher. African and Eritrean askari casualties on the Italian side were not systematically recorded.

pedagogy.hook: The British Empire's last new African territories were taken in 1941, not in the nineteenth century: Eritrea, Italian Somaliland, Libya and much of Ethiopia.

misconception.belief: The empire only shrank after 1918.
misconception.correction: Britain administered more African territory in 1945 than in 1939, and in 1946 and 1949 proposed keeping Somalia united under British trusteeship and Cyrenaica as a British trust territory. Both proposals failed at the United Nations. Expansion stopped because other powers stopped it, not because Britain had lost interest.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains a stretch of British African history that most accounts skip entirely, and it is where the borders of the modern Horn of Africa were finally settled.

evidence.author: Ashley Jackson
evidence.work: The British Empire and the Second World War
evidence.supports: The East African campaign and the wartime administrations.

events.title: The Tanganyika Groundnut Scheme
events.summary: Britain planned to clear 3.2 million acres of Tanganyikan bush and grow groundnuts for margarine, using war-surplus bulldozers and tractors. About 50,000 acres were cleared, the soil and rainfall defeated the machines, and the scheme was abandoned having cost roughly 36 million pounds.
events.significance: It is the standard case of late-colonial development planned in London for land nobody had surveyed. It also shows what colonial development was for: post-war Britain needed cooking fat and dollars, and the scheme was designed to supply Britain, not Tanganyika.

places.name: Kongwa
places.note: The main clearing site; the soil set like concrete in the dry season.

people.name: John Strachey
people.role: minister of food who championed the scheme and defended it in Parliament until it failed

people.name: Frank Samuel
people.role: managing director of the United Africa Company, whose proposal started it

pedagogy.hook: Britain spent about 36 million pounds clearing African bush for groundnuts and in some years harvested less seed than it had planted.

misconception.belief: Colonial development schemes were about helping colonies develop.
misconception.correction: The Colonial Development and Welfare Acts did fund schools, clinics and roads. But the groundnut scheme was designed to solve a British problem - a shortage of cooking fats and of dollars to buy them - on land chosen from aerial photographs, with no soil survey and no consultation. When it failed, Tanganyika was left with the debt on its own development account.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest evidence that late-colonial development was a British interest before it was an African one - and it made Tanganyikan nationalists sceptical of every scheme that followed.

evidence.author: John Iliffe
evidence.work: A Modern History of Tanganyika
evidence.supports: The groundnut scheme and post-war colonial development.

events.title: The Mau Mau emergency
events.summary: Kenya's colonial government declared an emergency, arrested the nationalist leadership, and over eight years detained tens of thousands of Kikuyu without trial, hanged 1,090 people, and moved about a million people into guarded villages to break the Kenya Land and Freedom Army.
events.significance: It is the most fully documented case of British counter-insurgency violence at the end of empire - because the documents were removed to Britain, hidden at Hanslope Park, and disclosed only in 2011 during litigation. In 2013 the British government paid 19.9 million pounds to 5,228 claimants and expressed regret.

places.name: Nyeri and the Aberdares
places.note: The forest bases of the Land and Freedom Army.

places.name: Lari
places.note: 26 March 1953: a Mau Mau attack on loyalist families, followed by security-force reprisals.

places.name: Kapenguria
places.note: Where Kenyatta was tried in 1953 before a judge later shown to have been paid.

people.name: Dedan Kimathi
people.role: field marshal of the Kenya Land and Freedom Army; captured 21 October 1956 and hanged 18 February 1957

people.name: Waruhiu Itote (General China)
people.role: commander on Mount Kenya, captured in 1954 and later used as a negotiator

people.name: Muthoni Kirima
people.role: field marshal, one of very few women to hold the rank, who stayed in the forest until 1963

people.name: Jomo Kenyatta
people.role: convicted in 1953 of managing Mau Mau on evidence historians regard as worthless; imprisoned until 1961, prime minister in 1963

people.name: Evelyn Baring
people.role: governor who declared the emergency and authorised the detention system

people.name: Ndiku Mutua and Paulo Nzili
people.role: two of the five elderly Kenyans whose 2009 High Court case forced disclosure of the hidden archive

toll.note: Official counts: 11,503 Mau Mau killed, 1,090 hanged, 32 European settlers killed and about 1,800 African civilians killed by Mau Mau. Caroline Elkins argues for far higher totals and mass unrecorded deaths; John Blacker's demographic study estimates about 50,000 excess deaths, roughly half of them children; David Anderson works from documented executions and questions the highest figures. Records were destroyed at independence.
toll.source: Colonial government returns for the official counts; Caroline Elkins, Britain's Gulag (2005); John Blacker's demographic study in African Affairs (2007); David Anderson, Histories of the Hanged (2005).

pedagogy.hook: Britain hanged 1,090 people in Kenya during the emergency - more than it executed in any other colonial insurgency - and then flew the files out and hid them.

misconception.belief: Decolonisation was a planned, peaceful handover.
misconception.correction: In Kenya the colonial government detained tens of thousands without trial, used what the files call dilution technique - beating detainees into compliance - and moved about a million people into guarded villages. In 2011 the Foreign Office admitted holding 1,500 removed Kenyan files at Hanslope Park, part of about 8,800 files from 37 colonies. In 2013 it paid 5,228 claimants 19.9 million pounds.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows both the violence at the end of empire and how we know about it: through a court case, a hidden archive and a government admission - evidence no one can dismiss as bias.

evidence.author: David Anderson
evidence.work: Histories of the Hanged: Britain's Dirty War in Kenya and the End of Empire
evidence.supports: The emergency, the courts and the hangings.

evidence.author: Caroline Elkins
evidence.work: Britain's Gulag: The Brutal End of Empire in Kenya
evidence.supports: The detention camps and villagisation.

evidence.author: Huw Bennett
evidence.work: Fighting the Mau Mau: The British Army and Counter-Insurgency in the Kenya Emergency
evidence.supports: Army conduct and the legal framework of the emergency.

contested.note: The scale is contested and the system is not. Elkins's higher estimates are challenged by demographers, including Blacker, and by Anderson; all agree on mass detention without trial, forced villagisation and systematic beatings, which the British government did not deny in the 2013 settlement.

events.title: The Central African Federation
events.summary: Britain federated Southern Rhodesia, Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland against the near-unanimous opposition of their African populations, promising a partnership of the races. It lasted ten years and five months.
events.significance: The federation pooled Copperbelt revenue under a government in Salisbury dominated by white Southern Rhodesians, and its collapse produced three completely different outcomes: independence under majority rule for Zambia and Malawi in 1964, and a white unilateral declaration of independence in Rhodesia in 1965.

places.name: Salisbury (Harare)
places.note: Seat of the federal government.

people.name: Godfrey Huggins
people.role: first federal prime minister, who described partnership as that of the horse and its rider

people.name: Roy Welensky
people.role: federal prime minister from 1956; fought Britain to the last to keep the federation together

people.name: Hastings Kamuzu Banda
people.role: returned to Nyasaland in 1958 to break the federation, and did

people.name: Kenneth Kaunda
people.role: led the Northern Rhodesian campaign against the federation

people.name: Walter Monckton
people.role: chaired the 1960 commission that found African opposition to be almost universal

pedagogy.hook: The federation's first prime minister described the partnership of black and white as the partnership of the horse and its rider, and then asked why anyone objected.

misconception.belief: Britain always handed independence to its colonies as single, obvious units.
misconception.correction: Britain repeatedly tried to build federations - Central Africa, the West Indies, Malaysia, South Arabia - because larger units looked economically viable and easier to defend. Most failed. The Central African Federation was imposed in 1953 on populations that had already said no, and it broke when the Monckton Commission reported in 1960 that opposition was almost universal.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Its dissolution on 31 December 1963 is the hinge of central African history: two countries went to majority rule within a year, and the third declared UDI within two.

evidence.author: Andrew Roberts
evidence.work: A History of Zambia
evidence.supports: The federation from the northern side.

evidence.author: John McCracken
evidence.work: A History of Malawi, 1859-1966
evidence.supports: Nyasaland's resistance to the federation and the 1959 emergency.

events.title: The Suez Crisis
events.summary: Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company. Britain, France and Israel agreed in secret at Sevres that Israel would attack and the other two would intervene to separate the combatants. The plan worked militarily and collapsed politically within a week.
events.significance: A run on sterling, an American refusal to support it, and a United Nations emergency force forced Britain out by 22 December. Eden resigned. The crisis proved that Britain could no longer act against American wishes, and every colonial nationalist movement in the world drew the conclusion.

places.name: Port Said
places.note: Anglo-French landings on 5 November 1956; several hundred Egyptian civilians were killed here.

places.name: Sevres
places.note: Where the secret protocol was signed on 24 October 1956. Britain's copy was destroyed.

people.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser
people.role: nationalised the canal company and emerged from military defeat as the political victor

people.name: Anthony Eden
people.role: British prime minister; told the House of Commons there had been no foreknowledge of the Israeli attack, and resigned on 9 January 1957

people.name: Dwight Eisenhower
people.role: refused to support sterling until Britain announced a withdrawal

people.name: Dag Hammarskjold
people.role: UN Secretary-General; assembled the first UN peacekeeping force

people.name: Hugh Gaitskell
people.role: Labour leader who opposed the operation in Parliament and was accused of betraying the country

toll.note: Egyptian deaths, military and civilian, are usually put between 1,000 and 3,000, with several hundred civilians killed at Port Said. There was no impartial count. British losses were 22 killed, French 10, Israeli about 190.

pedagogy.hook: Britain's prime minister denied in the House of Commons that there had been any collusion with Israel; the document proving otherwise had been signed six days earlier at Sevres, and Britain's copy was destroyed.

misconception.belief: Suez was a military failure.
misconception.correction: Militarily the operation worked: paratroops took Port Said and the canal was within reach. It failed financially and diplomatically. Britain had a run on its reserves, the United States refused to let the International Monetary Fund help until a withdrawal was announced, and the United Nations General Assembly voted overwhelmingly against. Britain stopped because it could not pay.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Suez is where informal empire ended. Macmillan, who had backed the operation, made his Wind of Change speech three years later, and Britain left almost all of Africa within a decade.

evidence.author: Keith Kyle
evidence.work: Suez: Britain's End of Empire in the Middle East
evidence.supports: The collusion at Sevres, the operation and the withdrawal.

events.title: The Hola camp killings
events.summary: At Hola detention camp in Kenya, eleven detainees who refused to work were beaten to death by guards and 77 more were injured. The colonial government first said they had died from drinking contaminated water.
events.significance: The cover-up unravelled in the House of Commons, where the Conservative MP Enoch Powell said that a British subject could not be treated by different standards because he had a black face. Together with the Devlin Report on Nyasaland, published four months later, it destroyed political support for holding Africa by force.

places.name: Hola
places.note: A detention camp on the Tana River for detainees classed as irreconcilable.

people.name: Enoch Powell
people.role: Conservative MP whose speech on 27 July 1959 forced the government to accept responsibility

people.name: Barbara Castle
people.role: Labour MP who had campaigned on Kenyan detention for years and pressed the case in the Commons

people.name: Evelyn Baring
people.role: governor, who had approved the dilution technique under which the beatings took place

people.name: The eleven men killed
people.role: detainees at Hola, beaten to death for refusing to work; among them Kabiru Kagoi and Ndungu Kibaki

toll.note: Eleven detainees killed and 77 injured. The figures come from the subsequent inquest and parliamentary inquiry and are not disputed; the first official explanation, contaminated water, was false.

pedagogy.hook: The colonial government said eleven men at Hola had died from drinking bad water. They had been beaten to death, and a Conservative MP said so in the House of Commons.

misconception.belief: Nobody in Britain knew what was being done in the colonies.
misconception.correction: Hola was debated in Parliament, reported in the newspapers, and denounced by MPs of both parties within months. The same summer the Devlin Commission called Nyasaland a police state. The information was public; what was hidden was the scale, and the files that showed it were removed to Britain in 1963 and concealed until 2011.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the moment the political cost of holding Africa by force became too high in Britain itself - eight months before Macmillan's Wind of Change speech.

evidence.author: David Anderson
evidence.work: Histories of the Hanged: Britain's Dirty War in Kenya and the End of Empire
evidence.supports: Hola, the cover-up and the political consequences.

evidence.author: Caroline Elkins
evidence.work: Britain's Gulag: The Brutal End of Empire in Kenya
evidence.supports: The dilution technique and the camp system.

events.title: The Wind of Change speech
events.summary: Harold Macmillan told the South African parliament in Cape Town that a wind of change was blowing through the continent, that African national consciousness was a political fact, and that Britain could not support a policy of racial supremacy.
events.significance: It announced to white settlers across Africa that Britain would not fight to keep them in power. Within five years Nigeria, Tanganyika, Uganda, Kenya, Zambia, Malawi and a dozen others were independent - and South Africa left the Commonwealth, and Rhodesia's settlers declared independence rather than accept the message.

places.name: Cape Town
places.note: Macmillan spoke in the South African parliament on the last day of a six-week African tour.

people.name: Harold Macmillan
people.role: British prime minister; had commissioned a secret audit of whether each colony was worth holding before making the speech

people.name: Hendrik Verwoerd
people.role: South African prime minister, who replied from the floor that white South Africans were also an African people entitled to justice

people.name: Iain Macleod
people.role: Colonial Secretary from 1959, who then accelerated African independence faster than anyone expected

pedagogy.hook: A British prime minister stood in the South African parliament and told his hosts, to their faces, that their policy was one Britain could not support.

misconception.belief: Britain decolonised because it decided colonialism was wrong.
misconception.correction: Macmillan's government had just commissioned a cost-benefit audit of the colonies. Suez had shown Britain could not act alone, the Hola killings and the Devlin Report had made force politically expensive at home, and the Cold War made African goodwill valuable. Moral argument and hard calculation pointed the same way, and the calculation came first in the cabinet papers.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest single statement of when and why the British retreat from Africa was decided in London - and the moment settler communities realised they were on their own.

evidence.author: Saul Dubow
evidence.work: Apartheid, 1948-1994
evidence.supports: The speech, its reception in South Africa and the road to the 1961 republic.

events.title: South Africa becomes a republic and leaves the Commonwealth
events.summary: After a whites-only referendum carried the republic by 52.29 per cent in October 1960, South Africa applied to stay in the Commonwealth as a republic. Faced with attacks on apartheid from India, Ghana, Nigeria, Malaya and Canada, Verwoerd withdrew the application in March 1961.
events.significance: It was the first time Commonwealth membership was made conditional on domestic racial policy, and it was newly independent Asian and African members who did it. The Commonwealth stopped being a club of white dominions and became something a state could be excluded from.

people.name: Hendrik Verwoerd
people.role: South African prime minister who withdrew the application rather than accept criticism of apartheid

people.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
people.role: Indian prime minister, who led the argument that a Commonwealth of equals could not include a state built on racial rank

people.name: John Diefenbaker
people.role: Canadian prime minister whose insistence on a statement of racial equality made South Africa's position impossible

people.name: Albert Luthuli
people.role: ANC president and Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 1961, who welcomed South Africa's exclusion

pedagogy.hook: South Africa did not walk out of the Commonwealth in 1961 for freedom's sake; it walked out rather than be told that apartheid was unacceptable, by India, Ghana, Nigeria, Malaya and Canada.

misconception.belief: The Commonwealth is the empire's friendly afterlife, and always was.
misconception.correction: It began in 1926 and 1931 as an arrangement among white dominions. India's decision in 1949 to stay in as a republic changed what it was for, and by 1961 the newly independent members could force a founding member out over apartheid. It now includes Mozambique, Rwanda, Gabon and Togo, which Britain never ruled.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the moment when the countries Britain had governed had enough weight inside the Commonwealth to set its terms.

evidence.author: Saul Dubow
evidence.work: Apartheid, 1948-1994
evidence.supports: The referendum, the Commonwealth conference and the republic.

events.title: The Zanzibar revolution
events.summary: Five weeks after independence, armed insurgents overthrew the Sultan and the Arab-led government in a night. Thousands of Zanzibaris of Arab and South Asian descent were killed, tens of thousands fled, and in April Zanzibar joined Tanganyika to form Tanzania.
events.significance: It is the sharpest demonstration in Africa of what happens when a colonial power hardens social categories into racial ones and then hands over on an electoral system that gives power to the side which lost the popular vote. The union with Tanganyika that followed created Tanzania and still shapes its politics.

places.name: Zanzibar Town
places.note: The Sultan's palace was taken before dawn on 12 January 1964.

people.name: John Okello
people.role: Ugandan-born labourer who organised and led the insurrection, and was excluded from power within weeks

people.name: Abeid Amani Karume
people.role: Afro-Shirazi Party leader who became president of Zanzibar and negotiated the union

people.name: Jamshid bin Abdullah
people.role: the last Sultan, who fled and lived in exile in Britain for 56 years

people.name: Julius Nyerere
people.role: president of Tanganyika, who agreed the union in April 1964

toll.note: One of the least settled death tolls in modern African history. Contemporary diplomatic reports suggested a few thousand; later accounts, including film footage, have supported much higher figures. No administration existed to count, and the new revolutionary government and the deposed sultanate's supporters each had reasons to shape the number.

pedagogy.hook: Zanzibar was an independent country for 33 days.

misconception.belief: Post-colonial violence shows that people were not ready for independence.
misconception.correction: Zanzibar's categories - Arab, Shirazi, African, Asian - were sharpened by a British census and a British electoral system, and the 1963 constituencies handed government to a party that won 46 per cent of the vote against the opposition's 54. The violence had local causes and a colonial architecture; saying so is not saying Zanzibaris were unready to govern themselves.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the origin of Tanzania, and it shows the cost of an electoral system designed to produce a particular result.

evidence.author: Jonathon Glassman
evidence.work: War of Words, War of Stones: Racial Thought and Violence in Colonial Zanzibar
evidence.supports: How colonial racial categories shaped the politics that ended in the revolution.

contested.note: Estimates of the dead range from about 2,000 to 20,000. There was no count, foreign journalists were largely excluded, and figures have been used politically ever since.

events.title: Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence
events.summary: Ian Smith's government declared Southern Rhodesia independent, in a document echoing the American Declaration of Independence, to prevent Britain imposing majority rule. About 220,000 white Rhodesians claimed a country of four million Africans.
events.significance: Britain declared it illegal, imposed sanctions, and refused to use force. No state ever recognised Rhodesia. The rebellion lasted fourteen years and was ended by a guerrilla war, not by London, and Britain briefly resumed direct rule in December 1979 to run the election that made Zimbabwe.

places.name: Salisbury (Harare)
places.note: Where the declaration was signed and broadcast on 11 November 1965.

people.name: Ian Smith
people.role: prime minister; said in 1976 that he did not believe in majority rule, not in a thousand years

people.name: Harold Wilson
people.role: British prime minister who ruled out using force and predicted sanctions would work in weeks rather than months

people.name: Joshua Nkomo
people.role: ZAPU leader, detained without trial from 1964 to 1974

people.name: Robert Mugabe
people.role: ZANU leader, imprisoned from 1964 to 1974, then led ZANLA from Mozambique

people.name: Humphrey Gibbs
people.role: the Governor, who stayed in Government House for four years as the legal authority nobody obeyed

pedagogy.hook: Rhodesia declared independence from Britain in order to stop black Rhodesians from getting the vote - and quoted the American Declaration of Independence while doing it.

misconception.belief: Declaring independence from Britain was always an anti-colonial act.
misconception.correction: UDI was a settler rebellion against decolonisation. Britain's condition for independence was progress towards majority rule; the Rhodesian Front declared independence to avoid it. The people who wanted the vote were in prison or in exile, and it took a fourteen-year war to get it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the exception that defines the rule: the only case where a British colony seized independence in order to keep the majority of its people out of power.

evidence.author: Luise White
evidence.work: Unpopular Sovereignty: Rhodesian Independence and African Decolonization
evidence.supports: UDI's legal claims, its self-understanding and its collapse.

events.title: The Lancaster House conference
events.summary: Fourteen weeks of talks in London between the Patriotic Front, the internal Zimbabwe Rhodesia government and Britain produced a ceasefire, a constitution and an election, after a war that had killed at least 20,000 people.
events.significance: It ended the last white-ruled British territory in Africa and produced Zimbabwe in April 1980. It also entrenched, for ten years, that white farmland could only be bought on a willing-seller basis with compensation - which pushed the land question to the year 2000 and the violent seizures that followed.

places.name: Lancaster House, London
places.note: Where the constitution was negotiated between 10 September and 15 December 1979.

people.name: Robert Mugabe
people.role: ZANU leader; won the February 1980 election with 57 of 80 African seats

people.name: Joshua Nkomo
people.role: ZAPU leader and co-leader of the Patriotic Front

people.name: Josiah Tongogara
people.role: ZANLA commander who pressed for the settlement and died in a car crash in Mozambique days after it was signed

people.name: Peter Carington
people.role: British foreign secretary who chaired the conference

people.name: Abel Muzorewa
people.role: prime minister of the unrecognised Zimbabwe Rhodesia, who won three seats in the 1980 election

people.name: Samora Machel
people.role: president of Mozambique, whose pressure on ZANU to settle was decisive

toll.note: Deaths in the war of 1972-79 are usually given between 20,000 and 30,000, the great majority African civilians. There was no counting authority and the Rhodesian security forces published their own figures.

pedagogy.hook: Britain took back legal control of Rhodesia for four months in 1979 - a governor, a flag and a ceasefire - solely in order to hand it over properly.

misconception.belief: Independence settlements settle everything.
misconception.correction: Lancaster House ended the war and produced a democratic election, and it also locked the land question shut. For ten years white-owned farms could only be bought willingly, at market prices, in foreign currency, with Britain and the United States expected to help fund it. When the funding fell short and the ten years expired, the unresolved question returned - violently, from 2000.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the closest thing to a model British decolonisation settlement, and studying what it postponed is as instructive as studying what it solved.

evidence.author: David Martin and Phyllis Johnson
evidence.work: The Struggle for Zimbabwe: The Chimurenga War
evidence.supports: The war and the negotiations.

evidence.author: Luise White
evidence.work: Unpopular Sovereignty: Rhodesian Independence and African Decolonization
evidence.supports: The end of the Rhodesian state.

events.title: The migrated archives and the Mau Mau settlement
events.summary: During a High Court case brought by five elderly Kenyans, the Foreign Office admitted it held about 8,800 files removed from 37 colonies at independence, hidden at Hanslope Park. In June 2013 Britain paid 19.9 million pounds to 5,228 Kenyan claimants and expressed regret.
events.significance: It is the only occasion on which the British state has admitted in court to the systematic concealment of colonial records and paid compensation for colonial abuses. Historians have since used the released files to rewrite the history of the end of empire, and other claims - from Cyprus, Malaya and Aden - followed.

places.name: Hanslope Park
places.note: The Foreign Office facility in Buckinghamshire where the files were held.

people.name: Ndiku Mutua, Paulo Nzili, Wambugu Wa Nyingi, Jane Muthoni Mara and Susan Ngondi
people.role: the five Kenyan claimants whose case forced the disclosure; two died before the settlement

people.name: David Anderson
people.role: historian whose expert evidence for the claimants prompted the search that found the archive

people.name: Caroline Elkins
people.role: historian and expert witness whose research underpinned the claim

people.name: William Hague
people.role: Foreign Secretary who announced the settlement and the regret in the Commons on 6 June 2013

toll.money: 19.9 million pounds paid to 5,228 claimants, an average of about 3,800 pounds each, plus a memorial in Nairobi.
toll.note: The settlement was made without admission of liability, with an expression of sincere regret. The figures were stated in the Commons and are not disputed.

pedagogy.hook: In 2011 the Foreign Office admitted it had been keeping 8,800 secret colonial files in a warehouse in Buckinghamshire, some of them for fifty years.

misconception.belief: We cannot know what really happened at the end of empire because the records are lost.
misconception.correction: Many were deliberately destroyed under Operation Legacy, and many others were removed to Britain and hidden. Their existence was denied until a court case forced the admission in 2011. The gaps in the colonial record are not accidents of time; they are the result of a documented policy, and knowing that is part of knowing the history.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows how historical evidence is made and unmade, and it is the strongest possible answer to anyone who says accounts of colonial violence rest only on testimony.

evidence.author: David Anderson
evidence.work: Guilty Secrets: Deceit, Denial and the Discovery of Kenya's 'Migrated Archive'
evidence.supports: The discovery of the archive and the destruction policy.

evidence.author: Caroline Elkins
evidence.work: Britain's Gulag: The Brutal End of Empire in Kenya
evidence.supports: The research that underpinned the claim.

events.title: South Sudan becomes independent
events.summary: After two civil wars lasting nearly forty years and a peace agreement in 2005, 98.83 per cent of voters in southern Sudan chose separation. South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011, along a line that had been a British provincial boundary in 1956.
events.significance: It is the only redrawing of a colonial-era border by referendum in African history, and the clearest long-run consequence in this atlas of a colonial administrative decision - Britain's Southern Policy, which governed the south as a separate country from 1922 to 1946 and then joined it to the north with nine years' notice.

places.name: Juba
places.note: Where southern chiefs were persuaded to accept a single Sudanese legislature in June 1947.

people.name: John Garang
people.role: founder of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement, who argued for a reformed united Sudan rather than secession; died in a helicopter crash in 2005

people.name: Salva Kiir Mayardit
people.role: Garang's successor and first president of South Sudan

people.name: Omar al-Bashir
people.role: Sudan's president, who accepted the referendum result

toll.note: Combined estimates for the two Sudanese civil wars of 1955-72 and 1983-2005, mostly deaths from war-induced famine and displacement rather than combat. These are demographic reconstructions with wide margins.

pedagogy.hook: The border between Sudan and South Sudan was drawn by British administrators as a provincial boundary, and became an international one 55 years later after two wars and about two million deaths.

misconception.belief: African borders have never been changed because the Organisation of African Unity froze them in 1964.
misconception.correction: The principle of inherited borders has held remarkably well, and South Sudan is the major exception - agreed by referendum under a peace agreement, not seized. Eritrea in 1993 is the other, and it too restored a colonial-era boundary rather than inventing a new one.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the longest causal chain in this atlas: an ordinance in 1922, a policy reversed in 1946, a mutiny in 1955, two wars, and a new country in 2011.

evidence.author: Douglas H. Johnson
evidence.work: The Root Causes of Sudan's Civil Wars
evidence.supports: The colonial origins of the north-south division and the wars that followed.
